entry.title: Suspected fentanyl supplier linked to overdose death arrested after chase on I-95
entry.summary: A suspected drug trafficker linked to a deadly fentanyl overdose investigation is behind bars after investigators say he fled from detectives, hit a law enforcement vehicle and led authorities on a high-speed chase on I-95 in St. Lucie and Martin counties. Investigators said the arrest of James Arthur Green, 43, came after a weeks-long narcotics investigation that also uncovered a suspected connection to a fatal fentanyl overdose. According to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, detectives with the Special Investigations Division conducted multiple undercover purchases of drugs, gathering evidence during those operations that identified Green as the suspected supplier of fentanyl to a person who later died from an overdose. On Oct. 13, detectives used the deceased victim's cellphone during another controlled narcotics operation and placed an order for fentanyl. Investigators said Green returned to the victim's residence, delivered about two grams of fentanyl and sent a photograph showing where he left the drugs. Later that day, detectives conducted a separate undercover operation in which Green allegedly participated in a transaction involving about two ounces of fentanyl and one pound of methamphetamine. When detectives attempted to arrest him, Green fled, allegedly hitting a sheriff's office vehicle and fleeing onto southbound I-95. Authorities said the pursuit reached speeds of approximately 115 mph. During the chase, detectives reported seeing Green throw suspected narcotics and a cellphone out of his vehicle. The Florida Highway Patrol and Martin County Sheriff's Office joined the pursuit as it entered Martin County. Troopers deployed stop sticks before performing a PIT maneuver near Kanner Highway, bringing the chase to an end. Investigators recovered the one pound of methamphetamine and two ounces of fentanyl associated with the controlled purchase, along with an additional 22 grams of methamphetamine, two grams of crack cocaine and one gram of fentanyl. As part of the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office investigation, Green faces charges including trafficking of fentanyl, trafficking of cocaine, four counts of trafficking methamphetamine, sale of cocaine and unlawful use of a two-way communication device. entry.title: 'FIRST OF MANY': Attorney General discusses Nick Mimms conviction, warns of more corruption cases
entry.summary: Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier highlighted the recent conviction of former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms at a press conference Wednesday, calling it the first major outcome from the state's newly created public corruption unit and warning that more investigations are underway across Florida. Speaking at the Attorney General's Office in West Palm Beach, Uthmeier said public officials who abuse their positions for personal gain will face increased scrutiny from his office and the Florida Department of Law Enforcement (FDLE). 'Public officials are held to an even higher standard,' Uthmeier said. 'If you work in a city hall, serve on a commission, if you hold public office or work for a state agency, you have a duty to serve the public and not use your job to enrich yourself.' Last week, a St. Lucie County jury found Mimms guilty of official misconduct, a third-degree felony, but acquitted him on a bid-tampering charge. The case centered on a city-owned parcel near the historic Lincoln Theater in Fort Pierce. Prosecutors alleged that in 2024, Mimms used his position to benefit a nonprofit organization on whose board his niece served by helping secure the land deal and later concealing his involvement. During the trial, prosecutors presented evidence that Mimms failed to disclose his familial relationship and took steps to influence and cover up the transaction. Uthmeier said the case represented the type of conduct the state's public corruption unit was created to investigate. 'The facts make clear that shenanigans took place to ensure that that nonprofit ended up with the award, and ultimately the city manager covered it up,' Uthmeier said. The incident unfolded Wednesday afternoon near Woolbright Road, where a large law enforcement presence prompted the closure of the roadway in both directions. PBSO previously confirmed that the encounter involved deputies and resulted in a death. entry.title: Trump made Alaska push for Sullivan with Senate control at stake
entry.summary: Its a long way from Washington, has a small population and hasn't backed a Democrat for Senate in nearly 20 years. Yet President Donald Trump on Tuesday devoted a big chunk of his dwindling time ahead of crucial midterm elections to head to Alaska attempting to bolster a Republican incumbent senator in another sign of GOP fears about retaining control of Congress after Election Day on Nov. 3. Trump headlined a rally for Sen. Dan Sullivan in Wasilla, about 45 miles north of Anchorage famous for being the hometown of former Republican vice presidential nominee Sarah Palin and the headquarters of the Iditarod sled dog race across the state. Trump's stop is part of a western swing also taking him to rallies in Arizona and Montana on Wednesday. The president noted to the crowd that he had flown eight hours to rally for Sullivan, whom he called one of the best and most respected senators in D.C. Sullivan, seeking a third term, faces Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman who is running to put Alaska first and emphasizing cost-of-living issues. Trump also said the Federal Communications Commission would vote in the coming weeks on investing an additional $162 million in expanding high-speed internet access in Alaska. entry.article_text: It’s a long way from Washington, has a small population and hasn't backed a Democrat for Senate in nearly 20 years.Yet President Donald Trump on Tuesday devoted a big chunk of his dwindling time ahead of crucial midterm elections to head to Alaska — attempting to bolster a Republican incumbent senator in another sign of GOP fears about retaining control of Congress after Election Day on Nov. 3.Trump headlined a rally for Sen. Dan Sullivan in Wasilla, about 45 miles north of Anchorage — famous for being the hometown of former Republican vice presidential nominee Sarah Palin and the headquarters of the Iditarod sled dog race across the state.Trump's stop is part of a western swing also taking him to rallies in Arizona and Montana on Wednesday.The president noted to the crowd that he had flown eight hours to rally for Sullivan, whom he called “one of the best and most respected senators in D.C.” Sullivan, seeking a third term, faces Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman who is running to put “Alaska first” and emphasizing cost-of-living issues.During Tuesday's rally, Trump announced that Taiwan would purchase gas from a proposed mega-gas project that he has been highlighting amid Sullivan's campaign and that it would invest more than $4 billion. There was no immediate confirmation from Taiwan, the self-governing island that China claims as its own. The White House did not immediately provide further details.Trump also said the Federal Communications Commission would vote in the coming weeks on investing an additional $162 million in expanding high-speed internet access in Alaska. And he announced pardons for two men who had pleaded guilty in 2022 to Clean Air Act violations for tampering with federally mandated monitoring devices on certain vehicles.Trump and Vance have been trying to boost Sullivan repeatedlyDemocrats last won a Senate seat in Alaska in 2008, and the state hasn’t elected a governor from that party since 1998. The only time Alaska didn’t vote Republican for president was during Lyndon B. Johnson’s landslide 1964 reelection.Yet high gasoline prices from the Iran war and persistently elevated inflation have damaged Trump’s approval ratings enough to leave Democrats dreaming of Alaska upsets.Alaska pollster Ivan Moore said he's seen a decline in Trump's support statewide that mirrors the president's falling approval ratings nationally. That means the Senate race may be decided by Trump 2024 voters who are now unsure they still back him.“The visit is certainly appropriate. Whether the visit will be effective or not is another matter," said Moore, who said when he first heard that Trump would visit Alaska, he didn't believe it would actually happen.The Trump administration has prioritized expanding oil and gas drilling in the state. Vice President JD Vance last week campaigned in Fairbanks for Sullivan and Republican Rep. Nick Begich.Sullivan recently joined Trump in the Oval Office, where the president announced a $54 billion investment by South Korea's government into the proposed Alaska gas project. That's despite South Korea saying the deal, and its total value, haven't been finalized.Versions of a gas project have been proposed in Alaska for decades.Trump trekking four time zones west to get to Sullivan’s home turf — an unusually long trip so close to the midterms — is his strongest show of support for the incumbent.Trump last campaigned in Alaska to try to defeat a fellow RepublicanAlaska is home to around 740,000 people, making it slightly less populous than Denver. It ranks 48th out of 50 states in population, smaller than all but Vermont and Wyoming.Trump nonetheless headlined a 2022 rally in Anchorage opposing Republican Alaska Sen. Lisa Murkowski after she voted to convict him on a charge of incitement of insurrection during his second impeachment trial, following the attack on the U.S. Capitol by a mob of his supporters on Jan. 6, 2021.Trump endorsed Kelly Tshibaka, who challenged Murkowski that year, but that didn't stop incumbent Murkowski from winning reelection.In Wasilla, Max Christensen was waiting in line for the rally and said he hoped to hear more specifics from Trump about the natural gas project, and said he was “really curious just to see how he’s going to handle things like inflation and gas prices and things like that.”Christensen, 22, said he thinks Trump has been a great president “despite all his flaws and stuff," adding, “I think he really does genuinely care about the people of the United States of America.”This year, there are two Dan Sullivans on the ballotTrump has complained about Alaska’s unique elections system. The state has open primaries, in which the four top vote-getters — regardless of party affiliation — advance to the general election, which uses ranked choice voting.RELATED STORY | Republicans are flooding Senate races with ad money, but paying a premiumThat's led to a scenario where there also will be another Dan Sullivan on the November ballot: retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan, whom Trump and other allies of Sen. Sullivan have called a sham candidate. Sullivan has denied this, but Trump continued to hammer the other Sullivan at his rally.“They found a guy named Dan Sullivan, they put him up to get things a little confused,” Trump said, as he repeatedly urged his supporters to vote for “the real Dan Sullivan.”Trump also touted Begich, who is facing a competitive challenge from Bill Hill, an independent.Alaska has a history of rewarding candidates with an independent streak — something Vance acknowledged during his trip to Fairbanks last week."In very deep red years, Alaska is competitive. In very deep blue years, Alaska is still competitive,” Vance said. “I think it’s just a reality of the politics of the state.”Independence has been hard to find in the Republican Party, where Trump for years has had total control. Some Republicans facing tough elections have begun tiptoeing away from the president on key issues such as Iran and tariffs, but not Sullivan, who has been vocal in supporting both.Trump also questioned why three Republicans were running against a Democrat for governor and endorsed Bernadette Wilson, who finished third in the August primary but was the top vote-getting Republican. This came at the same time state GOP leaders — including outgoing Gov. Mike Dunleavy — are urging voters to rank Republicans on the ballot.Many Republicans — despite reservations with ranked voting — have seen a ranking strategy in that race as crucial for Republicans trying to win the seat.Trump's trade war with Canada may also be a factorTrump has also triggered a trade war with Canada, which shares a 1,500-plus-mile border with Alaska and is among the state's most important trading partners.The U.S. banned nearly $1 billion worth of imports from its neighbor — including alcoholic beverages, dairy products and motorcycles — after previously imposing 50% tariffs on about $20 billion in Canadian products. Canada has responded with reciprocal bans and its own import levies, and the back-and-forth could raise prices for Alaska consumers.RELATED STORY | 'I had the flu': Talarico returns to campaign trail, dismisses online rumorsMaking Canada an enemy of sorts is "discomforting" for many Alaskans, said pollster Moore.“We associate, I think, probably more closely with the Canadians — more than a lot of the Lower 48," he said.

entry.title: Jupiter Goodwill employee celebrates 19 years on the job during Disability Employment Awareness Month
entry.summary: October marks National Disability Employment Awareness Month, an annual observance recognizing the contributions people with disabilities make to workplaces across the country. The observance dates back to 1945, when it began as a weeklong national recognition of the contributions of people with physical disabilities. WATCH BELOW: Jupiter Goodwill employee celebrates 19 years on the job National Disability Employment Awareness Month highlights value and talent in the workplace In 1988, Congress expanded the commemoration to a month, and it evolved to recognize the importance of increasing employment opportunities for people with disabilities, including those with mental health conditions and other nonobvious disabilities. The U.S. Department of Labor's Office of Disability Employment Policy, created in 2001, now leads the annual observance. At a Goodwill store in Jupiter, that message can be seen through an employee who has spent nearly two decades putting his own talents to work. WPTV reporter Christy Waite spoke with Jeffrey McFadden Jr., who has worked at the Jupiter Goodwill for 19 years, but for him, going to work is about much more than earning a paycheck. entry.summary: Florida AG vows public corruption crackdown after Fort Pierce city manager Nicholas Mimms conviction    WPBF
entry.article_text: Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier is promising a broader crackdown on public corruption following the conviction of former Fort Pierce City Manager Nicholas Mimms. Lucie County jury found Mimms guilty of official misconduct but acquitted him of bid tampering. The case centered on two vacant, city-owned parcels in Fort Pierce and a nonprofit connected to Mimms’ niece. Prosecutors said Mimms used his position to benefit the nonprofit and later concealed his involvement. Mimms’ niece served on the nonprofit’s board. The organization received a $500,000 grant from a Catholic charitable organization for a community center that was never built. Uthmeier pointed to the conviction as an example of the state’s efforts to hold public officials accountable. “We want to ensure the public that we are protecting their trust, that we are protecting taxpayers and that we are going to hold public officials to the oaths that they take,” Uthmeier said. Uthmeier said the evidence showed that “shenanigans took place” to ensure the nonprofit received the award and that Mimms ultimately covered up his involvement. “He will be punished for abusing his office,” Uthmeier said. Uthmeier said his office’s Public Corruption Unit has more than 25 active investigations or cases underway and described the Mimms case as the first of many public corruption cases the state expects to announce. Florida Department of Law Enforcement Commissioner Larry Keefe said his agency is making public corruption investigations a priority. “No one is too big, no one is too powerful to be held accountable,” Keefe said. Uthmeier declined to comment on what sentence Mimms should receive. Official misconduct is a third-degree felony punishable by up to five years in prison. Mimms is scheduled to be sentenced Dec. entry.summary: Fort Pierce police investigate after body found in Lincoln Park lake    WPEC
entry.article_text: A man in his 30s was found dead in a lake at Lincoln Park in Fort Pierce Wednesday morning, and police are investigating how he ended up in the water. An officer was flagged down by a citizen just after 9 a.m. who reported seeing a body floating in the lake near the 400 block of North 13th Street, Fort Pierce Police Major Michael Santiago said. Officers say they arrived and found a man face down in the water. Rescue crews pulled him out, but he was pronounced dead. Police identified the man but are waiting to notify his next of kin. Santiago described him as a Black man believed to be between 30 and 32 years old. Investigators are working to determine how the man entered the water and what he was doing before his death. See also: Man fatally shot by PBSO deputy after Boynton Beach pursuit identified There were no apparent signs of trauma to the man's body, Santiago said, but he noted the body appeared to have been in the water for some time. Police are canvassing the area, speaking with potential witnesses and looking for surveillance footage that could help investigators determine how the man ended up in the lake, per FPPD. Santiago said investigators are also looking into whether currents in the waterway could have played a role in where the body was found. It is too early to determine whether foul play or drugs were involved. Investigators are waiting for the medical examiner's findings, including autopsy and toxicology results, to help determine the cause of death. CBS12 News will provide updates as more information becomes available.

entry.title: Court records reveal man shot by PBSO deputies had a lengthy criminal history
entry.summary: Palm Beach County sheriff's deputies shot and killed a 51-year-old man Tuesday afternoon following a strong-arm robbery report and a pursuit that began in Lake Park, which continued along Interstate 95 and ended in a deadly confrontation near Boynton Beach. On Wednesday, PBSO identified Gregory Dobkins as the man who was fatally shot. Court records show his final encounter with law enforcement was not his first. WATCH BELOW: Man shot by deputies had lengthy criminal history, records show Court records reveal man shot by PBSO deputies had a lengthy criminal history Deputies said Dobkins was a suspect in a strong-arm robbery that happened Monday night when they located him in Lake Park using license plate readers. Deputies and state troopers then pursued him down I-95 before a confrontation in Boynton Beach ended in the shooting. At the scene Tuesday, Sheriff Ric Bradshaw described the moment his deputy fired. 'He was actually in a kneeling position and raised up his hands in the shooting position, and that's when our deputy fired, struck him, and he was neutralized right there,' Bradshaw said. 'During this whole time, he's yelling too at the officers, right? 'You're gonna have to kill me. You're gonna have to kill me, you're gonna have to kill me.'' At the scene, Bradshaw told reporters Dobkins had a lengthy criminal history. 'He's obviously a serious bad guy,' Bradshaw said. WPTV dug through court records across Florida and found a history of theft, assault, drug convictions and other charges that go back decades. Arrest affidavits repeatedly reference a battle with addiction. Most recently in 2025, Dobkins was accused of stealing merchandise from a Walgreens in Sarasota. Deputies wrote that when they confronted Dobkins, he was acting erratically, so they Baker Acted him. Court records show Dobkins pleaded guilty to petit theft and paid a fine. Tuesday's deadly confrontation is still actively under investigation by state and county law enforcement. We're going to keep digging into this to better understand what happened, and will bring details as they are uncovered. So, on a lot of issues that they feel touch on, their identities, or their rights, or their rights for their peers, their friends, their communities, that can be something really, really powerful for young people in terms of their ideology or their political views,” he said.Multiple surveys in 2026 show cost of living and economic issues are a top concern among young voters. Another big issue for them is combating corruption and big money in politics.MORE ON MIDTERMS | Scripps News poll: 43% of voters say they’ve been fooled by AI ads this campaign"They want to improve their communities. They want to improve their own lives. And so they look at our political system and go, okay, ‘What's in the way of me having power?’ of me being able to affect change?’” Medina said.One advantage for politicians and advocacy groups – young voters are more persuadable than other voting blocs and they're willing to consider new ideas.

entry.title: Jury finds Tyreek Hill liable for 2 battery counts, awards $500,000 to the NFL star's estranged wife
entry.summary: A Miami jury on Tuesday found Tyreek Hill liable for two counts of battery but not liable for the eight remaining claims made by Lakeeta Vaccaro ending the high-profile civil trial involving the NFL wide receiver and his estranged wife. Hill, who has played for the NFL's Kansas City Chiefs and Miami Dolphins, was found liable for two counts of battery one stemming from an incident in January 2024, and another from April 2025. The jury awarded Vaccaro $500,000 in compensatory damages but did not award her punitive damages. The jury found Hill, 32, not liable for eight other counts that included battery, assault and continuing domestic violence. The trial involved allegations of abuse made by Vaccaro, 30, who on the stand described instances in which Hill allegedly pulled her hair and 'treated me like I was, just, a man.' Hill took the stand last week and mostly denied what he called 'false allegations' made by his estranged wife, while saying in one instance he shoved Vaccaro and created a hole in the wall.' Hill, wearing a dark polo shirt on Tuesday, embraced one of his attorneys and shook hands with others following the verdict before leaving the courtroom by himself. It wasn't immediately clear what the verdict means for Hill's return to the NFL. He is still working his way back from a dislocated knee and torn ligaments suffered in September 2025 while he was with the Dolphins, but his agent, Drew Rosenhaus, has indicated that he could be ready to play by November.

entry.title: Death sentence handed down for 66-year-old Otto Lenke in Fort Pierce killing case - WPEC
entry.summary: Death sentence handed down for 66-year-old Otto Lenke in Fort Pierce killing case    WPEC
entry.article_text: Otto Lenke, convicted of killing Fort Pierce motorcycle shop owner Richard Benson, was sentenced to death Wednesday. "The court's independent evaluation of this case herein leads to the conclusion that the death sentence is appropriate and a just sentence for the murder of Richard Benson. Therefore, Otto Lenke, I hereby sentence you to death for the first-degree murder of Richard Benson," said Circuit Court Judge Michael Linn. Lenke sat motionless as he learned his fate. "He did a horrific act he's going to pay the price. And up until the day that he dies, he's going to be in solitary confinement. For years, this case has been pending and today, the family of Richard Benson got justice. So, I'm very, very relieved for that," said Brandon White, Asst. "We're relieved and the judge's decision is, we respect it and that's what we were hoping for in this case and we're glad that justice could be served," said Justin Cormier, Asst. Lenke, 67, was found guilty of first-degree murder and arson in May 2026 for Benson’s 2021 death. See also: Man fatally shot by PBSO deputy after Boynton Beach pursuit identified Prosecutors said Lenke shot Benson at Fast Frank’s Custom Cycle Components, then poured denatured alcohol on him and set him on fire while he was still alive. The crime happened just down the street from the Fort Pierce Police Department. Investigators say the motive stemmed from a personal relationship. According to prosecutors, Benson had been dating a woman who previously had a relationship with Lenke. During the murder trial, prosecutors argued that the murder was fueled by jealousy, claiming that Lenke could not accept that Benson was dating someone from his past. The prosecutor says Lenke carefully planned the murder and used a car that day that belonged to his daughter, a car which people would not associate him with and he cut up the gun and disposed of it in pieces. Lenke is a former Melbourne police officer and Indian River County firefighter. A close friend of Richard Benson, who attended every day of the trial, had this to say about the sentence Lenke received. "I like that he got the death penalty. I don't like the fact that we may be back here two or three more times on the appeals," said Skip Thompson, a friend who helped Benson in his motorcycle repair shop. Lenke did not testify in his own defense during the trial. Florida law requires the State Supreme Court to review every death sentence. So Lenke still has a legal path to challenge his conviction and sentence. That process could take years.

entry.title: $900 a month in fees: West Boca condo owner feels squeeze of rising HOA costs
entry.summary: Stephanie Donner saw my report this week on local leaders discussing HOA fees and assessments in Florida and immediately contacted me. 'It is a problem in the state, to the point where they will put a sign on the highway coming from the north (that says) 'Turnaround,'' she told me outside her West Boca condo on Wednesday. WATCH BELOW: West Boca condo owner says rising HOA fees could force her to move West Boca condo owner says rising HOA fees could force her to move Where she lives, she says her total fees are around $900 a month. 'We're going to have an assessment and, to be honest, a lot of people have already moved,' Donner said. 'This is really tough,' state Sen. Mack Bernard said Tuesday at the HOA Fee forum in West Palm Beach. 'But we dont want another Surfside, but at the same time what we want to do is create new affordable housing.' The discussion comes as Florida communities rank among those with the nation's highest HOA burdens. A Realtor.com analysis previously reported by WPTV found seven of the nation's 10 metro areas with the highest HOA fees relative to estimated mortgage payments were in Florida. Port St. Lucie ranked fifth, while the Sebastian-Vero Beach area ranked ninth. Among the potential solutions raised Tuesday at the forum were additional financial assistance for seniors and more state oversight of HOAs. As for Donner, who is semi-retired, she says that with HOA fees, insurance and overall inflation, she's enduring the situation as long as she has her stay-at-home remote job. 'If I lose that, I have to move,' she said

entry.title: DOJ threatens California with legal action over claim of noncitizens on voter rolls
entry.summary: The U.S. Department of Justice has threatened California with possible legal action over what it says are noncitizens believed to have received mail ballots for next months midterm elections. California mails ballots to all registered voters. The letter obtained by The Associated Press gives the state 48 hours to determine whether any citizens are included on the list. entry.article_text: Department of Justice has threatened California with possible legal action over what it says are noncitizens believed to have received mail ballots for next month’s midterm elections.A letter sent Tuesday to Secretary of State Shirley Weber from Trent McCotter, the acting deputy U.S. attorney general, says the department has provided officials in Los Angeles County with a password-protected thumb drive that contains a list of names the federal government believes are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots to participate in the Nov. 3 election.California mails ballots to all registered voters.The letter obtained by The Associated Press gives the state 48 hours to determine whether any citizens are included on the list. For individuals whose citizenship cannot be independently verified, the state is to instruct local election officials to segregate their mail-in ballots until their status can be determined, and to not provide a ballot to anyone who has not yet received it. The letters warns that legal action may follow if the state does not meet the 48-hour deadline to review the list.“If you cannot implement this process by then, given the ongoing federal election, the United States will have no choice but to seek emergency relief,” the letter states.RELATED STORY | Records show ICE reviewed tens of millions of voter records looking for noncitizen votersA separate, similar letter was sent to the registrar's office in Los Angeles County, which the U.S. attorney's office had investigated during the state's June primary.Unclear how many names DOJ flaggedLos Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan confirmed in a statement that his office received the letter and a thumb drive, along with a “hand written note providing a password” to access the list of alleged noncitizens on the voter rolls.He said he did not consider the thumb drive a secure device and hasn't yet accessed any files. The letter, which Logan made public, does not specify the number of individuals flagged by the federal government.Logan said his office is working with the secretary of state and attorney general's offices to decide how to proceed. Neither of those two offices immediately responded to an emailed request for comment.“Federal and state laws are clear on how voter eligibility is established,” Logan wrote. “And any action to remove a voter from eligibility must be based on verifiable information, not assertions of unconfirmed data matching.”Nationwide search for alleged noncitizen votersThe Trump administration has made the hunt for noncitizen voters a priority this year, even though the problem is exceptionally rare. The Justice Department has charged about 90 people for various types of election misconduct so far this year, including 50 who are alleged to have voted as noncitizens. There were more than 227 million registered voters in the United States during the 2024 presidential election.In July, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin sent letters to California, Nevada, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, alleging that as many as 250,000 noncitizens were registered in those states. Election officials there were skeptical of the claim, including Weber, the California secretary of state.“I have serious doubts about the reliability of your data and accuracy of your claims, since my office has not shared our statewide voter registration list with DHS or any other federal agency or official,” Weber said in response.That same month, the Republican administration claimed Nevada had 1,500 noncitizen voters on its voter rolls. But after the federal government identified them to the state, the number of actual registered noncitizens turned out to be zero.IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Young voter turnout could be pivotal in this year's midtermsAs part of its project to find noncitizens on the voter rolls, the Justice Department has been seeking detailed voter information — including dates of birth, addresses, driver's license numbers and partial Social Security numbers — from the states. Some Republican-led states have turned over the information, which has been run through a U.S. Department of Homeland Security database that has been criticized as inaccurately flagging U.S. citizens.The Justice Department has sued 30 states and the District of Columbia for that information, but so far has lost those cases in court. California is among the states that successfully sued, in part by arguing that turning over the data would violate state privacy laws.Election official calls 48-hour deadline “unreasonable”Santa Cruz County Clerk Tricia Webber, who is president of the California Association of Clerks and Election Officials, said she had not seen the letters but said the 48-hour deadline to vet voters flagged by the federal government was “completely unreasonable.”She said when there is a report of an ineligible voter incorrectly on the rolls, her office does due diligence to investigate. That involves looking at the voter’s registration history, identifying whether that person had voted before and, most importantly, reaching out to the voter, she said.“It would take more than 48 hours to even begin to get the full picture,” Webber said. She also questioned how the federal government came up with a list of alleged noncitizen voters since it doesn’t have access to the state's detailed voter information.Webber added that throughout the course of her decades-long career working for local election agencies, she has “never seen anything that would make me believe that our voter records are filled with fraudulent voters.”

entry.title: Neighbors ask for solutions on deadly roadway in Port St. Lucie
entry.summary: WPTV is continuing to follow up after the tragic death of a 14-year-old student who was struck by a vehicle on Port St. Lucie Boulevard last Wednesday. Neighbors told WPTV the road can be dangerous during ongoing construction. 'I don't even come down this road no more,' neighbor Selene Gabriele said. I go all the way down to I-95, come up on Gatlin to take my child to school. It's very dangerous. A 14-year-old was struck by an SUV on Port St. Lucie Boulevard while walking to school just before sunrise on Oct. 7. He later died from his injuries. Neighbors like Howard Shapiro said the roadway lacks lighting, especially during the early morning and at night. 'I don't walk around here... no lighting outside at nighttime. Kids walk along all the time because there's school back there, school down there, Shapiro said. To protect those kids, pedestrians and drivers, Shapiro said they need lights. 'They are putting in a sidewalk, so that's gonna be helpful. But street lights need to follow, he said. WATCH: WPTV's Tyler Hatfield is listening to neighbors' concerns following the fatal crash Hearing your concerns after fatal crash on Port St Lucie Blvd. The Florida Department of Transportation is in charge of the project along a segment of Port St. Lucie Boulevard from Alcantara Boulevard to Parr Drive. FDOT started construction back in 2025 and, according to its website , crews are widening the road from two to four lanes as well as adding new sidewalks and lights. Scott Samples with the City of Port St. Lucie said this will make the roadway safer. 'We'll see a significant improvement in the safety as well as the traffic flow for this roadway,' Samples said. WPTV asked Samples if city staff can provide any temporary safety measures to address neighbors' concerns. Samples said the work being done is FDOTs responsibility. 'It's tough when there is active, ongoing construction, because people still need to utilize it,' Samples said. 'That's why we encourage everyone to do it as safely as they possibly can.' WPTV reached out to FDOT to see if there will be any added safety measures in the wake of last week's tragedy. WPTV is still working on getting a response. FDOT said on its website that the SW Port St. Lucie Boulevard Project is expected to be completed in the winter of 2028.

entry.title: Court records reveal man shot by PBSO deputies had a lengthy criminal history
entry.summary: Palm Beach County sheriff's deputies shot and killed a 51-year-old man Tuesday afternoon following a strong-arm robbery report and a pursuit that began in Lake Park, which continued along Interstate 95 and ended in a deadly confrontation near Boynton Beach. On Wednesday, PBSO identified Gregory Dobkins as the man who was fatally shot. Court records show his final encounter with law enforcement was not his first. WATCH BELOW: Man shot by deputies had lengthy criminal history, records show Court records reveal man shot by PBSO deputies had a lengthy criminal history Deputies said Dobkins was a suspect in a strong-arm robbery that happened Monday night when they located him in Lake Park using license plate readers. Deputies and state troopers then pursued him down I-95 before a confrontation in Boynton Beach ended in the shooting. At the scene Tuesday, Sheriff Ric Bradshaw described the moment his deputy fired. 'He was actually in a kneeling position and raised up his hands in the shooting position, and that's when our deputy fired, struck him, and he was neutralized right there,' Bradshaw said. 'During this whole time, he's yelling too at the officers, right? 'You're gonna have to kill me. You're gonna have to kill me, you're gonna have to kill me.'' At the scene, Bradshaw told reporters Dobkins had a lengthy criminal history. 'He's obviously a serious bad guy,' Bradshaw said. WPTV dug through court records across Florida and found a history of theft, assault, drug convictions and other charges that go back decades. Arrest affidavits repeatedly reference a battle with addiction. Most recently in 2025, Dobkins was accused of stealing merchandise from a Walgreens in Sarasota. Deputies wrote that when they confronted Dobkins, he was acting erratically, so they Baker Acted him. Court records show Dobkins pleaded guilty to petit theft and paid a fine. Tuesday's deadly confrontation is still actively under investigation by state and county law enforcement. We're going to keep digging into this to better understand what happened, and will bring details as they are uncovered. entry.title: Former Melbourne police officer sentenced to death for killing Fort Pierce motorcycle mechanic
entry.summary: A former Melbourne police officer and Treasure Coast first responder has been sentenced to death. Otto Lenke was found guilty in May of shooting and killing Richard Benson inside the victim's bike shop, Fast Frank's , back in February 2021. WATCH BELOW: Former police officer sentenced to death for killing mechanic Former police officer sentenced to death for killing mechanic The crime happened just down the street from Fort Pierce Police Department headquarters. Prosecutors showed the jury surveillance video of the crime during the trial back in May. Lenke not only shot Benson, but spread denatured alcohol over his body and set him on fire while he was still alive. As to a motive, prosecutors noted Benson was dating a woman that Lenke had once been romantically involved with. Assistant State Attorney Brandon White told WPTV that justice was served and he's pleased that this part of the legal process is done.

entry.title: Suspected fentanyl trafficker arrested after 115 mph chase on I-95 in St. Lucie County - WPBF
entry.summary: Suspected fentanyl trafficker arrested after 115 mph chase on I-95 in St. Lucie County    WPBF
entry.article_text: A suspected fentanyl trafficker is behind bars after investigators say he sold drugs to a person who later died of an overdose, then led law enforcement on a high-speed chase that reached 115 mph and ended in Martin County. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro identified the suspect as 43-year-old James Arthur Green, who he said is a 10-time convicted felon. According to the sheriff, the investigation began after a fatal fentanyl overdose on Oct. Detectives used the victim’s phone to contact Green, who allegedly returned to the victim’s home Tuesday to deliver more fentanyl. Investigators say Green even sent a picture to the victim’s phone showing where he had left the drugs, unaware that he had been communicating with law enforcement the entire time. "Obviously, he didn’t know that this person had passed away. We were communicating with them," Del Toro said. Later that day, investigators say Green attempted to sell more fentanyl during an undercover operation. When detectives moved in to arrest him, Green fled, striking an unmarked St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office cruiser before leading law enforcement on a pursuit down Interstate 95. Authorities say the chase reached speeds of 115 mph and continued into Martin County. The pursuit eventually ended near Kanner Highway after Florida Highway Patrol troopers deployed stop sticks and performed a PIT maneuver to stop Green’s vehicle. Del Toro emphasized the dangers of fentanyl and the importance of removing suspected traffickers from the community. This is killing our citizens and our community and preying upon people that have substance abuse problems," Del Toro said. "So I’m very, very happy this person’s off the streets right now." Green now faces multiple drug-related charges, along with additional charges connected to the pursuit. He is being held on a $440,000 bond. According to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, detectives with the Special Investigations Division conducted multiple undercover purchases of drugs, gathering evidence during those operations that identified Green as the suspected supplier of fentanyl to a person who later died from an overdose. On Oct. 13, detectives used the deceased victim's cellphone during another controlled narcotics operation and placed an order for fentanyl. Investigators said Green returned to the victim's residence, delivered about two grams of fentanyl and sent a photograph showing where he left the drugs. Later that day, detectives conducted a separate undercover operation in which Green allegedly participated in a transaction involving about two ounces of fentanyl and one pound of methamphetamine. Authorities said the pursuit reached speeds of approximately 115 mph. During the chase, detectives reported seeing Green throw suspected narcotics and a cellphone out of his vehicle. The Florida Highway Patrol and Martin County Sheriff's Office joined the pursuit as it entered Martin County. Troopers deployed stop sticks before performing a PIT maneuver near Kanner Highway, bringing the chase to an end. entry.title: 'FIRST OF MANY': Attorney General discusses Nick Mimms conviction, warns of more corruption cases
entry.summary: Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier highlighted the recent conviction of former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms at a press conference Wednesday, calling it the first major outcome from the state's newly created public corruption unit and warning that more investigations are underway across Florida. Speaking at the Attorney General's Office in West Palm Beach, Uthmeier said public officials who abuse their positions for personal gain will face increased scrutiny from his office and the Florida Department of Law Enforcement (FDLE). 'Public officials are held to an even higher standard,' Uthmeier said. 'If you work in a city hall, serve on a commission, if you hold public office or work for a state agency, you have a duty to serve the public and not use your job to enrich yourself.' Last week, a St. Lucie County jury found Mimms guilty of official misconduct, a third-degree felony, but acquitted him on a bid-tampering charge. The case centered on a city-owned parcel near the historic Lincoln Theater in Fort Pierce. Prosecutors alleged that in 2024, Mimms used his position to benefit a nonprofit organization on whose board his niece served by helping secure the land deal and later concealing his involvement. Uthmeier said the case represented the type of conduct the state's public corruption unit was created to investigate. 'The facts make clear that shenanigans took place to ensure that that nonprofit ended up with the award, and ultimately the city manager covered it up,' Uthmeier said. entry.title: Santaluces star Jayvon Dawson transforms from QB to elite edge rusher on his way to the University of Miami
entry.summary: In life, they say it's not how you start; it's how you finish, and for Jayvon Dawson, his football start is one of a kind. 'Back in Little League, I first played as a quarterback trying to dab on everybody,' said Dawson. WATCH BELOW: Jayvon Dawson went from QB to elite edge rusher at Santaluces, earning offer from Miami From QB to the U: Jayvon Dawson's path to Miami Dawson was a solid quarterback, but it wasnt until he got to high school at Santaluces that he was humbled. 'My coaches were saying, 'You're not going D1 playing quarterback,'' said Dawson. Dawson is 6-foot-4 and more than 200 pounds, so coaches got creative in his first three years on where they'd pay him. 'He played receiver before we were able to get him on the defensive side of the ball,' head coach Samuel Putmon said. That defensive side of the ball is where he shined. His junior year, he was a man amongst boys and had nearly every school you could think of calling. 'Miami, (the University of North Carolina), Georgia and many others,' said Dawson. Dawson was a game-wrecker the last two seasons, getting to the quarterback at ease and stopping almost every run game the Chiefs faced. He was so good the University of Miami pulled out the big dogs during his recruitment. '(Defensive coordinator Corey) Hetherman and (defensive line coach) Jason Taylor,' said Dawson. Dawson wasn't born when Taylor was dominating the NFL for the Miami Dolphins, so he didnt even know who was recruiting him until days later. 'I was looking up d-ends trying to work some moves on my game and get better at my game, and then he popped up playing for the Dolphins. That's how I started to know him,' said Dawson. Star-struck by his lead recruiter and the Hurricanes' facilities, Dawson made his coach a promise. 'I already told my coach if Miami offers me, I'm fully committed,' Dawson said. During a visit to Coral Gables, Miami did just that and offered the three-star edge rusher. Dawson committed to the school on the spot. 'I kept God first, always kept him first, I just kept going and being consistent and disciplined, said Dawson. That positive mindset has him ready to become an early enrollee at The U this December, and before he steps on the campus, his head coach has glowing reviews for the Us coaches and fans. 'He's a great kid, a humble kid, a hard worker who does what's asked of him. It's easy to coach kids like that,' Putmon said.

entry.title: 'We don't need to lose another child': Port St. Lucie residents push for safer walking routes - WPBF
entry.summary: 'We don't need to lose another child': Port St. Lucie residents push for safer walking routes    WPBF
entry.article_text: Lucie continues building sidewalks across the city, residents advocating for safer school bus stops and routes say more immediate measures are needed to protect children walking along busy roads. Lucie resident and grandmother, has been pushing city officials for safer bus stops, pedestrian stop signs and painted walkways, saying children should not have to risk their lives getting to and from school. Green said her concerns grew after watching her granddaughter and other children navigate traffic near their neighborhood off Southwest Paar Drive, where a sidewalk only exists on one side of the street. Green said once the bus drops the children off, the bus driver helps them cross the street to where the sidewalk is. However, the children who live on the opposite side of the street then have to cross back over without help. "Once the bus stopped and the kids were walking, cars were flying by. Literally, if you crossed your foot across that line, a child would have been run over or an adult. So that started my campaign to email our city officials, transportation officials, and we did get an opportunity to speak," she said. Green said she has continued communicating with city officials and transportation officials about potential safety improvements. She is calling for more sidewalks, pedestrian stop signs and marked walkways. Stay up to date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 "Kids should be able to just walk along the street and make it home safely, walk to school safely," Green said. She mentioned the recent tragic incident in which a 14-year-old Treasure Coast High School student died after being struck by a vehicle while walking to school in Port St. "My heart goes out to the family. I, too, have lost a child before, so I understand that grief. When I met with city officials right there at the corner, I literally said, 'We don't need to lose another child,'" she told WPBF. Sidewalk projects underway across the city The city says sidewalks are currently being installed through its Capital Improvement Projects and Sidewalk Master Plan. Active projects include Port St. Lucie Boulevard from Alcantarra to Paar, Floresta Drive from Crosstown Parkway to Prima Vista, Kestor Drive, Volucia Drive and Lakehurst Drive. Recently completed projects include sidewalks on Abingdon Avenue, Import Drive, Brescia Street and Grand Drive, as well as Berkshire Boulevard Phase 1 and a Veterans Memorial Parkway connection to the Publix plaza and post office. Upcoming projects include California Boulevard from Crosstown Parkway to Prima Vista and the Peacock Trail at O.L. Park, from Dreyfuss Boulevard to Open View Drive. City officials say the public works department continues to evaluate existing priorities and identify additional locations for future improvements. An updated plan, including proposed future sidewalk locations, is expected to be presented to the City Council for approval in 2027. What about safety before sidewalks are built? The city says it has met with the St. Lucie County School Board as part of the master plan review to discuss school bus stops. City officials say the school board determines bus stop locations, which can change annually based on transportation needs and where children live. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app. The city also says crosswalks are evaluated as part of new projects. Under federal accessibility requirements, crosswalks must connect to compliant sidewalks and curb ramps at both ends, meaning they cannot be installed independently where accessible pedestrian infrastructure is absent. A push for more neighborhood input According to the city, the previous sidewalk master plan prioritized major roadways, particularly within 2 miles of schools, with the goal of connecting existing sidewalks rather than building isolated sections. The updated plan is expected to expand those connections into more neighborhoods, while continuing to prioritize heavily traveled areas and routes connecting schools, parks and recreational destinations. A call for action For Green, the issue goes beyond her own family. She said every resident has a connection to a child who could face similar dangers. She started a petition asking the city to implement several safety measures to protect children, including: Immediate transverse pedestrian crosswalks Immediate in-street pedestrian crossing signs Speed bumps to permanently slow down reckless drivers "Collectively, together, we’re stronger," Green said. The petition can be found here.

entry.title: Death sentence handed down for 67-year-old Otto Lenke in Fort Pierce killing case - WPEC
entry.summary: Death sentence handed down for 67-year-old Otto Lenke in Fort Pierce killing case    WPEC
entry.article_text: Otto Lenke, convicted of killing Fort Pierce motorcycle shop owner Richard Benson, was sentenced to death Wednesday. "The court's independent evaluation of this case herein leads to the conclusion that the death sentence is appropriate and a just sentence for the murder of Richard Benson. Therefore, Otto Lenke, I hereby sentence you to death for the first-degree murder of Richard Benson," said Circuit Court Judge Michael Linn. Lenke sat motionless as he learned his fate. "He did a horrific act he's going to pay the price. And up until the day that he dies, he's going to be in solitary confinement. For years, this case has been pending and today, the family of Richard Benson got justice. So, I'm very, very relieved for that," said Brandon White, Asst. "We're relieved and the judge's decision is, we respect it and that's what we were hoping for in this case and we're glad that justice could be served," said Justin Cormier, Asst. Lenke, 67, was found guilty of first-degree murder and arson in May 2026 for Benson’s 2021 death. See also: Man fatally shot by PBSO deputy after Boynton Beach pursuit identified Prosecutors said Lenke shot Benson at Fast Frank’s Custom Cycle Components, then poured denatured alcohol on him and set him on fire while he was still alive. The crime happened just down the street from the Fort Pierce Police Department. Investigators say the motive stemmed from a personal relationship. According to prosecutors, Benson had been dating a woman who previously had a relationship with Lenke. During the murder trial, prosecutors argued that the murder was fueled by jealousy, claiming that Lenke could not accept that Benson was dating someone from his past. The prosecutor says Lenke carefully planned the murder and used a car that day that belonged to his daughter, a car which people would not associate him with and he cut up the gun and disposed of it in pieces. Lenke is a former Melbourne police officer and Indian River County firefighter. A close friend of Richard Benson, who attended every day of the trial, had this to say about the sentence Lenke received. "I like that he got the death penalty. I don't like the fact that we may be back here two or three more times on the appeals," said Skip Thompson, a friend who helped Benson in his motorcycle repair shop. Lenke did not testify in his own defense during the trial. Florida law requires the State Supreme Court to review every death sentence. So Lenke still has a legal path to challenge his conviction and sentence. That process could take years.

entry.title: Celebrities tee off for a cause at Par for the Culture golf tournament in Greenacres, Florida
entry.summary: GREENACRES, Fla. Golf, celebrities, and community impact will come together on Monday, October 19th as Par for the Culture celebrity golf tournament takes over Palm Beach National Golf Country Club, raising awareness and support for people experiencing homelessness in Palm Beach County. The event, organized by Darren Wingate, will bring together professional athletes, celebrities, influencers, and community leaders for a day of golf with a purpose. Proceeds from the tournament will benefit The Lord's Place, a Palm Beach County nonprofit organization that provides housing assistance, supportive services and programs designed to help individuals and families experiencing homelessness rebuild their lives. For Wingate, the mission goes beyond the golf course. The tournament is designed to use the influence of sports and entertainment to bring attention to affordable housing, homelessness and the importance of community involvement. The event also aims to introduce new audiences to golf while creating opportunities for people from different backgrounds to connect through a shared cause. The Lord's Place works to address homelessness through services that include street outreach, housing support, employment training and programs that help people achieve greater independence. Organizers hope the tournament will encourage athletes and community leaders to use their platforms to support housing initiatives, not just in Palm Beach County, but in communities across the country. entry.title: 'We need help': Martin County transit cuts put strain on United Way's Ride United program
entry.summary: The United Way of Martin County is calling on the community for support as transit services for residents face mounting challenges. The organization says the MARTY bus shutdown last week was just the tip of the iceberg. The United Way has been seeing an increased need for transit services following state budget cuts earlier this year. WATCH BELOW: United Way's Ride United program strained by surge in transit requests United Way's Ride United program strained by surge in transit requests Henry Hayden relies on community transit services to get to and from work. As an adult on the autism spectrum, he and his mom, Leigh Hayden, say his job gives him purpose. 'It feels like I'm independent. I can do stuff on my own,' Henry Hayden said. 'I like working because I like to talk to people. I like to get some knowledge.' 'The gifts that come with having Henry employed they're so huge,' Leigh Hayden said. In August, state budget cuts reduced funding for Community Coach, a program that helps disabled people like Henry get around. The cuts meant any disabled riders under age 70 had to find a new means of transportation. 'I said I don't know what to do,' Henry Hayden said. 'It was like having the bottom drop out. This is our lifeline, and until you know that, you really don't understand how important something like transportation is,' Leigh Hayden said. Carol Houwaart-Diez, president and CEO of the United Way of Martin County, says many turned to the organization's 'Ride United' program following the Community Coach cuts. It is the same program that Martin County residents are now using amid the MARTY Bus shutdown. 'When that closed, everything fell on the United Way. It's just really put a strain on us financially,' Houwaart-Diez said. Last year alone, 'Ride United' provided over 7,600 trips. In the last three and a half months, the organization says it has already completed over 2,800 trips. 'We need help, we need people to really start looking at how we can get that funding restored because we shouldn't be the only solution,' Houwaart-Diez said. Without services like 'Ride United,' people like Henry Hayden would lose their independence. 'I'm eternally grateful,' Henry Hayden said. 'Transportation is the piece of the puzzle that hooks to self-esteem to groceries to purpose to his character,' Leigh Hayden said. The United Way is calling on the community for help to support the increased need for community transit services. This story was reported on-air by a journalist

entry.title: Palm Springs police seek potential witness in fatal Lake Worth Road hit-and-run
entry.summary: Police are asking for the public's help identifying a potential witness as they continue investigating a fatal hit-and-run crash that happened in Palm Springs nearly four months ago. The Village of Palm Springs Police Department said Wednesday that investigators have released additional surveillance footage connected to the June 20 crash in the 4100 block of Lake Worth Road, between Kirk Road and South Military Trail. WATCH BELOW: Police seek to ID potential witness of fatal hit-and-run Palm Spring police seek to ID potential witness of fatal hit-and-run Police are trying to identify a person seen walking in the area who investigators believe may have information that could help them determine the circumstances surrounding the crash. Investigators stressed that the person is not considered a suspect. Police simply want to speak with the individual to determine whether they witnessed the crash or have information that could help the investigation. Police are asking anyone who recognizes the potential witness or has information about the crash, vehicle or driver to contact Officer Fardella at 561-584-8369 or BFardella@vpsfl.org.

entry.title: Motorcyclist killed in Palm Springs crash
entry.summary: A motorcyclist was killed in a crash involving a car Wednesday afternoon in Palm Springs, police said. The Palm Springs Police Department said the crash happened at approximately 2:14 p.m. at the intersection of South Congress Avenue and 2nd Avenue North. Officers responding to the scene found that the crash involved a motorcycle and a red Toyota Corolla. Police have not released the identity of the person who died or provided details about what led to the collision. Investigators remained at the scene Wednesday afternoon gathering evidence and investigating the circumstances surrounding the crash. Drivers should expect delays near the intersection and are encouraged to use alternate routes. Anyone who witnessed the crash or has video or other information is asked to contact Palm Springs police Officer Fardella at 561-584-8369 or BFardella@vpsfl.org .

entry.title: Palm Beach Gardens Latina entrepreneur Mary Nava builds beauty business by opening doors for other women
entry.summary: For Mary Nava, building a beauty business in Palm Beach Gardens has meant more than creating a career. After leaving Venezuela and starting over in South Florida, the Latina entrepreneur says she is now able to create opportunities for other women while building the future she wanted for her family through her business, Lashes Brows and Beauty by Mary. Nava told WPTV she came to South Florida about a decade ago with a clear goal, even though she did not yet know what her path would look like. WATCH: Palm Beach Gardens entrepreneur opens doors for Latinas Palm Beach Gardens Entrepreneur Opens Doors for Latinas | WPTV 'I need to build a future for my family, for my kids, for me,' Nava said. Today, Nava works alongside a team of Latina beauty professionals, an accomplishment she once did not imagine for herself. Starting over in South Florida Building that future required Nava to leave behind the life she knew in Venezuela. 'I left behind my country. I left behind my family, my profession,' she said. After becoming certified in Lake Worth, Nava decided to establish herself in Palm Beach Gardens. The transition presented new challenges. Nava said she had to adapt to a different culture, learn a new language and earn the trust of clients in a community where English was predominantly spoken. 'One of the biggest challenges I had was build a client from scratch,' Nava said. 'I needed people trusting in me and my services.' But Nava said quitting was never an option. 'I don't know how, but the only thing I need to know is I couldn't give up,' she said. Creating opportunities for other Latina professionals As Nava's business grew, so did her ability to help other women pursue their own careers. 'Now I can open the door for other women to grow with me together,' Nava said. For Nava, that opportunity represents a full-circle moment. 'This country gave me opportunities, and now I can bring opportunities to someone else,' she said. Her story also reflects a deeply personal definition of success. Rather than measuring it only by her own achievements, Nava said she values the opportunities she can create for others and the example she can set for the next generation. entry.title: West Palm Beach residents push back on high-rise development along Flagler Drive
entry.summary: More than 100 people gathered Wednesday evening to weigh in on development rules covering 12 acres along South Flagler Drive, where residents say high-rise construction is increasing traffic and encroaching on historic neighborhoods. The city of West Palm Beach held the public workshop at St. Catherine Greek Orthodox Church to collect feedback on zoning regulations within the South Flagler Overlay District. WPTV reporter Zitlali Solache attended the workshop and spoke with residents about their concerns. City staff focused the discussion on parking, building density and height. Residents, however, used the meeting to voice broader concerns about what they described as excessive development along the waterfront. The traffic has increased exponentially, one attendee said. West Palm Beach residents push back on Flagler waterfront development Residents question neighborhood impact West Palm Beach has undergone a major transformation, with new construction reshaping its downtown and waterfront. Several residents said they do not oppose development but want city leaders to consider its cumulative effects on traffic, infrastructure and surrounding neighborhoods. Im not against developing and making better and bringing value to our neighborhood, but can we take into consideration the overall impact? one resident asked. WPTV identified at least six new or planned developments along Flagler Drive. Longtime residents said the projects are changing the character of the waterfront and could place increasingly tall buildings next to historic homes. If we want high-rises, they have a place, downtown or near downtown, resident Amy Triggs said. Its not appropriate to build a high-rise near a 1920s neighborhood. Resident Jeff Eagle said he opposes a building approaching 200 feet in height near a historic neighborhood. I dont want a 190-some-odd-foot-tall building in a historic neighborhood, Eagle said. City reviewing waterfront zoning In July, the West Palm Beach City Commission paused waterfront redevelopment approvals for six months while the city reviews its zoning regulations. City officials said property owners have development rights, but the review is intended to keep residents informed and give the community an opportunity to comment before projects move forward. The city is expected to review feedback collected through its community survey on Nov. 4. The majority of the people all want the same thing, Eagle said. entry.title: Florida ordered license plate readers off state roads. Why does Palm Beach County still have them?
entry.summary: The Palm Beach County Sheriffs Office says it has received an exemption allowing the agency to continue using license plate reader cameras on state roads, despite a statewide push to remove the technology from those roads. Sheriff Ric Bradshaw told WPTV's Michael Hoffman the exemption is connected to the agencys role in protecting President Donald Trump when he is in Palm Beach County. WATCH: Why PBSO can keep license plate readers on state roads Florida ordered license plate readers off state roads. Why does Palm Beach County still have them? The cameras, often referred to as Flock-type cameras or automated license plate readers, capture license plate information that law enforcement can use to help locate vehicles and people. PBSO has used the technology for years, including in searches for criminal suspects and endangered people. The thing that I want people to understand is this: Its a very good tool to find people that were looking for in a law enforcement capacity, Bradshaw said. Not just for the heck of it. The technology has also played a role in several high-profile investigations. PBSO used license plate reader technology during the search for Ryan Routh after the apparent assassination attempt against Trump at Trump International Golf Club in West Palm Beach. Most recently, the sheriffs office said the cameras were used Tuesday while deputies tracked a robbery suspect. That incident ultimately ended in a deputy-involved shooting. But the continued presence of the cameras on state roads comes after Gov. Ron DeSantis directed the Florida Department of Transportation in August to take action to remove them from state roads. entry.article_text: The Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office says it has received an exemption allowing the agency to continue using license plate reader cameras on state roads, despite a statewide push to remove the technology from those roads.Sheriff Ric Bradshaw told WPTV's Michael Hoffman the exemption is connected to the agency’s role in protecting President Donald Trump when he is in Palm Beach County.WATCH: Why PBSO can keep license plate readers on state roadsThe cameras, often referred to as Flock-type cameras or automated license plate readers, capture license plate information that law enforcement can use to help locate vehicles and people.PBSO has used the technology for years, including in searches for criminal suspects and endangered people.“The thing that I want people to understand is this: It’s a very good tool to find people that we’re looking for in a law enforcement capacity,” Bradshaw said. “Not just for the heck of it.”The technology has also played a role in several high-profile investigations.PBSO used license plate reader technology during the search for Ryan Routh after the apparent assassination attempt against Trump at Trump International Golf Club in West Palm Beach.Most recently, the sheriff’s office said the cameras were used Tuesday while deputies tracked a robbery suspect. That incident ultimately ended in a deputy-involved shooting.But the continued presence of the cameras on state roads comes after Gov. Ron DeSantis directed the Florida Department of Transportation in August to take action to remove them from state roads.Bradshaw said Palm Beach County’s situation is different.“We filed a brief with the Department of Highway Safety up there in Tallahassee that, along with the Secret Service, and says, ‘Hey, this is why we can’t take them down,’ and they granted us that exemption,” Bradshaw said.That raised another question: If the exemption is connected to protecting the president, why can PBSO use those cameras for unrelated law enforcement investigations?WPTV’s Michael Hoffman put that question directly to Bradshaw.“There were some people who reached out to me and said, ‘Well, if they have an exemption to protect the president, why are they using it for other law enforcement activities?’ How would you respond to somebody with that concern?” Hoffman asked.“Well, because the law enforcement activities came first, the president came second,” Bradshaw responded. “We’ve been using them for six years, so he just became part of the system.”The cameras have also faced scrutiny over privacy and the potential for law enforcement misuse.Hoffman asked Bradshaw what safeguards PBSO has in place to prevent its system from being abused.“If you have the right guardrails, you have the right policies and procedures, you can stop that from happening,” Bradshaw said.“You can’t just put the information in there and say, ‘Gee, I’d like to see where my girlfriend was yesterday.’ This has to be a bona fide law enforcement investigation,” he added.Bradshaw said somebody audits the agency’s use of the system every week.The sheriff also pushed back against broader concerns that license plate readers amount to surveillance.“They call them surveillance. It’s not surveillance,” Bradshaw said. “Surveillance is when I think you committed a crime, and we’re going to follow you 24 hours a day, wherever you go. We’re going to be there watching you. This is just a snapshot of a particular point in time.”Bradshaw also argued there is no expectation of privacy when a person is traveling in public.Hoffman asked, "is there any scenario in which you you would take down these cameras?" "No," Sheriff Bradshaw said"Why is that?" Hoffman followed up. Because they're legal," he said. "They're a great investigative tool. We help the public with them, and it's a crime prevention tool that we use to solve cases."The sheriff said PBSO has license plate reader cameras on county roads in addition to those it has been allowed to keep on state roads.

entry.title: Death sentence handed down for 67-year-old Otto Lenke in Fort Pierce killing case - WPEC
entry.summary: Death sentence handed down for 67-year-old Otto Lenke in Fort Pierce killing case    WPEC
entry.article_text: Otto Lenke, convicted of killing Fort Pierce motorcycle shop owner Richard Benson, was sentenced to death Wednesday. "The court's independent evaluation of this case herein leads to the conclusion that the death sentence is appropriate and a just sentence for the murder of Richard Benson. Therefore, Otto Lenke, I hereby sentence you to death for the first-degree murder of Richard Benson," said Circuit Court Judge Michael Linn. Lenke sat motionless as he learned his fate. "He did a horrific act he's going to pay the price. And up until the day that he dies, he's going to be in solitary confinement. For years, this case has been pending and today, the family of Richard Benson got justice. So, I'm very, very relieved for that," said Brandon White, Asst. "We're relieved and the judge's decision is, we respect it and that's what we were hoping for in this case and we're glad that justice could be served," said Justin Cormier, Asst. Lenke, 67, was found guilty of first-degree murder and arson in May 2026 for Benson’s 2021 death. See also: Man fatally shot by PBSO deputy after Boynton Beach pursuit identified Prosecutors said Lenke shot Benson at Fast Frank’s Custom Cycle Components, then poured denatured alcohol on him and set him on fire while he was still alive. The crime happened just down the street from the Fort Pierce Police Department. Investigators say the motive stemmed from a personal relationship. According to prosecutors, Benson had been dating a woman who previously had a relationship with Lenke. During the murder trial, prosecutors argued that the murder was fueled by jealousy, claiming that Lenke could not accept that Benson was dating someone from his past. The prosecutor says Lenke carefully planned the murder and used a car that day that belonged to his daughter, a car which people would not associate him with and he cut up the gun and disposed of it in pieces. Lenke is a former Melbourne police officer and Indian River County firefighter. A close friend of Richard Benson, who attended every day of the trial, had this to say about the sentence Lenke received. "I like that he got the death penalty. I don't like the fact that we may be back here two or three more times on the appeals," said Skip Thompson, a friend who helped Benson in his motorcycle repair shop. Lenke did not testify in his own defense during the trial. Florida law requires the State Supreme Court to review every death sentence. So Lenke still has a legal path to challenge his conviction and sentence. That process could take years.

entry.title: Former police officer sentenced to death for Fort Pierce bike shop murder - WPBF
entry.summary: Former police officer sentenced to death for Fort Pierce bike shop murder    WPBF
entry.article_text: Otto Lenke, a former Melbourne police officer and Indian River County firefighter, has been sentenced to death for the 2021 murder of Richard Benson, a bike shop owner in Fort Pierce. Assistant State Attorney Brandon White, who prosecuted the case, called the sentence justice. "The jury got it right," White said. "This was probably one of the most heinous crimes in the history of our circuit. It was all caught on camera. It was well planned out." During the sentencing hearing, prosecutors showed the jury security video from inside the bike shop. They said the video showed Lenke not just killing Benson but torturing him. "He tormented him and basically made Richard's life a living hell, those last two minutes of his life by pouring that accelerant on him and lighting him on fire," White said. White stated that jealousy was the motive behind the murder, as Benson had started dating a woman Lenke previously dated. White said because he was a former police officer, Lenke thought he knew how he could get away with murder. "The defendant used his 20-plus years of experience in law enforcement to plan this attack, to carry out this attack," White said. Benson's family, who appeared via Zoom from out of state, was not present in the courtroom as the judge sentenced Lenke to death. "I think this is something they wanted for Rich. This was justice," White said. The case is not yet concluded, as Florida law requires the state Supreme Court to review all death sentences. Lenke is also expected to appeal the decision. entry.title: Trump warns Democrats ‘will take your guns away’ at Montana rally
entry.summary: President Donald Trump used a Western campaign swing on Wednesday to pitch Republicans as vigilant supporters of gun rights and to defend his acceptance of a luxury jet from Qatar to use as Air Force One. At an evening rally in Montana, Trump hewed close to the kind of attack lines that his party wants to hear as the president travels the country, and he warned that the Second Amendment would be under siege' if Democrats win in Novembers midterm elections. But his message was more off script earlier in the day as he visited an economically struggling corner of rural Arizona. Trump opened his remarks there by describing how the new jet parked behind him was a gift from the Qatari royal family. RELATED STORY | Trump in Arizona to support GOP candidates in close midterm races When youre given gifts, you take em, right? Trump told the crowd in Bullhead City. When they give you a 747, you say two words: Thank you. Trumps comments came during the second and final day of a Western swing, part of a midterm roadshow designed to rally the Republican Party ahead of Nov. 3 elections that will determine control of Congress. His first stop was Alaska on Tuesday, where he announced Taiwan would purchase gas from a proposed mega-gas project there and pardoned two Alaskans who had pleaded guilty in 2022 to Clean Air Act violations. The president continued to bestow favors in Montana, where he announced a new military testing range that had been sought by the state's Republicans. entry.title: WHERE'S WALTER? Getting into the fall spirit at Bedner's Farm Fresh Market
entry.summary: Fall has arrived in South Florida, and this week I headed to one of the season's most popular destinations: Bedner's Farm in western Palm Beach County. I had one mission when I arrived: conquer the corn maze. WATCH: 1 hospitalized with life-threatening injuries after shooting in Hobe Sound I've been looking forward to conquering the maze, but once I stepped inside, I quickly realized it was bigger and trickier than I expected. After plenty of twists, turns and dead ends, I started wondering if I'd ever find my way out. Along the way, I met fellow maze explorers, made a few new friends and even ran into a zombie. But the biggest victory came when I finally spotted the exit. Once I escaped, it was time to enjoy some of the other fall attractions around the farm. I hopped on a hayride and took in the festive atmosphere that has made Bedner's a favorite fall tradition for so many local families. Then came one of the biggest surprises of the day. While exploring the farm's animal area, I got the chance to meet and pet a baby kangaroo. It was definitely a highlight of my visit and a moment I won't soon forget. My adventure also took me through fields of beautiful sunflowers. Not only are they stunning to look at, but its cool how they follow the sun throughout the day, turning their faces as it moves across the sky. Of course, no trip to a fall festival would be complete without a visit to the pumpkin patch. I spent some time searching for the perfect pumpkin, checking out pumpkins of every size and shape while imagining all the creative jack-o'-lantern designs they could become. If you're looking for a great way to celebrate the season with family and friends, Bedner's Farm offers plenty of opportunities to make lasting memories while enjoying the outdoors. That's where I was!
