entry.article_text: Palm Beach County commissioners unanimously advanced a new micromobility device ordinance Tuesday that would establish speed limits, age restrictions and enforcement rules for e-bikes, electric scooters and similar devices, citing hundreds of injuries and concerns about rider and pedestrian safety. The proposal comes as local governments across Palm Beach County continue grappling with the growing popularity of e-bikes and e-scooters, particularly among younger riders.County staff told commissioners that since January 2023, the Healthcare District of Palm Beach County has documented 613 micromobility-related injuries, with 59% involving children ages 12 to 15. Officials also reported eight micromobility-related deaths across January 2025 and September 2026. The proposed ordinance would require riders to be at least 14 years old, carry a government-issued photo ID, obey a 15 mph speed limit on bicycle paths and shared-use areas, and slow to 10 mph when within 50 feet of pedestrians. The rules would also prohibit dangerous stunts and other unsafe riding behaviors.For many residents, the idea of more regulation is welcome."They should have some regulations at least, there should be more at least to restrict kids under 18 or people with no license," said Ryan Kuhnau of Palm Beach Gardens. "They've definitely popped up out of nowhere, they're pretty common to see in every side walk and every neighborhood."Others pointed to the growing number of riders in busy areas."More regulations for sure," said former teacher Pia Kresse.College student Melanie Zayas, who said e-scooters are popular on the Florida Atlantic University campus, said some limits make sense."For people getting around town that's good, but they can get a little crazy, especially when they're there's a lot of pedestrians out on the road," Zayas said.The proposal would require riders to slow down around pedestrians, something Zayas said she has experienced firsthand."So you've come close to getting hit by an e-scooter?" asked WPTV's Joel Lopez."Yes, I have and... It's, like, coming straight at me and I'm like 'hi, watch where you're going please,'" Zayas said.Kresse said the age and identification requirements could help improve accountability."As an ex-teacher I saw too many injuries. This is a big risk for a lot of kids and I want to see it get better before it gets worse," Kresse said. "I'm excited to see the ordinances actually take place."During the commission discussion, officials emphasized that the ordinance is largely driven by injury trends among young riders.Criminal Justice Commission Executive Director staff told commissioners that approximately 60% of the documented injuries involved children between ages 12 and 15, while 39% of injured adults were between 46 and 65 years old. Commissioners also debated how enforcement would work and whether younger riders could face disproportionate scrutiny."Is there concern youth will be over-policed, disproportionately stopped because they are young?" asked Bobby Powell.County staff and law enforcement officials repeatedly stressed that the focus will be education first."The intent is education and awareness," staff told commissioners. "They are not going to start writing and ticketing these kids as soon as they see it."The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said initial enforcement efforts would focus on outreach, safety campaigns and distributing helmets, particularly at schools where e-bike use is common. Officials said they secured grant funding to provide helmets and plan to launch a countywide awareness campaign directed at both children and parents."A lot of the parents don't understand that these items can be jailbroken and they can go from 20 miles an hour to 40 miles an hour," said County Commissioner Joel Flores.Flores said he routinely sees young riders weaving through traffic and riding at unsafe speeds."In my opinion this is not to jam them up. It's a way to protect them," said Flores. Some commissioners argued that e-bikes should be treated more like motorized vehicles than traditional bicycles."These are not bicycles. They're motor vehicles and they need to be treated like motor vehicles," said Gregg Weiss. Weiss also called for statewide action, saying better crash reporting and more consistent regulations are needed because current data collection remains limited.The ordinance could have impacts beyond unincorporated Palm Beach County.County staff told commissioners that many municipalities have expressed interest in adopting similar regulations and were waiting for the county to take the lead. Officials said both Wellington and the Town of Palm Beach already have ordinances on the books, with Palm Beach's rules being stricter than the county proposal. "A majority are interested. They were waiting for Palm Beach County to adopt this," staff told commissioners. Flores added that while the discussion was taking place, he received messages from officials in multiple cities interested in seeing the ordinance move forward.The ordinance was approved on first reading by a 7-0 vote and will return for additional consideration before becoming final. entry.title: Boynton Beach Mall tenants told to leave by Jan. 15 as questions surround property's future
entry.summary: After more than four decades as a shopping destination in Palm Beach County, the future of Boynton Beach Mall is raising questions for the businesses and shoppers who have made it part of their lives. Tenants at the mall say they recently received lease termination notices from property owner Washington Prime Group, instructing them to vacate by Jan. 15, 2027. The notices come as questions swirl about a potential sale and what could happen to the property next. However, the City of Boynton Beach tells WPTV it has not been notified of a finalized sale. WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW: After 41 years, Boynton Beach Mall faces questions about what's next For some business owners, the uncertainty means preparing to leave a place that has been part of their livelihood for decades. For longtime shoppers, it could mean saying goodbye to a familiar community landmark. Kevin Ng has a personal connection to Boynton Beach Mall that stretches back decades. Sarku Japan, the restaurant he operates, has been at the mall since 1992. His father took over the business in 2006, and Ng assumed responsibility in 2020. After his father's death, Ng continued running the restaurant, preserving a piece of his family's legacy. While the possibility of leaving the mall was not entirely unexpected, the termination notice made the situation more concrete. 'It wasn't shocking for sure, but I knew this day was going to come,' Ng said. The notice informed Ng that his lease would be terminated on Jan. 15, 2027. 'It just said, unfortunately, your lease will be terminated Jan. 15; we just have to pack up and go,' he said. Now, Ng is trying to determine what comes next for him and the family business he has worked to maintain. 'What's next? I'm trying to figure that out right now,' he said. Boynton Beach Mall first opened on Oct. 9, 1985. Over the years, it became a familiar destination for shopping, dining and spending time with family. Today, the property presents a different picture, with sparse parking lot activity, a quieter food court and vacant storefronts. Some shoppers say the mall could benefit from a fresh start. entry.title: Democrats fear slippage with Black voters makes Michigan Senate race feel ‘far closer than it should’
entry.summary: Abdul El-Sayed often talks about building a new and broad coalition of Michigan voters. A looming question in the states pivotal Senate race is whether he can keep the old one intact particularly with the Black voters who are pivotal to any Democratic victory. The Republican nominee, former Rep. Mike Rogers, has spent months working to make inroads with traditional Democratic constituencies that did not support El-Sayed, a progressive former public health official, in his bitter primary battle against Rep. Haley Stevens. POLITICAL ANALYSIS | Battle for the control of Congress Political analysis: Battle for the control of Congress And even though more than $280 million has been spent on television advertisements in Michigan since the 2026 midterm election cycle began, with billboards and campaign yard signs dotting the landscape alongside the fall colors, some political leaders wonder whether there is sufficient enthusiasm among Black voters for El-Sayed at this late stage. It only takes this much of Detroit to defect. It only takes this much of Flint to defect, said the Rev. Charles Williams II, pastor of the Historic King Solomon Baptist Church in Detroit, holding his fingers about an inch apart to drive home his point. If even a sliver of people dont turn out, you run into a huge challenge in trying to get your candidate over that line. Holding the Democratic coalition Michigan is crucial to Democrats hopes of the net four-seat gain the party needs on November 3 to win control of the Senate. If the party fails to retain the seat of retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters, its path to a majority would grow much more difficult and would run almost exclusively through much redder states than this upper Midwestern perpetual political battleground. El-Sayed defeated Stevens in the August primary by just 1 percentage point a narrow victory fueled by his strong support among Arab American and Muslim communities, young voters and progressives in college towns. But Stevens had clear strengths, too: Black voters in and around Detroit largely aligned behind her, as did Jewish voters who have long expressed deep concerns with El-Sayed, who is Muslim and a strident critic of Israels actions in Gaza. entry.article_text: “If even a sliver of people don’t turn out, you run into a huge challenge in trying to get your candidate over that line.”Holding the Democratic coalitionMichigan is crucial to Democrats’ hopes of the net four-seat gain the party needs on November 3 to win control of the Senate. If the party fails to retain the seat of retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters, its path to a majority would grow much more difficult — and would run almost exclusively through much redder states than this upper Midwestern perpetual political battleground.El-Sayed defeated Stevens in the August primary by just 1 percentage point — a narrow victory fueled by his strong support among Arab American and Muslim communities, young voters and progressives in college towns.But Stevens had clear strengths, too: Black voters in and around Detroit largely aligned behind her, as did Jewish voters who have long expressed deep concerns with El-Sayed, who is Muslim and a strident critic of Israel’s actions in Gaza.IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Poll: El Sayed holds slight edge in Michigan Senate race, but struggles with older swing votersRogers has made reaching those constituencies a central focus of his campaign in the race’s closing weeks, as he looks to assemble a coalition of voters more favorable to Republicans than in 2018, the last midterm election with President Donald Trump in office. That year, Democrats won four statewide races in Michigan, all by a range of about 7 to 9 percentage points.At a Detroit Economic Club forum on Tuesday, Rogers bragged that he has “built coalitions that really are very untraditional for a Republican candidate.”He pointed to plans to incentivize new home construction in Detroit, connect those construction efforts to high school apprenticeships, and eliminate “food deserts” in the city. He also said many Democrats have told him they fear the rising influence of democratic socialists within the party.“We’ve spent a lot of time here in Detroit, Flint, Pontiac,” he said, listing cities with large Black populations. “I think if we’re going to get our state right, we have to have everybody included in its forward progress.”In a bid to ease lingering Democratic doubts about El-Sayed, former President Barack Obama is set to visit Michigan, where he’ll attend a Saturday rally in Detroit with El-Sayed and the party’s nominee for governor, Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson.Other prominent Black Democrats have visited Michigan in recent weeks, including former Vice President Kamala Harris, who held a roundtable focused on Black maternal healthcare with El-Sayed. Raphael Warnock of Georgia is also set to campaign with El-Sayed, as are several members of the Congressional Black Caucus.“As much as he thinks he’s making inroads, folks are smart,” El-Sayed told CNN. “Mike Rogers is simply a rubber stamp on what Donald Trump wants. They understand exactly who Mike Rogers is.”While conversations with Black leaders and voters across Detroit show widespread support for El-Sayed, quiet concerns emerged about whether questions pertaining to the nominee’s background could dampen support. Historic tensions between Arab American and Black communities also were raised as points of anxiety.“In a close race, even a sliver of doubt about Abdul could lead to defeat,” one prominent Black leader told CNN, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss concerns frankly. “And this race feels far closer than it should.”El-Sayed mocks Rogers’ Black outreachEven as prominent Black Democratic leaders in Michigan express concern about the Senate race, El-Sayed — who spent recent days campaigning in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula, a sparsely populated region where he hopes his populist pitch will chip away at the GOP’s traditionally strong margins — is downplaying and even mocking Rogers’ efforts to win over Black voters.At a campaign stop in Flint, a majority-Black city, a few hundred supporters turned out for an El-Sayed rally on Sunday afternoon. Only about a dozen members of the audience who packed into a large hotel conference room were Black, which was striking for a Democratic campaign event two weeks before the election.As he spoke to reporters afterward, El-Sayed said he saw no reason for concern.“Look, one of the hardest things about this economy is that too often folks are having to work multiple jobs and having to work on weekends,” he told CNN. “We know because of exactly the policies architected by folks like Donald Trump, that falls hardest on Black folks.”He was joined at the rally by Democratic Rep. Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts, one of several Black members of Congress who have traveled to campaign alongside him.“We feel really strong about the relationship we’ve built and will continue to build,” El-Sayed said of his outreach to Black voters.When asked about the Rogers campaign opening a storefront office on Livernois Avenue in Detroit as part of its effort to win over Black voters, El-Sayed answered with a laugh.“I saw he opened a cute little office in Detroit where he brought all his friends from the suburbs to come clap him in. It was nice, yeah,” El-Sayed said. “He’s got no actual message for anyone who is struggling to make ends meet.”RELATED STORY | Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez tours for Michigan progressive Abdul El-Sayed in close Senate raceMarcia Turner, who attended the Flint rally, said she was optimistic about El-Sayed, who she called “the right person at the right time.” But even her kind words underscored a history of some tension between the Black and Arab communities of Michigan.“I love that he’s running,” Turner said. “I think people are looking past his religion and seeing him as a man who wants what we want for our children and grandchildren.”Rogers steps ‘out of his space’Naura Evans, a teacher and mother of two from Sterling Heights, is a proud Black Republican. She appears in a television commercial, saying: “I voted for Barack Obama, but this year, I’m voting for Mike Rogers.”She said she grew up in a Democratic family but has become more conservative since her 2008 vote for Obama. She said she thinks schools and neighborhoods haven’t improved under Democratic rule and believes in Rogers’ plans for both.She said she feels that Democrats have taken Black voters for granted over the years, so she spends time going door-to-door in Warren, Troy and Sterling Heights, trying to persuade voters to join her in supporting Rogers.“It’s very important that we elect the right people,” Evans said. “As Blacks in our community, we show that our vote matters. We’re not just giving the vote away.”She said the Rogers campaign should get credit for opening an office in Detroit.“I’ve seen Mike Rogers definitely step out of his space and go into the Black community,” Evans said. “I think it’s practical and I think it’s also symbolic that he cares about Detroit.

entry.article_text: Florida carried out its 18th execution of the year on Tuesday under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis' aggressive use of the death penalty in his final term.William Reaves, 77, was pronounced dead at 6:12 p.m. following a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison near Starke. He was convicted of first-degree murder in the 1986 shooting death of Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski.WATCH REPORT BELOW:Reaves was the eighth Florida prisoner over age 70 put to death this year, highlighting the nation's aging death-row population as Florida continues to far outpace the rest of country in total executions. Last year, Florida set a state record with 19 executions in a single year. Another execution is scheduled for November, which would tie that mark if both are carried out as planned.DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said previously that his goal is to bring justice to victims' families who have waited decades for the death sentences to be carried out.The U.S. Supreme Court rejected Reaves' final appeal without comment Tuesday afternoon.Reaves awoke at 5 a.m. Tuesday and remained compliant during the day, Florida Department of Corrections spokesman Jordan Kirkland said at an afternoon news conference Tuesday.The inmate had a last meal of crackers and juice and met with four visitors, including his sister, his brother, his nephew and a friend. Reaves also met with a spiritual adviser.According to court records, Raczkowski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store in September 1986. Reaves acknowledged that he had placed the call at a payphone outside the store.While Raczkowski and Reaves spoke, a gun fell out of Reaves' shorts, officials said. The men struggled over the firearm, and Reaves eventually regained control over it. Investigators said the deputy attempted to run away before Reaves shot him four times. The deputy later died from his wounds.Reaves was initially convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. The Florida Supreme Court reversed the conviction because of a conflict of interest with the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death a second time in 1992, and subsequent appeals have been unsuccessful.The Florida Supreme Court rejected Reaves' final appeals last week.One issue raised by his attorneys was Florida's method of execution. All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections.The court has previously upheld this lethal injection protocol against similar challenges. It differs from the single-drug injection used by states like Tennessee, where death row inmate Christa Pike was rushed to the hospital last month after surviving two lethal doses of pentobarbital.Defense attorneys also argued that the jurors who recommended the death penalty for Reaves were never told that the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs rated Reaves, an Army veteran, as 100% disabled by post-traumatic stress disorder, which was caused by his service in the Vietnam War. More than 100 veterans sent DeSantis a letter on Monday asking him to stop the execution.A total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half of the 31 total executions in the U.S. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so.Jesse Guardado, 64, is next scheduled to die by injection in Florida on Nov. He was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004.

entry.article_text: WPTV is learning that the Vero Beach City Council approved an extension for developers of the Three Corners project — but time is ticking.City council members told the developers, ClearBlue, that they need to negotiate and come to an agreement by Dec. 8 or the city may need to go back to the drawing board.WATCH BELOW: Developers get 4th extension for Three Corners project"I've been on this thing since 2019," Vero Beach Mayor John Cotugno said. "We need to negotiate the best, we'll call it a deal, for our citizens." The development project is located at the old Vero Beach Power Plant at the base of the 17th Street Bridge. Plans include hotels, a marina, restaurants, walking paths and more.This is the fourth extension the city council approved for developers to negotiate agreements on financing and lease terms."Some progress had been made on the financial aspects of the developer proposal," Cotugno said.But the mayor said if the council and ClearBlue aren't on the same page, they might have to change course."We need to listen and to see if this aligns with our goals and objectives. And if it does, great, we're going to work out a deal that's mutually beneficial," Cotugno said. "If not, then you know well we'll have to see what happens."Cotugno said the city council is also appointing a liaison to aid in negotiations and the developers come to discuss the project in person.Bob Salera, a spokesperson for ClearBlue, said they are meeting with city council Oct. 27."It's something that we've actually been asking for for several months," Salera said. "We're glad we finally have one on the books now."Salera said they're committed to the project and have invested over $1 million."We wouldn't have put in 21,000 hours of time into this project if we weren't serious," Salera said. "We're happy that these negotiations are moving forward, and we're ready to bring it home to a close."Cotugno said he hopes they do."I'm willing to stay at that the table if progress is being made," Cotugno said.

entry.summary: Man convicted of killing Indian River County deputy in 1986 set to be executed tonight    WPEC
entry.article_text: Florida is scheduled to execute William Reaves at 6 p.m. Tuesday, 40 years after Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkoski was shot and killed outside a convenience store near Vero Beach. Reaves, 77, will die by lethal injection at Florida State Prison unless Gov. Supreme Court denied his final appeal Tuesday, after the Florida Supreme Court rejected his last state appeals on Oct. The Florida Department of Corrections says Reaves had 5 visitors. His brother, sister, nephew, friend, and spiritual advisor all visited Reaves Tuesday. A spokesperson with the department said his final meal was crackers and juice. According to court records, Raczkoski was called to the store around 3 a.m. 23, 1986, to help Reaves get a cab. A gun fell from Reaves’ shorts and the two struggled over it. Records say Reaves shot the deputy in the back four times as he turned away. His son was born after his death. Reaves was arrested two days later in Albany, Georgia. In a taped interview with Indian River County detectives, he admitted to the shooting and said he had been using cocaine. I’ve never met a finer officer in my life, he told them, according to a transcript filed by the state. Reaves was convicted in 1987, but the Florida Supreme Court threw out that verdict in 1991 because one of the prosecutors had previously represented him. A second jury convicted him in 1992 and voted 10-2 to recommend death. DeSantis signed his death warrant Sept. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers, who pushed the governor to sign the warrant, plans to witness the execution. He told CBS12 News on Monday that his goal is that the last thing that he sees is an Indian River County Sheriff’s Office uniform, knowing that justice finally came. Flowers said Raczkoski’s brother is expected to be among the witnesses. Flowers said the brother told him Christmas was never the same for our family after Richard was killed. See also: 124 cats, some deceased, surrendered in disturbing Port St. Lucie hoarding case Reaves’ attorneys fought the execution to the end. In court filings, they argued he is a Vietnam veteran rated 100% disabled for post-traumatic stress disorder by the Department of Veterans Affairs, and that the jury that sentenced him never heard the details of his combat service. They also argued he was shut out of the clemency process. The governor denied clemency the same day he signed the death warrant. The Department of Corrections is expected to hold a briefing after the execution. CBS12 News is at Florida State Prison and will update this story.

entry.summary: A 20-year-old Martin County woman is being honored after she used CPR to help save a 3-year-old girl she found motionless at the bottom of a swimming pool. Nearly two months after the August rescue, Martin County Fire Rescue recognized Madison Isler with the department's Heroic Heart Award. WATCH: Martin County woman honored for saving 3-year-old Woman Honored After Using CPR to Save 3-Year-Old Girl | WPTV The rescue happened Aug. 23 as Isler walked past the pool at her apartment complex. She told WPTV something in the water caught her attention. 'It kind of looked like a smudge in your sunglasses,' Isler said. 'And then, so I took my glasses off, and I looked, and then I realized that it was a little girl.' That little girl was 3-year-old Luna. 'I jumped in and grabbed her' Isler said Luna was motionless at the bottom of the swimming pool when she spotted her. 'I jumped in and grabbed her and pulled her out, and she was blue,' Isler said. Isler called for her boyfriend to contact 911 and began CPR, using skills she said she learned at a young age from her parents, who both work in fire rescue. 'You just don't really think; you just kind of do, especially in a situation when it's a little baby,' Isler said. 'I pulled a lifeless baby out of a pool.' A family friend who is a pediatric intensive care unit nurse heard the commotion and joined the rescue effort, according to the account shared by Martin County Fire Rescue. 'Together, they continued their life-saving efforts till finally Luna responded,' Martin County Fire Rescue Chief Chad Cianciulli said. Fire rescue officials said Luna was alert and oriented by the time paramedics transported her to the hospital. entry.title: Dolphins release kicker Riley Patterson, add Zane Gonzalez to practice squad
entry.summary: The Miami Dolphins released kicker Riley Patterson amid a series of roster moves on Tuesday. The Dolphins brought back kicker Zane Gonzalez, signing him to the practice squad after the veteran spent part of training camp with the team before being released in August with an injury settlement. Miami also waived cornerback Storm Duck and edge Andre Jones Jr. and signed edge Rodney McGraw off the practice squad. Patterson made seven of his nine field-goal attempts this season and was 5 of 6 on extra points. The moves come as the Dolphins try to improve one of the league's worst special teams units, which allowed an 81-yard return on the opening kickoff against Cincinnati in Week 5. Coach Jeff Hafley has pointed to a lack of execution as a reason for some of Miami's special teams struggles and said the team would evaluate all units during its bye week and explore changes if necessary. 'Were counting on those veteran players to do their job to the best of their ability,' Hafley said last week, before Miami's Week 6 bye. Whether its in the punt game, whether its making our PATs and our extra points, whether its kicking the ball, whether its were trying to kick a touchback or were trying to kick the ball deep left, just like any other position, were counting on those veterans to do their job and do them at a high level. Thats what theyre here for. Gonzalez is 115 of 142 in his career on field goals and 18 of 28 on attempts of 50 or more yards.

Meanwhile, the Falcon 9's first stage made another spectacular landing about nine minutes after launch, touching down on a drone ship called 'A Shortfall of Gravitas.'

entry.article_text: More than 100 cats were found in unsanitary conditions inside a Port St. Lucie home, including deceased kittens, prompting a criminal investigation. Officers with the Port St. Lucie Police Department say 124 cats, both living and deceased, were recovered from a residence in the 2500 block of SW Warwick Street. Animal Control personnel responded to concerns about the number of cats and their living conditions on October 13. They documented accumulated feces and deceased kittens inside the home. See also: Wellington speed camera ticket tossed over missing state approval Two of the three residents have been issued citations for hoarding and failing to provide medical attention to animals, police said. The investigation remains active, and police have not provided details about potential future arrests. All 124 cats have been surrendered and are receiving care through Port St. Lucie Animal Control and the Humane Society of St. Several cats are being treated for ear mites and fleas. Others have needed surgery or additional veterinary care, with some transported to Veterinary Medical Center for treatment. Many of the surviving cats are friendly and could become available for adoption once their medical needs are addressed, police said. The case required a coordinated response involving animal control personnel, police officers, veterinarians and animal welfare organizations. Police said additional information will be released as the investigation continues.

entry.title: More than 100 cats rescued from hoarding situation in Port St. Lucie - WPBF
entry.summary: More than 100 cats rescued from hoarding situation in Port St. Lucie    WPBF
entry.article_text: More than 100 cats and kittens rescued from a hoarding situation in Port St. Lucie are now receiving medical care and nourishment at the Humane Society of St. Lucie Animal Control removed the animals over the course of three days last week, with the first group arriving at the shelter on Tuesday. "Some were clearly showing symptoms of upper respiratory. The majority of them had ear mites. They were all covered in fleas. There were a couple that had open sores, from scratching at the flea, scratching at the ear mites and some other issues," said Sarah Wees, executive director of the Humane Society of St. Three pregnant cats gave birth shortly after being rescued, with one too weak to care for her kittens. Those newborns were rushed to an emergency foster home for round-the-clock care, while others remain at the shelter. "We have kittens who are nursing on cats that may or may not be their mom because we really can't tell who belongs with whom because they were all in the same house together," Wees said. The Humane Society is receiving assistance from American Humane, a national organization that supports local communities during large intake cases or natural disasters. "She reached out to me, and by Thursday morning I was on property, and helping just work through those initial days, and also coordinating some volunteers and additional staffing to come in to help with additional personnel," said Taylor Nickelsen, a certified animal responder with American Humane. Nickelsen said their efforts are making a difference, with many of the cats showing significant improvement. "We stay as long as we need to be able to provide the relief that is needed, which ultimately our goal is to help get these animals on their way to foster and on their way to adoption," Nickelsen said. Lucie police are monitoring the case to determine if any criminal charges will be filed. In the meantime, the Humane Society is seeking donations and volunteers to help care for the rescued cats and kittens. entry.title: William Reaves: Man convicted of killing Indian River County deputy in 1986 scheduled to be executed Tuesday - WFLX
entry.summary: William Reaves: Man convicted of killing Indian River County deputy in 1986 scheduled to be executed Tuesday    WFLX
entry.article_text: Florida is set Tuesday to carry out its 18th execution of the year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis’ aggressive use of the death penalty in his final term. William Reaves , 77, was sentenced to death after being convicted of first-degree murder for the 1986 shooting of Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski. He would become Florida’s eighth prisoner over the age of 70 to be executed this year, which has highlighted the nation’s aging death-row population and underscored how Florida has outpaced the rest of the country in executions. Reaves was set to receive a three-drug injection starting at 6 p.m. at Florida State Prison near Starke. Last year, Florida set a state record with 19 executions in a single year. Another execution is scheduled for November, which would tie that mark if both are carried out as planned. DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said previously that his goal is to bring justice to victims’ families who have waited decades for the death sentences to be carried out. According to court records, Raczkowski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store in September 1986. Reaves acknowledged that he had placed the call at a payphone outside the store. While Raczkowski and Reaves spoke, a gun fell out of Reaves’ shorts, officials said. The men struggled over the firearm, and Reaves eventually regained control over it. Investigators said the deputy attempted to run away before Reaves shot him four times. The deputy later died from his wounds. Reaves was initially convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. The Florida Supreme Court reversed the conviction because of a conflict of interest with the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death a second time in 1992, and subsequent appeals have been unsuccessful. The Florida Supreme Court rejected Reaves’ final appeals last week. One issue raised by his attorneys was Florida’s method of execution. All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections. The court has previously upheld this lethal injection protocol against similar challenges. It differs from the single-drug injection used by states like Tennessee, where death row inmate Christa Pike was rushed to the hospital last month after surviving two lethal doses of pentobarbital. Defense attorneys also argued that the jurors who recommended the death penalty for Reaves were never told that the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs rated Reaves, an Army veteran, as 100% disabled by post-traumatic stress disorder, which was caused by his service in the Vietnam War. More than 100 veterans sent DeSantis a letter on Monday asking him to stop the execution. Final appeals for Reaves were still pending before the U.S. A total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half of the 31 total executions in the U.S. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so. Jesse Guardado, 64, is next scheduled to die by injection in Florida on Nov. He was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004.

entry.title: Oculina Bank: Rare Florida coral reef faces pivotal federal decision over return of shrimp trawling
entry.summary: A years-long fight over one of the world's rarest ecosystems has reached federal officials, as scientists and conservationists push back against a proposal that could reopen part of the protected Oculina Bank to shrimp trawling for the first time in decades. The Oculina Bank is a deep-water coral reef off Florida's Atlantic coast, with some of its most significant formations off Fort Pierce. Built by the rare Oculina varicosa coral, the reef sits hundreds of feet below the surface and provides habitat for thousands of marine species, including economically important snapper and grouper. entry.article_text: A years-long fight over one of the world's rarest ecosystems has reached federal officials, as scientists and conservationists push back against a proposal that could reopen part of the protected Oculina Bank to shrimp trawling for the first time in decades.The Oculina Bank is a deep-water coral reef off Florida's Atlantic coast, with some of its most significant formations off Fort Pierce. Built by the rare Oculina varicosa coral, the reef sits hundreds of feet below the surface and provides habitat for thousands of marine species, including economically important snapper and grouper.WATCH BELOW: Fight over rare coral reef reaches NOAA as public comment opensScientists say decades of shrimp trawling destroyed roughly 90% of the reef before federal protections were put in place. Parts of the Oculina Bank were closed to trawling beginning in the 1990s, with protections later expanded and made permanent.Now, conservationists fear some of that progress could be reversed."I'd say it's dire. It's a dire situation," said Mark Perry, executive director of the Florida Oceanographic Society. "We're desperate to get this protected."The latest battle began after a Trump administration executive order directed the nation's regional fishery councils to look for ways to reduce regulatory burdens, expand fishing opportunities and increase economic profitability.The South Atlantic Fishery Management Council subsequently considered proposals that would restore commercial shrimping access to portions of the Oculina Bank that have been protected from trawling for decades. Council documents described the areas as historically important fishing grounds and said the changes were intended to help achieve optimum yield in the rock shrimp fishery.Shrimpers say they need the additional fishing grounds."The shrimping industry is teetering on the brink of extinction," Bob Zales, executive director of the Southeastern Fisheries Association, previously told WPTV.Council data reviewed by WPTV shows the rock shrimp industry has declined dramatically. The number of annual trips fell from more than 700 in the mid-1990s to fewer than 100 annually since 2010. The number of active rock shrimpers also dropped from 144 in 1996 to fewer than 30 in later years.Zales has blamed the decline on factors including rising costs, imported shrimp and the loss of fishing grounds. Shrimpers have also faced increasing restrictions off Port Canaveral during space launches.Scientists and conservationists argue the potential benefit to the shrimp industry is small compared with the ecological and economic value of protecting the remaining reef.NOAA data previously reviewed by WPTV showed brown rock shrimp landings nationwide totaled about 600,000 pounds in 2023, worth roughly $1 million.Florida fishermen, by comparison, landed nearly 100 million pounds of fish worth just under $300 million that year, including species such as snapper and grouper that use the reef as habitat."We know how valuable this reef system is," Perry said.Scientists also warn that recovery from additional damage could take generations."It would take centuries to grow back even some semblance of the corals," Perry said.Supporters of reopening the area point to mapping that found no live coral, standing dead coral or coral rubble within the proposed trawling zones.But that same research warned sediment kicked up by trawling could drift into nearby living reef and smother coral. Scientists have also raised concerns that snapper and grouper could be caught as bycatch.WPTV Investigates has followed the debate as opposition grew locally and nationally.Earlier public comments to the council overwhelmingly opposed reopening the area. WPTV's review found about 120 of 150 comments opposed both proposals, while 25 supported both and five supported one proposal but not the other.A similar proposal approved by the council in 2022 ultimately failed to win federal approval, garnering thousands of opposing public comments from across the country. The latest proposal nevertheless continued moving forward.WPTV also previously reviewed financial disclosure records for members of the South Atlantic Fishery Management Council and found several disclosed financial interests tied to the fishing or seafood industries. Council officials told WPTV that conflicts of interest are governed by NOAA rules and federal law.Earlier this year, despite opposition from scientists, conservationists and members of the public, the council voted to recommend reopening as much as 24 square nautical miles to shrimp trawling — an area larger than Manhattan.The proposal has now reached the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, which will decide whether to approve it.The Agency has posted the proposals to its Federal Registry, asking the public to weigh in before it votes. The fight is also drawing attention from national conservation organizations.Mike Gravitz, with the Marine Conservation Institute, said the debate comes as coral reefs worldwide already face pressure from warming waters, pollution and overfishing — and as countries around the world work toward protecting more of the planet's oceans."For gosh sakes, it's the last 10% of something that occurs nowhere else on Earth," Gravitz said.He said the United States has close to 25% of its ocean protected in an effective way, while international conservation efforts are moving in the opposite direction."It's really ironic to us that people would be talking about weakening protections for these deep-sea corals at a time when the world needs to do even more, not less," Gravitz said. "This administration is rolling back those protections, especially for the very large marine protected areas, some of which have been protected since Teddy Roosevelt was president." For Perry, the federal review represents the latest — and potentially decisive — stage of a fight that has stretched for years."They understood it, and they protected it," Perry said of previous federal protections, "but now it's being attacked again."Public comment on the proposal is open through Nov. 17 before federal officials make a final decision.Click here to submit a public comment."And we just really need to, you know, stand up and fight for it," Perry said.Multiple organizations have also launched petitions opposing the proposals.

After a few minutes, the team warden shook Reaves’ shoulders and yelled his name, but there was no response.A medic was called into the chamber a short time later to check for a heartbeat or any other signs of life, and Reaves was pronounced dead about a minute later.Reaves was the eighth Florida prisoner over age 70 put to death this year, highlighting the nation’s aging death-row population as Florida continues to far outpace the rest of country in total executions.Last year, Florida set a state record with 19 executions in a single year and it would tie that mark if another execution is carried out next month as scheduled.DeSantis, who leaves office in January after two terms, has said his goal is to deliver justice to victims’ families who have waited decades for death sentences to be carried out.Raczkowski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store in September 1986, according to court records. Reaves later acknowledged he had placed the call from a payphone outside the store.While Raczkowski and Reaves spoke, a gun fell out of Reaves’ shorts, officials said. The two struggled over the weapon, and Reaves eventually regained control of it. Investigators said the deputy was trying to run away when Reaves shot him four times. The deputy later died from his wounds.Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. But the Florida Supreme Court overturned the conviction because of a conflict of interest with the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. Reaves was convicted again and sentenced to death in 1992, and subsequent appeals were unsuccessful.The U.S. Supreme Court on Tuesday afternoon rejected Reaves’ final appeal without comment.The Florida Supreme Court last week also rejected Reaves’ appeals to spare his life.One issue raised by his attorneys was Florida’s method of execution. All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections.The court has previously upheld this lethal injection protocol against similar challenges. It differs from the single-drug injection used by states such as Tennessee, where death row inmate Christa Pike was rushed to the hospital last month after surviving two lethal doses of pentobarbital.Defense attorneys also argued that the jurors who recommended the death penalty for Reaves were never told that the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs rated Reaves — an Army veteran — as 100% disabled by post-traumatic stress disorder, which was caused by his service in the Vietnam War. More than 100 veterans sent DeSantis a letter Monday urging him to stop the execution.A total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half of the 32 total executions in the U.S. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so.Jesse Guardado, 64, is next scheduled to die by injection in Florida on Nov. He was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004.

entry.title: More than 100 cats rescued from hoarding situation in Port St. Lucie - WPBF
entry.summary: More than 100 cats rescued from hoarding situation in Port St. Lucie    WPBF
entry.article_text: More than 100 cats and kittens rescued from a hoarding situation in Port St. Lucie are now receiving medical care and nourishment at the Humane Society of St. Lucie Animal Control removed the animals over the course of three days last week, with the first group arriving at the shelter on Tuesday. "Some were clearly showing symptoms of upper respiratory. The majority of them had ear mites. They were all covered in fleas. There were a couple that had open sores, from scratching at the flea, scratching at the ear mites and some other issues," said Sarah Wees, executive director of the Humane Society of St. Three pregnant cats gave birth shortly after being rescued, with one too weak to care for her kittens. Those newborns were rushed to an emergency foster home for round-the-clock care, while others remain at the shelter. "We have kittens who are nursing on cats that may or may not be their mom because we really can't tell who belongs with whom because they were all in the same house together," Wees said. The Humane Society is receiving assistance from American Humane, a national organization that supports local communities during large intake cases or natural disasters. "She reached out to me, and by Thursday morning I was on property, and helping just work through those initial days, and also coordinating some volunteers and additional staffing to come in to help with additional personnel," said Taylor Nickelsen, a certified animal responder with American Humane. Nickelsen said their efforts are making a difference, with many of the cats showing significant improvement. "We stay as long as we need to be able to provide the relief that is needed, which ultimately our goal is to help get these animals on their way to foster and on their way to adoption," Nickelsen said. Lucie police are monitoring the case to determine if any criminal charges will be filed. In the meantime, the Humane Society is seeking donations and volunteers to help care for the rescued cats and kittens. entry.title: Man convicted of killing Indian River County deputy set for execution Tuesday - WPEC
entry.summary: Man convicted of killing Indian River County deputy set for execution Tuesday    WPEC
entry.article_text: The man convicted of killing an Indian River County deputy nearly 40 years ago is scheduled to be executed Tuesday. William Reaves, 77, is set to die by lethal injection at 6 p.m. at Florida State Prison near Starke . Ron DeSantis signed the death warrant Sept. According to court records, Cpl. Richard Raczkoski was called to a Zippy Mart near Vero Beach around 3 a.m. 23, 1986, to help Reaves get a cab. During the encounter, a gun fell from Reaves’ shorts and the two struggled over it. Records say Reaves shot the deputy four times in the back. In a taped interview with Indian River County detectives in Albany, Reaves admitted to the shooting. I’ve never met a finer officer in my life, he said, according to a transcript filed by the state. When a detective asked why he would not give up the gun, Reaves said he was a convicted felon and feared prison. I know if I got caught with that gun, and the man take me down there, I’m gonna get a mandatory three years already for the gun, he said. Reaves also told detectives, I was all coked up and I panicked, both of us panicked. Prosecutors have long argued the shooting was premeditated. Court records show the deputy was running away when he was shot, and the .380 handgun required a separate trigger pull for each shot. See also: Florida secures state arrest warrant for Raúl Castro in 1996 shootdown Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death. The Florida Supreme Court rejected his latest appeals last week, and a request for the U.S. Supreme Court to review his case is still pending. His attorneys and supporters, including a group of military veterans, have asked DeSantis to spare his life, pointing to his service in Vietnam. Reaves was first convicted in 1987, but the Florida Supreme Court threw out that conviction in 1991 because one of the prosecutors had previously represented Reaves in another case. A second jury convicted him again in 1992 and voted 10-2 to recommend the death penalty. In a court filing last month, Reaves’ attorneys said he was deployed to Vietnam as a ground combat soldier in 1969, at age 20. They say the Department of Veterans Affairs rates him 100% disabled for post-traumatic stress disorder, and that the jury that sentenced him never heard the details of his combat service. His attorneys also argued that Reaves was shut out of the clemency process. They said the attorney assigned to represent him met with him about five minutes before his clemency interview and never gave him a copy of what was submitted on his behalf. A circuit judge ruled Reaves received a full clemency proceeding. The governor denied clemency the same day he signed the death warrant. In the same filing, the defense accused two former Indian River County deputies of taking bribes from a drug dealer in the 1980s. The defense also said one of them helped shape the testimony of a key witness against Reaves. Circuit Judge Anastasia Norman rejected the claim on Oct. 2, finding the allegations were not backed by any sworn statement and were merely speculative at best. Reaves did not raise that claim in his appeal to the Florida Supreme Court. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers, who pushed for the governor to sign the warrant, describes the moment when he learned the governor signed Reaves' death warrant. "It was not something that I had expected. At this point, our governor is wrapping things up in Tallahassee and finishing out his time. So for him to take time to make sure that this gets handled is just really a blessing," said Flowers. Flowers plans to attend the execution in Raiford on Tuesday. My goal with going tomorrow is ultimately the last thing that he sees is an Indian River County Sheriff’s Office uniform, knowing that justice finally came, Flowers said. Flowers said Raczkoski’s brother will also be there. Raczkoski’s parents have since died. Flowers said the brother told him, Christmas was never the same for our family after Richard was killed. The execution comes nearly a year after the agency lost Sgt. Terri Sweeting-Mashkow, who was killed in the line of duty in November 2025. Flowers said Tuesday will bring the agency some closure. It just really feels like coming full circle, like a moment of healing that we all needed, Flowers said. Supreme Court appeal still pending, Flowers said he will not rest easy until the execution is carried out. I’d hate to see it delayed in any way, he said.

entry.title: Year-long bridge closure in southern Martin County forces drivers onto detour, adds minutes to commutes
entry.summary: A major road closure is now in effect in southern Martin County, where the bridge at Southeast County Line Road is closed for a year-long reconstruction project. The detour could add several minutes to daily drives, so officials are urging commuters to plan ahead or find an alternate route. George May lives just off Southeast County Line Road, where a road block is now notifying drivers to turn around. 'It'll be inconvenient, for sure. People commuting to work and people that live in little club,' May said. May said the road closure is going to take some getting used to. 'I already drive over an hour to work everyday. It'll probably add about 20 minutes to my commute,' May said. Martin County says the bridge will be closed for a year, with a lot of work ahead. 'There are a lot of utilities ther,' Mark Aveni, Martin County public works deputy director, said. 'There's a lot of coordination that needs to occur. We're removing a pedestrian bridge and we're going to repurpose that somewhere else and unfortunately these things just take time.' Despite the closure, residents say they're glad to see the investment. 'There were large cracks under the bridge. It was deteriorating,' May said. 'It's a little bit of an inconvenience but I'm happy for that to have a new bridge and have better infrastructure in the area,' Daniel Von said. Six of the project's $7 million price tag is covered by state and federal grants. The new bridge will be two feet higher and built to be safer and more resilient. 'We're replacing it with a very resilient type of rebar that's going to be safer. There is a very sharp curve before that bridge, we're going to totally eliminate that and soften the curve. entry.title: William Reaves: Man convicted of killing Indian River County deputy in 1986 scheduled to be executed Tuesday - WFLX
entry.summary: William Reaves: Man convicted of killing Indian River County deputy in 1986 scheduled to be executed Tuesday    WFLX
entry.article_text: Florida is set Tuesday to carry out its 18th execution of the year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis’ aggressive use of the death penalty in his final term. William Reaves , 77, was sentenced to death after being convicted of first-degree murder for the 1986 shooting of Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski. He would become Florida’s eighth prisoner over the age of 70 to be executed this year, which has highlighted the nation’s aging death-row population and underscored how Florida has outpaced the rest of the country in executions. Reaves was set to receive a three-drug injection starting at 6 p.m. at Florida State Prison near Starke. Last year, Florida set a state record with 19 executions in a single year. Another execution is scheduled for November, which would tie that mark if both are carried out as planned. DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said previously that his goal is to bring justice to victims’ families who have waited decades for the death sentences to be carried out. According to court records, Raczkowski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store in September 1986. Reaves acknowledged that he had placed the call at a payphone outside the store. While Raczkowski and Reaves spoke, a gun fell out of Reaves’ shorts, officials said. The men struggled over the firearm, and Reaves eventually regained control over it. Investigators said the deputy attempted to run away before Reaves shot him four times. The deputy later died from his wounds. Reaves was initially convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. The Florida Supreme Court reversed the conviction because of a conflict of interest with the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death a second time in 1992, and subsequent appeals have been unsuccessful. The Florida Supreme Court rejected Reaves’ final appeals last week. One issue raised by his attorneys was Florida’s method of execution. All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections. The court has previously upheld this lethal injection protocol against similar challenges. It differs from the single-drug injection used by states like Tennessee, where death row inmate Christa Pike was rushed to the hospital last month after surviving two lethal doses of pentobarbital. Defense attorneys also argued that the jurors who recommended the death penalty for Reaves were never told that the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs rated Reaves, an Army veteran, as 100% disabled by post-traumatic stress disorder, which was caused by his service in the Vietnam War. More than 100 veterans sent DeSantis a letter on Monday asking him to stop the execution. Final appeals for Reaves were still pending before the U.S. A total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half of the 31 total executions in the U.S. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so. Jesse Guardado, 64, is next scheduled to die by injection in Florida on Nov. He was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004.

entry.title: Local court leaders urge residents to respond to jury summonses as turnout drops
entry.summary: Court officials in Floridas 19th Judicial Circuit are warning people who ignore jury duty summonses that they could face fines and other legal consequences. The circuit serves Indian River, Martin, St. Lucie and Okeechobee counties. Officials say low response rates are making it harder to select juries and can delay court proceedings. At a recent WPTV Lets Hear It meetup in Okeechobee , Jerald D. Bryant, clerk of circuit court and comptroller, spoke with WPTV reporter Brooke Chau about the problem. In April 2026, 300 people were summoned for jury duty, but only 60 reported. That means just one in five people showed up. Bryant said a jury summons is a court order and ignoring it can have legal consequences. It is contempt of court because a jury summons is a court order to appear, Bryant said. Why jury duty participation matters Court officials say low turnout can make it difficult to assemble a jury, potentially delaying trials and affecting defendants waiting for their cases to be heard, as well as victims and their families. Chief Judge Charles A. Schwab told WPTV that higher response rates could also help the court use its resources more efficiently. 'If we knew that return rate was going to be 75% to 85%, those other monies could then be diverted to things that we as a community would rather be spending those on,' Schwab said. What happens if you ignore a jury summons? Court leaders say they plan to enforce the consequences for people who fail to appear for jury duty. People who ignore their summonses could receive an order requiring them to explain their absence to a judge. They could face a $100 fine and still be required to serve on a jury. Failing to appear for that court hearing could lead to a bench warrant and potential arrest. Diamond Litty, public defender for the 19th judicial circuit, encouraged anyone with questions or a legitimate issue preventing them from attending to contact the court. It was murder," Uthmeier said Monday. "The evidence makes abundantly clear that there was a conspiracy."The Florida Attorney General's Office said its Office of Statewide Prosecution and the Florida Department of Law Enforcement secured the warrant. The state charges Castro with conspiracy to commit first-degree murder.The allegations date back to Feb. 24, 1996, when a Cuban military aircraft shot down two unarmed civilian planes operated by Brothers to the Rescue over international waters.The four men killed were Carlos Costa, Pablo Morales, Mario de la Peña and Armando Alejandre Jr.Brothers to the Rescue was a Miami-based Cuban exile organization whose missions included searching for Cuban migrants at sea."Raúl Castro called for the planes to be shot down," Uthmeier said. "He called for murder."According to the state attorney general's office, Castro is accused of participating in a conspiracy involving Cuban spies operating in South Florida who supplied intelligence to Havana.The arrest warrant affidavit alleges the goal was to kill people aboard the Brothers to the Rescue aircraft "using information provided by spies operating in Miami-Dade and Monroe counties."Florida's case does not stand alone.Federal prosecutors announced an indictment against Castro in May stemming from the same 1996 shootdown. The state prosecution is proceeding alongside that federal case.Former Palm Beach County State Attorney Dave Aronberg told WPTV that federal authorities would ordinarily take the lead on a case such as this."The federal government usually takes the lead on matters like this," Aronberg said.Aronberg questioned how much practical effect a state prosecution would have if Castro were ultimately brought to the United States."If he is brought to the United States to face justice at all, it'll be by the United States to face federal charges in a federal court and then get federal prison time," Aronberg said.Uthmeier, however, argued Monday that the state warrant has consequences. He said it could affect Castro's ability to travel internationally if he enters a country willing and legally able to assist with an arrest or extradition. Such an outcome would depend on the country's laws, applicable extradition arrangements and federal cooperation.The state announcement also brought questions about its timing.Monday marked the first day of early voting in Miami-Dade County, where Uthmeier is seeking election as attorney general.Aronberg told WPTV he believes politics played a role."I think the timing so close to the election is not a coincidence," Aronberg said. "This is a splash that the attorney general wanted to make, and perhaps it's justified under state law. But the timing does indicate that politics came into play here."Uthmeier's opponent also criticized the timing in a statement to WPTV."If we can arrest the murderous Raúl Castro from Tallahassee, I will be the first to do it as Attorney General," the statement said in part.The opponent argued that Uthmeier "somehow chose the first day of early voting in Miami-Dade to make this announcement" and called it "a smokescreen to distract from Hope Florida and Alligator Alcatraz."Beyond the legal and political questions, the case remains deeply personal for members of South Florida's Cuban American community.Hoffman spoke with Mirta Luaces, who said she fled Cuba 65 years ago in search of freedom."I came here in search of freedom, the freedom that I have lost in Cuba," Luaces said.Her son, she said, was a pilot with Brothers to the Rescue and could have been flying with the organization the day of the shootdown."The reason why he wasn't flying that day is because he had moved to Daytona, and he wasn't coming every week," Luaces said. "But otherwise, he could have been one of the victims."Luaces told WPTV she welcomed the new charges and hopes Cuba's political system will someday change."I hope that one day the political system in Cuba will change," Luaces said. "We will have free elections, and democracy will take place in Havana, in Cuba again."Thirty years after the shootdown, Florida's prosecution adds a state case to an already active federal effort to hold Castro accountable. Whether Castro will ever appear in a U.S. courtroom remains an open practical question, but the new warrant adds another legal avenue tied to a case that has remained significant to South Florida's Cuban exile community for decades.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Moskowitz, Singer discuss Israel, economy in Boca Raton congressional forum
entry.summary: Democratic U.S. Rep. Jared Moskowitz and Republican former Boca Raton Mayor Scott Singer faced off in Boca Raton as the race for Florida's 25th Congressional District enters its final stretch, focusing heavily on Israel, antisemitism and key economic issues affecting South Florida voters. The candidate forum, held at Congregation B'nai Israel in Boca Raton, drew residents eager to hear where the two candidates stand on issues ranging from U.S.-Israel relations and Cuba policy to homeowners insurance, housing costs and border security. Florida's 25th Congressional District now stretches from Delray Beach into Miami-Dade County, expanding the electorate both candidates are trying to reach. Candidates outline positions on Israel and antisemitism Israel and efforts to combat antisemitism emerged as major themes during the forum. Both Moskowitz and Singer emphasized support for Israel and discussed foreign policy issues that continue to resonate with many South Florida voters. Attendee Nadine Patz said she came to hear both perspectives before casting her vote. 'I love both sides of any conversation, so knowledge is power,' Patz said. The forum gave voters an opportunity to hear each candidate explain how they would approach international issues and address concerns raised by members of the local community. entry.title: Palm Beach County said no to Project Tango expansion, but data center space still triples
entry.summary: Palm Beach County zoning staff approved a plan that nearly triples the amount of data center space previously approved on part of the property associated with Project Tango, according to new documents obtained by WPTV reporter Michael Hoffman. The Oct. 7 approval came less than three months after county commissioners voted 5-1 to reject a much larger Project Tango expansion. Palm Beach County said no to Project Tango expansion, but data center space still triples. How is that possible? The new plan increases the approved data center space from 206,000 square feet to just under 700,000 square feet. That distinction is important because the new approval is separate from the Project Tango expansion commissioners rejected in July. Project Tango dates back to a 2016 approval In 2016, plans were approved for 206,000 square feet of data center space and 1.2 million square feet of warehouse space on the property. About 600,000 square feet remained unassigned. The site is next to what would later become the Arden community and Saddle View Elementary School. A decade later, a much larger proposal came before the Palm Beach County Commission. On July 15, commissioners spent roughly 12 hours reviewing the application known as Project Tango. That proposal sought to increase the project's data center footprint to more than 1 million square feet. Commissioners voted 5-1 to deny the expansion following significant opposition from nearby residents. The county also passed a moratorium on new data center applications while officials work on new rules. For residents who had fought the expansion, the July decision was a victory. Many believed it meant the 206,000 square feet of data center space approved in 2016 would remain the limit at the site. New documents show that was not the end of the story. entry.article_text: Palm Beach County zoning staff approved a plan that nearly triples the amount of data center space previously approved on part of the property associated with Project Tango, according to new documents obtained by WPTV reporter Michael Hoffman. 7 approval came less than three months after county commissioners voted 5-1 to reject a much larger Project Tango expansion.The new plan increases the approved data center space from 206,000 square feet to just under 700,000 square feet.That distinction is important because the new approval is separate from the Project Tango expansion commissioners rejected in July.In 2016, plans were approved for 206,000 square feet of data center space and 1.2 million square feet of warehouse space on the property. About 600,000 square feet remained unassigned.The site is next to what would later become the Arden community and Saddle View Elementary School.A decade later, a much larger proposal came before the Palm Beach County Commission.On July 15, commissioners spent roughly 12 hours reviewing the application known as Project Tango. That proposal sought to increase the project's data center footprint to more than 1 million square feet.Commissioners voted 5-1 to deny the expansion following significant opposition from nearby residents.The county also passed a moratorium on new data center applications while officials work on new rules.For residents who had fought the expansion, the July decision was a victory. Many believed it meant the 206,000 square feet of data center space approved in 2016 would remain the limit at the site.New documents show that was not the end of the story.Documents obtained by Hoffman show PBA Holdings, one of two companies that own property associated with Project Tango, had submitted a separate proposal before the July commission vote.Palm Beach County staff approved that plan Oct. 7 without another vote by county commissioners or a new public hearing before the commission.The approval increases the data center space on that portion of the property from 206,000 square feet to just under 700,000 square feet.The additional data center space uses square footage that had been unassigned under the 2016 approval.Under the newly approved plan, the property would include:Two 288,000-square-foot data center buildingsOne 122,000-square-foot data center building1.2 million square feet of warehouse spaceA utility building and offices occupying the remaining square footageThere is another significant difference between the 2016 plan and the October approval.The latest approval contains conditions governing development of the property. Palm Beach County zoning officials confirmed in July that the original 2016 approval did not include such conditions.Under the newly approved plan, data center buildings cannot be constructed within 850 feet of the property line near Arden.Noise at neighboring homes would be capped between 50 and 60 decibels, depending on the time of day. Sound monitors would run continuously, with the county receiving access to the monitoring data.The county's water utility would commit to providing no more than 100,000 gallons of water per day for the entire site.Battery storage would also be required to comply with fire safety requirements.Residents have contacted WPTV and Hoffman questioning how the plan could be approved without another commission vote and saying they believed the county's data center moratorium would prevent further movement on the property.Palm Beach County Zoning Director Wendy Hernandez told Hoffman by phone that the proposal was submitted before the moratorium took effect.Because it was already submitted, Hernandez said, county staff were able to continue reviewing it and ultimately approve it.Hernandez declined an on-camera interview.The Oct. 7 approval is not the only application involving the Project Tango property.According to Hernandez, WPB Logistics, the second owner of part of the property, has submitted its own proposal seeking to increase data center space on its roughly 60-acre portion of the site without approval from the County Commission.That proposal could result in approximately 1.2 million square feet of additional data center space.Unlike the PBA Holdings proposal approved Oct. 7, the WPB Logistics application remains under review.Hoffman also reached out to Ernie Cox, the main project manager for Project Tango, seeking a response to concerns from residents who said they felt the latest approval happened without their knowledge or an opportunity for public input.A member of Cox's staff returned Hoffman's call Tuesday and said the team would respond to the question.Hoffman had not received that response at the time of publication.

entry.article_text: A Vero Beach man accused of restraining a woman in a hotel room and throwing water on her after she tried to leave has been sentenced to nine months in jail. Frank Joseph Lagola pleaded no contest to charges of false imprisonment and battery and was sentenced Thursday, according to court records. Deputies with the Indian River County Sheriff's Office say they were called to Econo Lodge at 950 U.S. Highway 1 in Vero Beach on December 23, 2025, after a witness reported hearing a woman screaming for help. The witness told deputies she saw a man restraining a woman in the hotel doorway, preventing her from leaving. See also: Fort Pierce flasher? String of indecent exposure reports on bridge leads to arrest When deputies arrived, they found Lagola and the victim, who was visibly wet and shaken. Coppeto told deputies she had been staying at the hotel for about a week and wanted to leave the room. She alleged Lagola became increasingly agitated, threw "holy" water on her, and physically restrained her, telling her she wasn't going anywhere. According to the affidavit, Coppeto said Lagola pinned her down and struck her on the top of her head. She also told deputies she screamed for help because she did not have a cellphone and could not physically get away from him. Lagola told deputies he believed Coppeto was possessed by the devil after she began speaking in Latin. He said he was trying to perform an exorcism and admitted holding her down while reading Bible passages, according to the affidavit. Investigators also spoke with a witness who said she heard a woman yelling, Stop, Rape, Help Me, before seeing the man appear to drag the woman back into the room. Lagola was arrested on charges of false imprisonment and battery and was held in St. Lucie County Jail until his sentencing and was given 297 days time served.
