entry.title: Sheriff witnesses execution of man convicted in 1986 killing of Indian River County deputy - WPBF
entry.summary: Sheriff witnesses execution of man convicted in 1986 killing of Indian River County deputy    WPBF
entry.article_text: Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers witnessed the execution of William Reaves, who was convicted of killing Deputy Richard Raczkowski in 1986, at Florida State Prison on Tuesday night. Flowers said he positioned himself in the front row to ensure Reaves could see his sheriff’s office uniform. "I was in the front row; I was on the side of the room that he could see, so he saw my uniform, and I’m glad that he saw that," Flowers said. Reaves was convicted of killing Raczkowski at a convenience store near Vero Beach in 1986. Following the crime, Reaves was quickly arrested and sentenced to death. The case went through a retrial and several appeals, but the death sentence remained unchanged. "We will never forget Richard; we will never forget his sacrifice," Flowers said. Flowers described the execution process, which lasted about 12 minutes, and noted that Reaves did not make a final statement. "The real kicker on top of it was that he didn’t say anything; he didn’t make a last statement; he didn’t say anything to the family, ask God for forgiveness," Flowers said. Reaves’ last meal consisted of crackers and juice. Flowers said this was the first execution he had ever witnessed. "It’s closure but not justice; that chapter of the book is closed, but that man killed him in cold blood," Flowers said. Flowers also said his office will unveil a monument next month to honor its two fallen deputies.

entry.title: Man convicted of killing Indian River County deputy in 1986 executed tonight - WPEC
entry.summary: Man convicted of killing Indian River County deputy in 1986 executed tonight    WPEC
entry.article_text: Florida carried out the execution of William Reaves at 6 p.m. Tuesday, 40 years after Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkoski was shot and killed outside a convenience store near Vero Beach. Reaves, 77, died by lethal injection at Florida State Prison with an official time of death of 6:12 p.m. Supreme Court denied his final appeal Tuesday, after the Florida Supreme Court rejected his last state appeals on Oct. The Florida Department of Corrections says Reaves had 5 visitors. His brother, sister, nephew, friend, and spiritual advisor all visited Reaves Tuesday. A spokesperson with the department said his final meal was crackers and juice. William Reaves Execution Jack Wu's Reporter Notebook Before the execution 5:45 p.m. Notes say 29 people in the room, including 16 spectators: 8 men and 8 women. Sheriff Eric Flowers and Kevin Delisle are listed. The room is white, with no windows. A large viewing window takes up most of one wall. The room is quiet, with muffled talking heard on the other side of the glass. The door to the execution chamber is the same color as the wall, with covered glass and a tan border. Reaves is lying face-up, with his feet toward the witnesses. Three men in suits are in the room; one is on the phone. A spectator in the second row puts his hand on his wife’s shoulder. The man on the phone hangs up. Asked for any final words, Reaves says, No, I do not. Notes describe heavy breathing, his mouth opening and multiple IVs in his left arm. He is bound by brown leather straps. A man in a white shirt says "Reaves, Reaves" while shaking his shoulder. A man in the room is taking notes. (The note doesn’t specify further.) 6:11 p.m. A doctor walks in, puts a hand on Reaves’ face and shines a flashlight in his eyes. The doctor checks Reaves’ heart with a stethoscope. Notes say his face is blocked from view for 10 to 20 seconds. The doctor leaves; the man with the phone makes a call. Reaves is pronounced dead, and the curtain drops. According to court records, Raczkoski was called to the store around 3 a.m. 23, 1986, to help Reaves get a cab. A gun fell from Reaves’ shorts and the two struggled over it. Records say Reaves shot the deputy in the back four times as he turned away. His son was born after his death. Reaves was arrested two days later in Albany, Georgia. In a taped interview with Indian River County detectives, he admitted to the shooting and said he had been using cocaine. I’ve never met a finer officer in my life, he told them, according to a transcript filed by the state. Reaves was convicted in 1987, but the Florida Supreme Court threw out that verdict in 1991 because one of the prosecutors had previously represented him. A second jury convicted him in 1992 and voted 10-2 to recommend death. DeSantis signed his death warrant Sept. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers, who pushed the governor to sign the warrant, plans to witness the execution. He told CBS12 News on Monday that his goal is that the last thing that he sees is an Indian River County Sheriff’s Office uniform, knowing that justice finally came. Flowers said Raczkoski’s brother is expected to be among the witnesses. Flowers said the brother told him Christmas was never the same for our family after Richard was killed. See also: 124 cats, some deceased, surrendered in disturbing Port St. Lucie hoarding case Reaves’ attorneys fought the execution to the end. In court filings, they argued he is a Vietnam veteran rated 100% disabled for post-traumatic stress disorder by the Department of Veterans Affairs, and that the jury that sentenced him never heard the details of his combat service. They also argued he was shut out of the clemency process. The governor denied clemency the same day he signed the death warrant. The Department of Corrections is expected to hold a briefing after the execution. CBS12 News is at Florida State Prison and will update this story.

entry.title: 23 kids meet their idol Messi thanks to Inter Miami and Make-A-Wish
entry.summary: Tuesday was a day to remember for several youngsters who had the chance to meet their sports idols thanks to Make-A-Wish. I was so happy I started crying; its just an amazing experince, said Yulissa Morales Melendrez, a Make-A-Wish participant. Several kids from around the country had the opportunity to meet the defending MLS Champs, Inter Miami, a moment Make-A-Wish participant Jimmy Hoover could only dream of. I was super excited. I was a little in shock. I didnt really know what to do; it was kind of all surreal to me, Hoover said. Hoover said he's been playing soccer since he was just 7 years old. I started playing and started watching Messi, and he became my favorite player right away, said Hoover. On Tuesday afternoon, Hoover sat in the stands at Nu Stadium, watching his idol, Lionel Messi, and Inter Miami train. It was a simple moment, yes, but a moment that nearly didnt happen. I was going in (to the hospital) for a couple of months, and they were telling me it was just a stomach ache, said Hoover. entry.title: Martin County woman honored after using CPR to save 3-year-old girl from swimming pool - WPTV
entry.summary: Martin County woman honored after using CPR to save 3-year-old girl from swimming pool    WPTV
entry.article_text: A 20-year-old Martin County woman is being honored after she used CPR to help save a 3-year-old girl she found motionless at the bottom of a swimming pool. Nearly two months after the August rescue, Martin County Fire Rescue recognized Madison Isler with the department's Heroic Heart Award.WATCH: Martin County woman honored for saving 3-year-oldThe rescue happened Aug. 23 as Isler walked past the pool at her apartment complex. She told WPTV something in the water caught her attention."It kind of looked like a smudge in your sunglasses," Isler said. "And then, so I took my glasses off, and I looked, and then I realized that it was a little girl."That little girl was 3-year-old Luna.Isler said Luna was motionless at the bottom of the swimming pool when she spotted her."I jumped in and grabbed her and pulled her out, and she was blue," Isler said.Isler called for her boyfriend to contact 911 and began CPR, using skills she said she learned at a young age from her parents, who both work in fire rescue."You just don't really think; you just kind of do, especially in a situation when it's a little baby," Isler said. "I pulled a lifeless baby out of a pool."A family friend who is a pediatric intensive care unit nurse heard the commotion and joined the rescue effort, according to the account shared by Martin County Fire Rescue."Together, they continued their life-saving efforts till finally Luna responded," Martin County Fire Rescue Chief Chad Cianciulli said.Fire rescue officials said Luna was alert and oriented by the time paramedics transported her to the hospital.Luna's mother, Christine Hernandez, said she is grateful Isler happened to be nearby when her daughter needed help."It's God's work that He put her when we needed her, like at the right place at the right time," Hernandez said.Nearly two months after that frightening day, Isler and Luna reunited at Martin County Fire Rescue headquarters.This time, they were together to celebrate the outcome of the rescue.Martin County Fire Rescue presented Isler with its Heroic Heart Award to recognize her actions."Today, on behalf of Martin County Fire Rescue and our entire community, we honor Madison for her courage to act with Martin County Fire Rescue's Heroic Heart Award," Cianciulli said during the recognition.According to the department, Isler is the first person to receive its Heroic Heart Award.For Isler, however, the recognition is secondary to seeing Luna alive and able to grow up."What means the most to me is that Luna's here with us today and that she gets to grow up and experience life," Isler said.Isler affectionately calls Luna her "unicorn baby."For Hernandez, the outcome comes with overwhelming gratitude."I'm just very, very thankful, very thankful for Maddie and her family," Hernandez said.For Isler, a skill learned years before an emergency ever happened became critical in the moment Luna needed help, turning CPR training into an action Martin County Fire Rescue says helped save a child's life.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

The truck fire was reported just before 8 a.m. in the southbound lanes near mile marker 161, approximately nine miles south of the Okeechobee Road/State Road 70 exit. Officials initially closed all southbound lanes while crews worked to extinguish the blaze. One lane later reopened before a separate crash in the same area led to another closure. As of the latest update, all southbound lanes have reopened and traffic is beginning to move through the area. However, motorists may continue to experience residual delays as congestion clears. It’s unclear what caused the truck fire or whether anyone was injured in either incident. WFLX has reached out to the Florida Highway Patrol for additional information. This story will be updated if more information becomes available.

entry.title: Man convicted of killing Indian River County deputy in 1986 executed tonight - WPEC
entry.summary: Man convicted of killing Indian River County deputy in 1986 executed tonight    WPEC
entry.article_text: Florida carried out the execution of William Reaves at 6 p.m. Tuesday, 40 years after Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkoski was shot and killed outside a convenience store near Vero Beach. Reaves, 77, died by lethal injection at Florida State Prison with an official time of death of 6:12 p.m. Supreme Court denied his final appeal Tuesday, after the Florida Supreme Court rejected his last state appeals on Oct. The Florida Department of Corrections says Reaves had 5 visitors. His brother, sister, nephew, friend, and spiritual advisor all visited Reaves Tuesday. A spokesperson with the department said his final meal was crackers and juice. William Reaves Execution Jack Wu's Reporter Notebook Before the execution 5:45 p.m. Notes say 29 people in the room, including 16 spectators: 8 men and 8 women. Sheriff Eric Flowers and Kevin Delisle are listed. The room is white, with no windows. A large viewing window takes up most of one wall. The room is quiet, with muffled talking heard on the other side of the glass. The door to the execution chamber is the same color as the wall, with covered glass and a tan border. Reaves is lying face-up, with his feet toward the witnesses. Three men in suits are in the room; one is on the phone. A spectator in the second row puts his hand on his wife’s shoulder. The man on the phone hangs up. Asked for any final words, Reaves says, No, I do not. Notes describe heavy breathing, his mouth opening and multiple IVs in his left arm. He is bound by brown leather straps. A man in a white shirt says "Reaves, Reaves" while shaking his shoulder. A man in the room is taking notes. (The note doesn’t specify further.) 6:11 p.m. A doctor walks in, puts a hand on Reaves’ face and shines a flashlight in his eyes. The doctor checks Reaves’ heart with a stethoscope. Notes say his face is blocked from view for 10 to 20 seconds. The doctor leaves; the man with the phone makes a call. Reaves is pronounced dead, and the curtain drops. According to court records, Raczkoski was called to the store around 3 a.m. 23, 1986, to help Reaves get a cab. A gun fell from Reaves’ shorts and the two struggled over it. Records say Reaves shot the deputy in the back four times as he turned away. His son was born after his death. Reaves was arrested two days later in Albany, Georgia. In a taped interview with Indian River County detectives, he admitted to the shooting and said he had been using cocaine. I’ve never met a finer officer in my life, he told them, according to a transcript filed by the state. Reaves was convicted in 1987, but the Florida Supreme Court threw out that verdict in 1991 because one of the prosecutors had previously represented him. A second jury convicted him in 1992 and voted 10-2 to recommend death. DeSantis signed his death warrant Sept. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers, who pushed the governor to sign the warrant, plans to witness the execution. entry.title: Sheriff witnesses execution of man convicted in 1986 killing of Indian River County deputy - WPBF
entry.summary: Sheriff witnesses execution of man convicted in 1986 killing of Indian River County deputy    WPBF
entry.article_text: Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers witnessed the execution of William Reaves, who was convicted of killing Deputy Richard Raczkowski in 1986, at Florida State Prison on Tuesday night. Flowers said he positioned himself in the front row to ensure Reaves could see his sheriff’s office uniform. "I was in the front row; I was on the side of the room that he could see, so he saw my uniform, and I’m glad that he saw that," Flowers said. Reaves was convicted of killing Raczkowski at a convenience store near Vero Beach in 1986. Following the crime, Reaves was quickly arrested and sentenced to death. The case went through a retrial and several appeals, but the death sentence remained unchanged. "We will never forget Richard; we will never forget his sacrifice," Flowers said. Flowers described the execution process, which lasted about 12 minutes, and noted that Reaves did not make a final statement. "The real kicker on top of it was that he didn’t say anything; he didn’t make a last statement; he didn’t say anything to the family, ask God for forgiveness," Flowers said. Reaves’ last meal consisted of crackers and juice. Flowers said this was the first execution he had ever witnessed. "It’s closure but not justice; that chapter of the book is closed, but that man killed him in cold blood," Flowers said. Flowers also said his office will unveil a monument next month to honor its two fallen deputies. entry.article_text: A Vero Beach man accused of restraining a woman in a hotel room and throwing water on her after she tried to leave has been sentenced to nine months in jail. Frank Joseph Lagola pleaded no contest to charges of false imprisonment and battery and was sentenced Thursday, according to court records. Deputies with the Indian River County Sheriff's Office say they were called to Econo Lodge at 950 U.S. Highway 1 in Vero Beach on December 23, 2025, after a witness reported hearing a woman screaming for help. The witness told deputies she saw a man restraining a woman in the hotel doorway, preventing her from leaving. See also: Fort Pierce flasher? String of indecent exposure reports on bridge leads to arrest When deputies arrived, they found Lagola and the victim, who was visibly wet and shaken. Coppeto told deputies she had been staying at the hotel for about a week and wanted to leave the room. She alleged Lagola became increasingly agitated, threw "holy" water on her, and physically restrained her, telling her she wasn't going anywhere. According to the affidavit, Coppeto said Lagola pinned her down and struck her on the top of her head. She also told deputies she screamed for help because she did not have a cellphone and could not physically get away from him. Lagola told deputies he believed Coppeto was possessed by the devil after she began speaking in Latin. He said he was trying to perform an exorcism and admitted holding her down while reading Bible passages, according to the affidavit. Investigators also spoke with a witness who said she heard a woman yelling, Stop, Rape, Help Me, before seeing the man appear to drag the woman back into the room. Lagola was arrested on charges of false imprisonment and battery and was held in St. Lucie County Jail until his sentencing and was given 297 days time served.

entry.title: More than 120 cats, kittens found in Port St. Lucie home in alleged hoarding situation
entry.summary: WPTV is learning more about another animal hoarding situation on the Treasure Coast. Port St. Lucie police said more than 124 cats and kittens were found in a home off the 2500 block of Warwick Street. WATCH BELOW: More than 120 cats found in Port St. Lucie home 124 cats recovered from animal hoarding situation in Port St Lucie Investigators said they found the home in unsanitary conditions, including an accumulation of feces and dead kittens. Police said two of the three people living inside the home where the cats were found were issued citations for hoarding and failure to provide medical attention. Sarah Wees, executive director of The Humane Society of St. Lucie County, said they were brought in 106 cats and kittens. 'They likely had to fight for food, which is why some of them are underweight, and some of the kittens that are nursing, they might be nursing on the wrong mother,' Wees said. 'If they got them spayed or neutered, we wouldn't be where we are right now.' Wees said almost all of the cats had fleas and ear mites, and some with open sores needed immediate medical treatment. Now, Wees said staff and volunteers are scrambling to get them well. 'They're feeding them, they're cleaning them, they're doing medical intakes,' Wees said. Taylor Nickelson with the American Humane Society said the cats and kittens are getting better fast. 'We're seeing that in just their liveliness and eagerness to approach us and take food,' Nickelson said.  However, Wees said some of the cats and kittens are still in a dangerous situation and being treated in their sick room. 'They're responding well, but it's still an unknown situation,' Wees said. 'Any of them can fade at any time, so it's very dangerous at this time.' Wees said this situation has doubled their cat population. 'It overwhelms the staff,' Wees said. 'It overwhelms our resources.' Staff are asking for donations, volunteers and fosters during these recovery efforts. 'These little babies can't do it for themselves,' Wee said. 'So, we and the community need to do it for them.' Once medical needs are met, the cats and kittens will be up for adoption.

Ron DeSantis' aggressive use of the death penalty in his final term.William Reaves, 77, was pronounced dead at 6:12 p.m. following a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison near Starke. He was convicted of first-degree murder in the 1986 shooting death of Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski.WATCH REPORT BELOW:The death chamber curtain went up promptly at the 6 p.m. execution time, and Reaves was already strapped to a gurney with an IV in his arm. Asked if he had any last statement, he replied, "No, I do not."The injection began immediately after that. About 30 seconds later, Reaves took several big breaths and then stopped moving. After a few minutes, the team warden shook Reaves’ shoulders and yelled his name, but there was no response.A medic was called into the chamber a short time later to check for a heartbeat or any other signs of life, and Reaves was pronounced dead about a minute later.Reaves was the eighth Florida prisoner over age 70 put to death this year, highlighting the nation’s aging death-row population as Florida continues to far outpace the rest of country in total executions.Last year, Florida set a state record with 19 executions in a single year and it would tie that mark if another execution is carried out next month as scheduled.DeSantis, who leaves office in January after two terms, has said his goal is to deliver justice to victims’ families who have waited decades for death sentences to be carried out.Raczkowski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store in September 1986, according to court records. Reaves later acknowledged he had placed the call from a payphone outside the store.While Raczkowski and Reaves spoke, a gun fell out of Reaves’ shorts, officials said. The two struggled over the weapon, and Reaves eventually regained control of it. Investigators said the deputy was trying to run away when Reaves shot him four times. The deputy later died from his wounds.Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. But the Florida Supreme Court overturned the conviction because of a conflict of interest with the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. Reaves was convicted again and sentenced to death in 1992, and subsequent appeals were unsuccessful.The U.S. Supreme Court on Tuesday afternoon rejected Reaves’ final appeal without comment.The Florida Supreme Court last week also rejected Reaves’ appeals to spare his life.One issue raised by his attorneys was Florida’s method of execution. All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections.The court has previously upheld this lethal injection protocol against similar challenges. He was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004.

entry.summary: Tuesday was a day to remember for several youngsters who had the chance to meet their sports idols thanks to Make-A-Wish. 'I was so happy I started crying; it's just an amazing experience,' said Yulissa Morales Melendrez, a Make-A-Wish participant. Several kids from around the country had the opportunity to meet the defending MLS Champs, Inter Miami, a moment Make-A-Wish participant Jimmy Hoover could only dream of. 'I was super excited. I was a little in shock. I didn't really know what to do; it was kind of all surreal to me,' Hoover said. Hoover said he's been playing soccer since he was 7 years old. 'I started playing and started watching (Lionel) Messi, and he became my favorite player right away,' said Hoover. On Tuesday afternoon, Hoover sat in the stands at Nu Stadium, watching his idol, Lionel Messi, and Inter Miami train. It was a simple moment, yes, but a moment that nearly didn't happen. 'I was going in (to the hospital) for a couple of months, and they were telling me it was just a stomach ache,' said Hoover. Hoover and his family didn't think much of it until one day at his friend's house. 'My stomach was hurting so bad, I was in agonizing pain,' said Hoover. He rushed to the hospital, where doctors found out he had cancer, so for months he endured chemotherapy, and while he was fighting for his life, he didn't want to let his teammates down, so every day after treatment he'd be with his teammates. 'It was really difficult; I couldn't keep up with everyone; that was the hardest part,' said Hoover. Dedicated to playing soccer and again and again kicking cancer's butt he fought effortlessly, and last July he rang the bell as his cancer went into remission. 'It's been great. I'm still in a little bit of shock from everything,' said Hoover. That shock would soon wear off, and days ago he and his teammates hung out. He got the surprise of a lifetime: he'd be part of the Make-A-Wish Foundation's latest effort to help him and kids from around the world meet Messi and Inter Miami. 'It's super rewarding. entry.article_text: By: Scott Sutton Posted and last updated KISSIMMEE, Fla. — Florida's attorney general announced on Wednesday that a Central Florida mayor has been arrested. Attorney General James Uthmeier posted on X that Kissimmee Mayor Jackie Espinosa faces a charge of grand theft and organized scheme to defraud. Uthmeier said he hold a news conference at 2 p.m. in Orlando with CFO Blaise Ingoglia and Florida Department of Law Enforcement Commissioner Larry Keefe to provide more information. The city's website said that Espinosa has served as the city's mayor since November 2024. This morning, we arrested Kissimmee mayor Jackie Espinosa and are charging her with Grand Theft and Organized Scheme to Defraud. entry.summary: With controls in hand and drones in the air, students at Palm Beach State College (PBSC) are learning a skill that could lead to new career opportunities. WPTV reporter Christy Waite visited the college's Belle Glade campus, where students were putting those skills into practice as part of PBSC's first drone training class. WATCH BELOW: PBSC students take flight with drone training PBSC launches drone program The 12-week course combines classroom instruction with hands-on flight experience and helps students work toward earning the FAA certification required for most commercial drone operations. Student Marina Medina told Waite she believes the technology has a promising future. 'I heard that the drone industry is taking off, and I think it is taking off,' Medina said. 'It's the future.' The program is about more than simply learning how to control a drone. Instructor Scott Mitchell said the technology has applications across a number of industries, including one especially important to the Glades: agriculture. entry.title: Kamala Harris returns to campaign trail as 2028 speculation grows
entry.summary: Former Vice President Kamala Harris is back on the campaign trail Wednesday, kicking off a multistate push for Democrats. Harris is in Las Vegas, campaigning alongside Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford. Ford is trying to unseat Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo. RELATED STORY | Chants of run again! spur Kamala Harris to consider another White House bid Harris is also scheduled to speak to hundreds of casino and hospitality workers at a Culinary Union event. The trip is just the beginning. Harris heads to Mississippi on Thursday, followed by New Hampshire, Wisconsin and Georgia in the coming days. Harris is widely considered a potential contender for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination. Several polls have shown her leading other potential Democratic candidates, though the field could include several other high-profile Democrats. If Harris runs in 2028, it would mark her third presidential campaign in four election cycles. She lost the 2024 general election to Donald Trump after replacing Joe Biden at the top of the Democratic ticket less than four months before Election Day. Harris has not announced campaign stops in several Senate battleground states, including Ohio and Iowa, both of which she lost to Trump by wide margins in 2024. entry.title: Indian River State College trustees to consider eliminating men's, women's swimming and diving programs
entry.summary: Indian River State College trustees are expected to consider a major restructuring of the college's athletic programs next week that would eliminate men's and women's swimming and diving and move several remaining sports to Division II competition. The recommendations are included on the agenda for the college's Governance Legislative Affairs Committee meeting on Tuesday, Oct. 27, at the Dixon Hendry Campus in Okeechobee. The committee meetings begin at 9:30 a.m., followed by the full District Board of Trustees meeting at 1 p.m. WATCH THE LATEST REPORT BELOW: Indian River State College considers eliminating men's, women's swimming and diving programs Under the proposed athletic restructuring plan, both the men's and women's swimming and diving programs would be eliminated beginning with the fall 2027-28 academic year. The proposal would also transition baseball, softball and men's basketball to Division II competition beginning that same academic year. Volleyball already competes at the Division 2 level, according to the agenda. College administrators would also be directed to evaluate whether the women's basketball program could be reinstated for the 2028-29 season. The agenda says that possibility would depend on the availability of resources. The recommendations come from the college president and cabinet and are scheduled to be presented to the Governance Legislative Affairs Committee for approval. entry.title: El-Sayed, Rogers set to debate in closely watched Michigan Senate race
entry.summary: Less than two weeks before what could be a pivotal U.S. Senate race, Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed will debate Wednesday, with polling showing a deadlocked contest. El-Sayed is vying to become the first Muslim American elected to the U.S. Senate. Rogers is hoping to become the first Republican to represent Michigan in the Senate since Spencer Abraham, who lost his reelection bid in 2000. Democrats have won nine consecutive U.S. Senate races in Michigan. Although Democrats have maintained control of both of Michigans U.S. Senate seats, the state is considered a key battleground. President Donald Trump has won Michigan twice, demonstrating Republicans can compete statewide. Wednesdays debate begins at 7 p.m. ET. Scripps News will air a preview beginning at 6:30 p.m. The debate will also air live on Scripps News Groups Michigan stations, WXYZ in Detroit and WXMI in Grand Rapids. The debate will be moderated by Scripps News Group Detroit Editorial Director Chuck Stokes, along with Detroit-based anchors Carolyn Clifford and Alicia Smith. A Marist poll released Wednesday showed El-Sayed leading Rogers 50% to 48%, a difference within the polls margin of error. The poll also found both candidates had high unfavorable ratings. Forty-eight percent of likely voters viewed El-Sayed unfavorably, while 52% had an unfavorable view of Rogers. RELATED STORY | Abdul El-Sayed emphasizes Muslim faith after Trump calls him a jihadist The poll also indicated many Michigan families are struggling more financially than they were a year ago. Forty-three percent of likely voters said they were worse off financially, compared with 16% who said they were better off. El-Sayeds faith has come under attack during his campaign to become the countrys first Muslim U.S. senator. Republicans have sought to portray the Democratic nominee as sympathetic to interests connected to Islamic terrorism. Last week, Trump referred to El-Sayed as Mohammed and falsely called the former public health official a jihadist. Over the weekend, El-Sayed denounced the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamic political movement founded in Egypt in 1928. RELATED STORY | Democrats fear slippage with Black voters makes Michigan Senate race feel far closer than it should Meanwhile, El-Sayed has sought to tie Rogers to many of Trumps policies, including tariffs and the war in Iran. Rogers, a former member of the U.S. House, has at times sought to distance himself from some of Trumps more divisive policies.

entry.title: Sheriff witnesses execution of man convicted in 1986 killing of Indian River County deputy - WPBF
entry.summary: Sheriff witnesses execution of man convicted in 1986 killing of Indian River County deputy    WPBF
entry.article_text: Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers witnessed the execution of William Reaves, who was convicted of killing Deputy Richard Raczkowski in 1986, at Florida State Prison on Tuesday night. Flowers said he positioned himself in the front row to ensure Reaves could see his sheriff’s office uniform. "I was in the front row; I was on the side of the room that he could see, so he saw my uniform, and I’m glad that he saw that," Flowers said. Reaves was convicted of killing Raczkowski at a convenience store near Vero Beach in 1986. Following the crime, Reaves was quickly arrested and sentenced to death. The case went through a retrial and several appeals, but the death sentence remained unchanged. "We will never forget Richard; we will never forget his sacrifice," Flowers said. Flowers described the execution process, which lasted about 12 minutes, and noted that Reaves did not make a final statement. "The real kicker on top of it was that he didn’t say anything; he didn’t make a last statement; he didn’t say anything to the family, ask God for forgiveness," Flowers said. Reaves’ last meal consisted of crackers and juice. Flowers said this was the first execution he had ever witnessed. "It’s closure but not justice; that chapter of the book is closed, but that man killed him in cold blood," Flowers said. Flowers also said his office will unveil a monument next month to honor its two fallen deputies. entry.summary: Man convicted of killing Indian River County deputy in 1986 executed    WPEC
entry.article_text: Florida carried out the execution of William Reaves at 6 p.m. Tuesday, 40 years after Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkoski was shot and killed outside a convenience store near Vero Beach. Reaves, 77, died by lethal injection at Florida State Prison with an official time of death of 6:12 p.m. Supreme Court denied his final appeal Tuesday, after the Florida Supreme Court rejected his last state appeals on Oct. The Florida Department of Corrections says Reaves had 5 visitors. His brother, sister, nephew, friend, and spiritual advisor all visited Reaves Tuesday. A spokesperson with the department said his final meal was crackers and juice. William Reaves Execution Jack Wu's Reporter Notebook Before the execution 5:45 p.m. Notes say 29 people in the room, including 16 spectators: 8 men and 8 women. Sheriff Eric Flowers and Kevin Delisle are listed. The room is white, with no windows. A large viewing window takes up most of one wall. The room is quiet, with muffled talking heard on the other side of the glass. The door to the execution chamber is the same color as the wall, with covered glass and a tan border. Reaves is lying face-up, with his feet toward the witnesses. Three men in suits are in the room; one is on the phone. A spectator in the second row puts his hand on his wife’s shoulder. The man on the phone hangs up. Asked for any final words, Reaves says, No, I do not. Notes describe heavy breathing, his mouth opening and multiple IVs in his left arm. He is bound by brown leather straps. A man in a white shirt says "Reaves, Reaves" while shaking his shoulder. A man in the room is taking notes. (The note doesn’t specify further.) 6:11 p.m. A doctor walks in, puts a hand on Reaves’ face and shines a flashlight in his eyes. The doctor checks Reaves’ heart with a stethoscope. Notes say his face is blocked from view for 10 to 20 seconds. The doctor leaves; the man with the phone makes a call. Reaves is pronounced dead, and the curtain drops. According to court records, Raczkoski was called to the store around 3 a.m. 23, 1986, to help Reaves get a cab. A gun fell from Reaves’ shorts and the two struggled over it. Records say Reaves shot the deputy in the back four times as he turned away. His son was born after his death. Reaves was arrested two days later in Albany, Georgia. In a taped interview with Indian River County detectives, he admitted to the shooting and said he had been using cocaine. I’ve never met a finer officer in my life, he told them, according to a transcript filed by the state. Reaves was convicted in 1987, but the Florida Supreme Court threw out that verdict in 1991 because one of the prosecutors had previously represented him. A second jury convicted him in 1992 and voted 10-2 to recommend death. DeSantis signed his death warrant Sept. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers, who pushed the governor to sign the warrant, plans to witness the execution. He told CBS12 News on Monday that his goal is that the last thing that he sees is an Indian River County Sheriff’s Office uniform, knowing that justice finally came. Flowers said Raczkoski’s brother is expected to be among the witnesses. Flowers said the brother told him Christmas was never the same for our family after Richard was killed. See also: 124 cats, some deceased, surrendered in disturbing Port St. Lucie hoarding case Reaves’ attorneys fought the execution to the end. In court filings, they argued he is a Vietnam veteran rated 100% disabled for post-traumatic stress disorder by the Department of Veterans Affairs, and that the jury that sentenced him never heard the details of his combat service. They also argued he was shut out of the clemency process. The governor denied clemency the same day he signed the death warrant. The Department of Corrections is expected to hold a briefing after the execution. CBS12 News is at Florida State Prison and will update this story.

After a few minutes, the team warden shook Reaves’ shoulders and yelled his name, but there was no response.A medic was called into the chamber a short time later to check for a heartbeat or any other signs of life, and Reaves was pronounced dead about a minute later.Reaves was the eighth Florida prisoner over age 70 put to death this year, highlighting the nation’s aging death-row population as Florida continues to far outpace the rest of country in total executions.Last year, Florida set a state record with 19 executions in a single year and it would tie that mark if another execution is carried out next month as scheduled.DeSantis, who leaves office in January after two terms, has said his goal is to deliver justice to victims’ families who have waited decades for death sentences to be carried out.Raczkowski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store in September 1986, according to court records. Reaves later acknowledged he had placed the call from a payphone outside the store.While Raczkowski and Reaves spoke, a gun fell out of Reaves’ shorts, officials said. The two struggled over the weapon, and Reaves eventually regained control of it. Investigators said the deputy was trying to run away when Reaves shot him four times. The deputy later died from his wounds.Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. But the Florida Supreme Court overturned the conviction because of a conflict of interest with the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. Reaves was convicted again and sentenced to death in 1992, and subsequent appeals were unsuccessful.The U.S. Supreme Court on Tuesday afternoon rejected Reaves’ final appeal without comment.The Florida Supreme Court last week also rejected Reaves’ appeals to spare his life.One issue raised by his attorneys was Florida’s method of execution. All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections.The court has previously upheld this lethal injection protocol against similar challenges. It differs from the single-drug injection used by states such as Tennessee, where death row inmate Christa Pike was rushed to the hospital last month after surviving two lethal doses of pentobarbital.Defense attorneys also argued that the jurors who recommended the death penalty for Reaves were never told that the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs rated Reaves — an Army veteran — as 100% disabled by post-traumatic stress disorder, which was caused by his service in the Vietnam War. More than 100 veterans sent DeSantis a letter Monday urging him to stop the execution.A total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half of the 32 total executions in the U.S. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so.Jesse Guardado, 64, is next scheduled to die by injection in Florida on Nov. He was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004.

entry.title: Panthers fans make 100-mile trek from Port St. Lucie to cheer on their team - WPTV
entry.summary: Panthers fans make 100-mile trek from Port St. Lucie to cheer on their team    WPTV
entry.article_text: WPTV anchor and Panthers 360 host Mike Trim joined fans on a 100-mile, one-way trip to Amerant Bank Arena with one goal: cheer on the Panthers to a win.The group of six fans, including Maria Charles and Camilo Medina, meet up before their long rides from Port St. Lucie to Sunrise.WATCH BELOW: Port St. Lucie fans go the distance for Panthers"We have a strong following here in St. Lucie County," Medina told Trim.When we talked to these super fans on Thursday, Oct. 15, the Panthers were facing off against the Vancouver Canucks.Leaving Port St. Lucie just before 3:30 p.m., the group hoped to beat rush-hour traffic."And the length of the drive doesn't bother you at all?" Trim asked Medina."Not at all, no," Medina replied.The group is not only bonded by the love for the Panthers but also their prior military service. Nearly all in the road-tripping group are veterans.Trim joined Charles for most of the drive.As they departed to make the drive south, Trim asked Charles, "We're leaving Port St. Do you get in the zone while you're driving? What's the drive like?""I listen to music, and when it starts getting a little boring, that's when I put on the Latin music," Charles said.Charles, a Panthers season ticket holder, explained her route."I take the Florida Turnpike, drive all the way down until I hit Sawgrass Expressway and take Sawgrass Expressway to Oakland Park, which is the off-ramp for going to the arena," Charles told Trim."Do you keep a running tab of how many miles you've driven to Florida Panthers games?" Trim asked Charles."I can honestly say, 20 to 25,000 miles since 2023," Charles replied.In two separate vehicles, the Port St. Lucie fans arrived at Amerant Bank Arena about an hour before the puck dropped to start the game."We usually go straight in, order something to eat, and kind of hang out for a while," Medina told Trim.Charles has an arena routine she's had for many seasons."I got to go get my coffee and donuts," Charles told Trim as they headed up the escalator to their section.Medina and the rest of the Port St. Lucie crew sat in Section 305 and brought their fanhood to an exciting finish.In the third period, Brady Tkachuk scored two goals to tie the game 2-2.Then in overtime, Tkachuk scored his third goal, a game-winner, completing his hat trick for the night.Charles summed it up after the game."The Panthers won in overtime. Now it's time for that nice long drive back home. I had a nice large cup of coffee and a guava turnover, so I'm all set and super charged for the drive. Awesome game," Charles said.

entry.summary: Kissimmee Mayor Jackie Espinosa has been arrested on felony charges after state investigators accused her of using her position to improperly obtain money through a city program designed to help businesses recover from the COVID-19 pandemic. entry.article_text: Kissimmee Mayor Jackie Espinosa has been arrested on felony charges after state investigators accused her of using her position to improperly obtain money through a city program designed to help businesses recover from the COVID-19 pandemic.Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced Wednesday that Espinosa faces charges of grand theft and organized scheme to defraud.WATCH BELOW: Florida AG holds news conference on arrestDuring an afternoon news conference in Orlando, Uthmeier said the case involves Kissimmee's Business Boost 2.0 program. According to Uthmeier, Espinosa supported and voted to approve the program before later submitting applications seeking assistance for businesses tied to herself and family members."This was a program to try to help small businesses get back up on their feet after the COVID pandemic," Uthmeier said. "It was not designed to help government officials enrich themselves."Florida Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia said his office discovered what he described as irregularities while auditing COVID-19-related grant programs administered by several local governments.According to Ingoglia, seven businesses at properties owned or managed by Espinosa's family received a combined $90,000 through Kissimmee's Business Boost 2.0 program. He said $50,000 went to Espinosa's family businesses, while another $40,000 went to tenants.Ingoglia said investigators determined that Espinosa submitted grant applications on behalf of her family's businesses.Uthmeier alleged that Espinosa also participated in policy decisions that made it easier to apply for and receive money through the program. He said charging documents and bank records would provide further details about the allegations.Investigators eventually referred the matter to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, the Florida Commission on Ethics and a special prosecutor, according to Ingoglia.Ingoglia said investigators found that people within Espinosa's office had warned her against applying for the grant money."We started realizing that there were people within her own office that said this is not a good idea, you should not do it," Ingoglia said.He also said Espinosa was among the first to submit applications when the grant application period opened.FDLE Commissioner Larry Keefe said his agency worked with investigators from the CFO's office to develop the case before presenting its findings to prosecutors.During Wednesday's news conference, a reporter cited a statement from Espinosa's attorney maintaining her innocence and arguing that there is a fundamental difference between an alleged ethics violation and a criminal offense.Uthmeier responded that prosecutors believe the evidence supports criminal charges, pointing to applications he said Espinosa signed, money she allegedly received and decisions she allegedly made involving the program.The allegations will now be litigated in court. An arrest and criminal charges do not establish guilt, and Espinosa is presumed innocent unless proven guilty.Uthmeier said he had not spoken with Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis since Espinosa's arrest when asked whether the governor could take action concerning her position as mayor.State officials also said they plan to investigate how information about the impending arrest became public before it took place. Uthmeier said advance disclosure of an arrest can create safety risks for law enforcement and potentially cause problems involving evidence.The case comes as Uthmeier's office says it is increasing its focus on public-corruption investigations across Florida.The city's website said that Espinosa has served as mayor since November 2024.

entry.title: St. Lucie County Fire Board to discuss fire chief’s potential retirement after union vote - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County Fire Board to discuss fire chief’s potential retirement after union vote    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire District Board will discuss the future of Fire Chief Jeff Lee on Wednesday afternoon, about two weeks after the district’s firefighters union released the results of a no-confidence vote on its top leaders. The agenda for the board’s 3 p.m. regular meeting includes an item listed under Chair Shannon Martin titled Discussion Regarding Potential Retirement and Leadership Transition. The agenda does not say whose retirement will be discussed, and no supporting documents for the item have been made public. The Professional Fire Fighters and Paramedics of St. Lucie County, IAFF Local 1377, released its vote results Oct. According to the union, 423 of its 517 dues-paying members took part. Lee received 314 votes of no confidence and 108 votes of confidence. Assistant Fire Chief Brian Gonzalez received 390 votes of no confidence, and District Attorney Kim Sabol received 413. Under the rules the union set before the vote, at least 75% of participating members had to vote no confidence before the union would formally present the result to the Fire Board. Gonzalez and Sabol both passed that mark. The union said 74.23% of members voted no confidence in him. Local 1377 calls upon the Board to carefully consider these results and fulfill its responsibility to the employees who serve this county and to the public they have sworn to protect, the union said in its release. Since then, the district has reassigned Gonzalez from assistant chief to a battalion chief training role. The district said Gonzalez and Lee agreed to the move and that it had been discussed before the recent events. Sabol gave the district 90 days’ notice on Sept. 30 and is set to retire Dec. Wednesday’s agenda also includes the selection of a law firm and a new district attorney. See also: Former PBSO dispatcher sentenced after 2023 head-on DUI crash that killed mother The vote followed months of fallout from a hazing investigation. In July, the district f ired three veteran firefighters , Jordon Hutchinson, Christopher Baldwin and Douglas Boudrias, and suspended two others. Videos showed newer firefighters being shocked with a modified bug zapper . An outside investigation hired by the district concluded the conduct was hazing. The firefighters and their union say it was consensual horseplay, and a Fort Pierce Police report found no criminal matter. The union is pursuing arbitration to get the three firefighters reinstated. Board members have said the district has no policy for handling complaints against its top contracted employees, including the fire chief. They can’t investigate themselves. That’s not proper, board member and County Commissioner Jamie Fowler said at an Oct. 6, Lee withdrew a settlement offer that would have brought the three firefighters back with retroactive pay, citing guidance from counsel and the district’s insurance representatives. CBS12 News has also obtained a 2022 recording in which Lee, Gonzalez and Sabol declined to investigate a female firefighter’s complaint of unwanted touching by a coworker. Lee has said the problem is not one he can solve himself. The board has to fix that problem, Lee said at an Aug. County Commissioner James Clasby, who also sits on the fire board, has publicly called on Lee to resign. In August, a motion to suspend Lee and Sabol failed 2 to 4. In a statement after the vote, the district said it recognizes the results and will take appropriate action. It pointed to pay increases, about 100 additional uniformed personnel and three-person engine staffing during Lee’s tenure. Lee joined the district in 1997 after serving in the U.S. He became its 14th fire chief in May 2023. This is not the first time the board has faced this choice. In 2017, after a union no-confidence vote, the board accepted then Chief Buddy Emerson’s retirement effective immediately and paid him severance through the end of his contract. CBS12 News will be at Wednesday’s meeting and will update this story.

entry.summary: All lanes reopen on Florida's Turnpike after truck fire, crash in St. Lucie County    WFLX
entry.article_text: All lanes of Florida’s Turnpike have reopened in St. Lucie County after a truck fire and a separate crash caused major delays Tuesday morning. The truck fire was reported just before 8 a.m. in the southbound lanes near mile marker 161, approximately nine miles south of the Okeechobee Road/State Road 70 exit. Officials initially closed all southbound lanes while crews worked to extinguish the blaze. One lane later reopened before a separate crash in the same area led to another closure. As of the latest update, all southbound lanes have reopened and traffic is beginning to move through the area. However, motorists may continue to experience residual delays as congestion clears. It’s unclear what caused the truck fire or whether anyone was injured in either incident. WFLX has reached out to the Florida Highway Patrol for additional information. This story will be updated if more information becomes available.

entry.title: El-Sayed, Rogers set to debate in closely watched Michigan Senate race
entry.summary: Less than two weeks before what could be a pivotal U.S. Senate race, Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed will debate Wednesday, with polling showing a deadlocked contest. El-Sayed is vying to become the first Muslim American elected to the U.S. Senate. Rogers is hoping to become the first Republican to represent Michigan in the Senate since Spencer Abraham, who lost his reelection bid in 2000. Democrats have won nine consecutive U.S. Senate races in Michigan. WATCH | Talking to voters ahead of Michigan's closely-watched Senate midterm showdown Talking to voters ahead of Michigan's closely-watched Senate midterm showdown Although Democrats have maintained control of both of Michigans U.S. Senate seats, the state is considered a key battleground. President Donald Trump has won Michigan twice, demonstrating Republicans can compete statewide. Wednesdays debate begins at 7 p.m. ET. Scripps News will air a preview beginning at 6:30 p.m. The debate will also air live on Scripps News Groups Michigan stations, WXYZ in Detroit and WXMI in Grand Rapids. The debate will be moderated by Scripps News Group Detroit Editorial Director Chuck Stokes, along with Detroit-based anchors Carolyn Clifford and Alicia Smith. A Marist poll released Wednesday showed El-Sayed leading Rogers 50% to 48%, a difference within the polls margin of error. The poll also found both candidates had high unfavorable ratings. Forty-eight percent of likely voters viewed El-Sayed unfavorably, while 52% had an unfavorable view of Rogers. RELATED STORY | Abdul El-Sayed emphasizes Muslim faith after Trump calls him a jihadist The poll also indicated many Michigan families are struggling more financially than they were a year ago. entry.title: William Reaves: Man convicted of killing Indian River County deputy in 1986 scheduled to be executed Tuesday - WFLX
entry.summary: William Reaves: Man convicted of killing Indian River County deputy in 1986 scheduled to be executed Tuesday    WFLX
entry.article_text: Florida is set Tuesday to carry out its 18th execution of the year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis’ aggressive use of the death penalty in his final term. William Reaves , 77, was sentenced to death after being convicted of first-degree murder for the 1986 shooting of Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski. He would become Florida’s eighth prisoner over the age of 70 to be executed this year, which has highlighted the nation’s aging death-row population and underscored how Florida has outpaced the rest of the country in executions. Reaves was set to receive a three-drug injection starting at 6 p.m. at Florida State Prison near Starke. Last year, Florida set a state record with 19 executions in a single year. Another execution is scheduled for November, which would tie that mark if both are carried out as planned. DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said previously that his goal is to bring justice to victims’ families who have waited decades for the death sentences to be carried out. According to court records, Raczkowski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store in September 1986. Reaves acknowledged that he had placed the call at a payphone outside the store. While Raczkowski and Reaves spoke, a gun fell out of Reaves’ shorts, officials said. The men struggled over the firearm, and Reaves eventually regained control over it. Investigators said the deputy attempted to run away before Reaves shot him four times. The deputy later died from his wounds. Reaves was initially convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. The Florida Supreme Court reversed the conviction because of a conflict of interest with the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death a second time in 1992, and subsequent appeals have been unsuccessful. The Florida Supreme Court rejected Reaves’ final appeals last week. One issue raised by his attorneys was Florida’s method of execution. All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections. The court has previously upheld this lethal injection protocol against similar challenges. It differs from the single-drug injection used by states like Tennessee, where death row inmate Christa Pike was rushed to the hospital last month after surviving two lethal doses of pentobarbital. Defense attorneys also argued that the jurors who recommended the death penalty for Reaves were never told that the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs rated Reaves, an Army veteran, as 100% disabled by post-traumatic stress disorder, which was caused by his service in the Vietnam War. More than 100 veterans sent DeSantis a letter on Monday asking him to stop the execution. Final appeals for Reaves were still pending before the U.S. A total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half of the 31 total executions in the U.S. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so. Jesse Guardado, 64, is next scheduled to die by injection in Florida on Nov. He was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004.

entry.article_text: All lanes of Florida’s Turnpike have reopened in St. Lucie County after a truck fire and a separate crash caused major delays Tuesday morning. The truck fire was reported just before 8 a.m. in the southbound lanes near mile marker 161, approximately nine miles south of the Okeechobee Road/State Road 70 exit. Officials initially closed all southbound lanes while crews worked to extinguish the blaze. One lane later reopened before a separate crash in the same area led to another closure. As of the latest update, all southbound lanes have reopened and traffic is beginning to move through the area. However, motorists may continue to experience residual delays as congestion clears. It’s unclear what caused the truck fire or whether anyone was injured in either incident. WFLX has reached out to the Florida Highway Patrol for additional information. This story will be updated if more information becomes available.

entry.article_text: North Palm Beach County Airport could see some of its biggest changes in decades as county leaders explore proposals to help accommodate future growth. A proposal that could bring new aviation facilities, runway improvements and emerging air mobility technology to the airport is now headed to a competitive bidding process after a lengthy debate among Palm Beach County commissioners.WATCH BELOW: Major changes considered for North County AirportThe discussion focused on a proposal from Jet Greene LLC, owned by developer Jeff Greene, to purchase 131 acres of county-owned land near the airport, develop a second private aviation facility and help fund future airport improvements. But instead of moving forward exclusively with that proposal, commissioners unanimously voted to open the opportunity to other developers and aviation companies."What Jet Green has brought to the table is a starting point," Commissioner Maria Marino said.North County Airport, also known as F45, has been the subject of improvement discussions for years. The latest proposal called for a second private jet facility featuring hangars, fueling facilities, lounges and other aviation services while also supporting efforts to expand airport operations.The proposal quickly attracted interest from other aviation companies."We just don't want the plane to take off without us," said Stephen Abrams of Ellison Partners, speaking on behalf of Sky Harbour.Sky Harbour is one of several companies that appeared before commissioners expressing interest in competing for future development opportunities at the airport.One of those voices came from LuftCar, a company focused on advanced air mobility and infrastructure for electric aircraft capable of vertical takeoff and landing."Yeah, we're welcoming a wide variety of proposals," said Taniel Koushakjian, a representative working with LuftCar.They're in favor of the county starting a search for proposals. Unlike developers pursuing traditional aviation facilities, LuftCar says its role would be to build infrastructure that supports future transportation technologies."What LuftCar, my client, would like to see is the advancement of innovative technologies and the space to operate those programs," Koushakjian said.Koushakjian said North County Airport is well-positioned to become a testing ground for that technology because it is smaller than President Donald J. Trump International Airport."It is a prime area for eVTOL (electric vertical take-off and landing) and innovative technologies simply because it's a smaller airport," he said.The company envisions infrastructure that could support electric aircraft that do not require traditional runways."The energy infrastructure, the platform, the storage, the fueling area, as well as the platform itself for vertical takeoff and landing," Koushakjian said when describing what such a facility would require.He also pointed to increasing congestion in the region's airspace as one reason airport leaders are exploring future growth."I hear it's very congested and some people are experiencing flight delays because of the congested airspace, and that's why they're expanding the airport because we just need more space to accommodate that growth," he said.Supporters of airport improvements have argued that expanding North County Airport could help ease pressure on Trump International Airport by creating more capacity for private aviation activity.Airport officials, however, stressed the airport is not being expanded to attract commercial airline service. Instead, they described the discussion as part of long-term planning to avoid future congestion and accommodate continued growth in private and general aviation.While aviation companies see opportunity, some nearby residents are watching the conversation closely.Roberta Sorensen, who lives near the airport and under part of the flight path, said aircraft noise is not her biggest concern."Much more worried about the road. The traffic is really bad. The planes going over don't bother me at all," Sorensen said.She's more concerned that airport growth could bring more vehicles to already busy roads."People are going to be coming out here to fly. So there'll be more traffic on the roads. The roads are bad now up here. They're just getting worse, and by the time they finish all this building they're doing out here, it's going to be terrible," she said.Sorensen also hopes nearby residents remain part of the conversation."I think maybe the neighbors should be consulted because they've lived here a long time. I haven't," she said.Commissioners ultimately chose not to move forward directly with Jet Green's proposal. Instead, they directed staff to begin developing a competitive solicitation process that would allow multiple developers and aviation companies to submit their visions for the future of North County Airport.The move keeps the conversation alive while opening the door to a broader range of proposals that could shape the airport's future for decades to come.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Florida Senate president opposes Amendment 3 months after lawmakers put it on ballot
entry.summary: The president of the Florida State Senate says he is voting 'No' on Amendment 3, just months after the State Senate approved putting the referendum on the November ballot. 'As a native of Florida's Heartland, our rural communities are near and dear to my heart,' Albritton said in a post on the Florida Sheriffs Association's Instagram page. 'Amendment 3 would eliminate up to 30% of resources for Florida's rural counties, gutting essential support for law enforcement, emergency response services and critical infrastructure.' WATCH BELOW: Florida Senate president opposes Amendment 3 Florida Senate president opposes Amendment 3 Albritton also stated the Florida Taxation and Budget Reform Commission presents: 'An ideal opportunity to design property tax reform and create a solution that is meaningful, reasonable and balanced.' Amendment 3 would raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. It would also cut property taxes for homesteaded homeowners, excluding school taxes. Cities and counties stand to lose significant revenue and many local leaders say it will lead to budget cuts, reduced services and possibly creating other revenue streams. The referendum needs 60% approval on Election Day to become law in Florida.

entry.title: Indian River State College trustees to consider eliminating men's, women's swimming and diving programs
entry.summary: Indian River State College trustees are expected to consider a major restructuring of the college's athletic programs next week that would eliminate men's and women's swimming and diving and move several remaining sports to Division II competition. The recommendations are included on the agenda for the college's Governance Legislative Affairs Committee meeting on Tuesday, Oct. 27, at the Dixon Hendry Campus in Okeechobee. The committee meetings begin at 9:30 a.m., followed by the full District Board of Trustees meeting at 1 p.m. WATCH TYLER HATFIELD'S REPORT BELOW: Swimmers rally to save IRSC swim and dive teams Under the proposed athletic restructuring plan, both the men's and women's swimming and diving programs would be eliminated beginning with the fall 2027-28 academic year. The proposal would also transition baseball, softball and men's basketball to Division II competition beginning that same academic year. Volleyball already competes at the Division 2 level, according to the agenda. College administrators would also be directed to evaluate whether the women's basketball program could be reinstated for the 2028-29 season. The agenda says that possibility would depend on the availability of resources. The recommendations come from the college president and cabinet and are scheduled to be presented to the Governance Legislative Affairs Committee for approval. The agenda itself does not provide a reason for the proposed elimination of swimming and diving or detail the financial impact of the restructuring. All of this comes after Indian River State College's men's swim and dive team in March captured its 52nd consecutive national championship title, with the women's team also claiming its 48th national title. The meeting will take place at the Williamson Conference Center Auditorium on Indian River State College's Dixon Hendry Campus at 2229 NW 9th Avenue in Okeechobee.

entry.summary: St. Lucie County Fire Board terminates fire chief after union vote    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire District Board voted to terminate longtime fire chief Jeff Lee, about two weeks after the district’s firefighters union released the results of a no-confidence vote on its top leaders. Following the decision, the district voted 4-3 to appoint Deputy Chief Paul Langel as Interim Chief. The agenda for the board’s 3 p.m. regular meeting includes an item listed under Chair Shannon Martin titled Discussion Regarding Potential Retirement and Leadership Transition. The agenda does not say whose retirement will be discussed, and no supporting documents for the item have been made public. The Professional Fire Fighters and Paramedics of St. Lucie County, IAFF Local 1377, released its vote results Oct. According to the union, 423 of its 517 dues-paying members took part. Lee received 314 votes of no confidence and 108 votes of confidence. Assistant Fire Chief Brian Gonzalez received 390 votes of no confidence, and District Attorney Kim Sabol received 413. Under the rules the union set before the vote, at least 75% of participating members had to vote no confidence before the union would formally present the result to the Fire Board. Gonzalez and Sabol both passed that mark. The union said 74.23% of members voted no confidence in him. Local 1377 calls upon the Board to carefully consider these results and fulfill its responsibility to the employees who serve this county and to the public they have sworn to protect, the union said in its release. Since then, the district has reassigned Gonzalez from assistant chief to a battalion chief training role. The district said Gonzalez and Lee agreed to the move and that it had been discussed before the recent events. Sabol gave the district 90 days’ notice on Sept. 30 and is set to retire Dec. Wednesday’s agenda also includes the selection of a law firm and a new district attorney. See also: Former PBSO dispatcher sentenced after 2023 head-on DUI crash that killed mother The vote followed months of fallout from a hazing investigation. In July, the district f ired three veteran firefighters , Jordon Hutchinson, Christopher Baldwin and Douglas Boudrias, and suspended two others. Videos showed newer firefighters being shocked with a modified bug zapper . An outside investigation hired by the district concluded the conduct was hazing. The firefighters and their union say it was consensual horseplay, and a Fort Pierce Police report found no criminal matter. The union is pursuing arbitration to get the three firefighters reinstated. Board members have said the district has no policy for handling complaints against its top contracted employees, including the fire chief. They can’t investigate themselves. That’s not proper, board member and County Commissioner Jamie Fowler said at an Oct. 6, Lee withdrew a settlement offer that would have brought the three firefighters back with retroactive pay, citing guidance from counsel and the district’s insurance representatives. CBS12 News has also obtained a 2022 recording in which Lee, Gonzalez and Sabol declined to investigate a female firefighter’s complaint of unwanted touching by a coworker. Lee has said the problem is not one he can solve himself. The board has to fix that problem, Lee said at an Aug. County Commissioner James Clasby, who also sits on the fire board, has publicly called on Lee to resign. In August, a motion to suspend Lee and Sabol failed 2 to 4. In a statement after the vote, the district said it recognizes the results and will take appropriate action. It pointed to pay increases, about 100 additional uniformed personnel and three-person engine staffing during Lee’s tenure. Lee joined the district in 1997 after serving in the U.S. He became its 14th fire chief in May 2023. This is not the first time the board has faced this choice. In 2017, after a union no-confidence vote, the board accepted then Chief Buddy Emerson’s retirement effective immediately and paid him severance through the end of his contract. CBS12 News will be at Wednesday’s meeting and will update this story.

Police are asking anyone who witnessed suspicious activity or has information about the incidents to call the FPPD at 772-467-6800 . entry.summary: Seacoast Bank has surpassed a major milestone in the fight against breast cancer, raising more than $1 million for the American Cancer Society through its annual Waves initiative, a fundraising campaign supporting research, advocacy and patient services for people affected by the disease. The achievement comes as Breast Cancer Awareness Month shines a spotlight on early detection and support services. 'I was very close to my maternal grandmother.' entry.title: Girl Scout troop returns to Pleasant City Elementary, creating new opportunities for West Palm Beach girls
entry.summary: A Girl Scout troop is getting a fresh start at Pleasant City Elementary School in West Palm Beach, giving local girls an opportunity to make new friends, learn new skills and build confidence after the school lost its previous troop. The Related Ross Foundation helped restart the troop after Executive Director Jeremy Morse learned students at the school no longer had the opportunity to participate. For the girls now learning the Girl Scout sign and promise, the new troop is already becoming a place to set goals, help others and find a sense of belonging. Girls find friendship and a place to grow For Girl Scout Tanisha Smith, joining the troop is about learning while helping those around her. 'Girl Scouts is about learning to be ladylike and to help other people,' Smith said. Fellow Girl Scout Kennedy Harper said she is looking forward to the friendships that could come from participating. 'My favorite thing about Girl Scouts [is] because I feel like it's gonna help me make more friends,' Harper said. Smith said she also sees the troop as a welcoming place for girls who may be hesitant to speak up or meet new people. 'If you're shy, it could help,' Smith said. 'It can help you make friends, and if you don't know much, you can either ask questions or learn it.' Foundation helps restart Pleasant City troop The opportunity was not available at Pleasant City Elementary until the Related Ross Foundation stepped in to help bring the troop back. 'When I heard that Pleasant City Elementary School lost their troop, I thought, you know, this is our opportunity to restart it, so that they can have this opportunity to continue that journey,' Morse said. The girls have already begun earning patches while deciding what they want to accomplish together. 'I hope to accomplish working together,' Harper said. It's not about one single decision that he's made. It's about bringing peace and calm and respect back to the district and the men and women that serve this community every day, and it just got to a point where he was not effective anymore,' said St. Lucie County Commissioner and Board Member Jamie Fowler. Other videos show water being dumped on two firefighters and a dead raccoon placed inside a fire vehicle.A third-party investigator concluded the videos depicted hazing. Veteran firefighters Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Chris Baldwin were fired following the investigation, though they disputed the characterization of hazing and said the incidents were "consensual" pranks that were done "all in good fun." “It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," said Hutchinson. “We’re all still friends," added Boudrias. Boudrias, Hutchinson, and Baldwin's firings sparked outcry from firefighters, former firefighters and community members, many of whom felt the punishment was too harsh. In Wednesday's Fire Board meeting, those community members packed the Fire Administration building, many of whom held signs or wore shirts in support of the three firefighters. "Not only have they lost their jobs, but they also lost their reputations," said one public commentator. "We need to restore faith in this fire district," said another. "I think it speaks loud and clear, exactly like the confidence vote that was reported to us. There was a large desire to have a change in leadership, and we delivered that today," said St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire Board member James Clasby. Lee had signaled days earlier that his tenure could be coming to an end. 15 letter to the board, Lee wrote that it may be time to consider a “mutually agreeable retirement and leadership transition," adding "the position of fire chief requires confidence." During the meeting's discussion, fire board member and business owner Travis Leonard said that gave him reason to begin the motion to Fire Lee. "Coming from the private sector, anytime an employee gives their notice, I terminate them; I found they've checked out," said Leonard. After terminating Lee’s contract, the board appointed Deputy Chief Paul Langel as interim fire chief. The district also plans to hire a recruiter to conduct a search for Lee’s permanent replacement."I am excited to move this district forward, to begin the healing process of the issues that we’ve been dealing with, as of recent, and to instill trust,” Langel said.Lee's departure comes with a high cost to the district. His severance package is expected to total about $350,000.The leadership change also comes as the firefighters union continues negotiations with the district in an effort to reinstate three veteran firefighters who were fired. Union Representative Ryan Sapp said he believed Lee's termination is a "positive step forward.""I think moving forward, the ultimate goal here is to just move forward and get things back to a level field and continue providing the services to our community," Sapp told investigative reporter Kate Hussey. "The biggest thing today is we worked together and came together as a local — glad to see my membership stepped up and let their voices be heard." The Fire Board is also searching for a replacement district attorney, who submitted her notice of retirement amid the ongoing controversy.
