entry.article_text: All lanes of Florida’s Turnpike have reopened in St. Lucie County after a truck fire and a separate crash caused major delays Tuesday morning. The truck fire was reported just before 8 a.m. in the southbound lanes near mile marker 161, approximately nine miles south of the Okeechobee Road/State Road 70 exit. Officials initially closed all southbound lanes while crews worked to extinguish the blaze. One lane later reopened before a separate crash in the same area led to another closure. As of the latest update, all southbound lanes have reopened and traffic is beginning to move through the area. However, motorists may continue to experience residual delays as congestion clears. It’s unclear what caused the truck fire or whether anyone was injured in either incident. WFLX has reached out to the Florida Highway Patrol for additional information. This story will be updated if more information becomes available.

entry.article_text: A long list of watches, warnings and advisories is in place across the Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches, with coastal flooding, strong winds and dangerous beach and boating conditions among the main concerns. Note: Alert expiration times may differ across the region because Palm Beach County is covered by the Miami forecast office, while Indian River, St. Lucie, Martin and Okeechobee counties are covered by the Melbourne office. Coastal Flood Warning A Coastal Flood Warning is in effect until 8 p.m. Wednesday, October 28th for coastal Palm Beach County. One is in effect until 2 a.m. Thursday, October 29th for coastal Indian River, St. Lucie, and Martin counties. Coastal roads may be closed. Low lying property including homes, businesses and some critical infrastructure will be inundated. Significant shoreline erosion will occur. Wind Advisory A Wind Advisory is in effect from 11 a.m. Monday, October 26th, until 8 p.m. Tuesday, October 27th, for metro and coastal Palm Beach County. One is in effect until 8 p.m. Monday, October 26th, for coastal Indian River, St. Lucie and Martin counties. Northeast winds of 20 to 25 mph are expected, with gusts up to 40 mph in Palm Beach County and up to 35 mph along the Treasure Coast. Gusts could blow around unsecured objects, break tree limbs and cause isolated power outages. High Surf Advisory A High Surf Advisory is in effect until 8 p.m. Wednesday, October 28th, for coastal Palm Beach County. One is in effect until 2 a.m. Thursday, October 29th, for coastal Indian River, St. Lucie and Martin counties. Breaking waves of 8 to 13 feet are possible along the Palm Beaches, with 7 to 11 feet forecast for the Treasure Coast. Dangerous swimming and surfing conditions are expected, along with localized beach erosion. High Rip Current Risk A High Rip Current Risk is in effect through Wednesday evening, October 28th, for coastal Palm Beach County. One is in effect through late Wednesday night for coastal Indian River, St. Lucie and Martin counties. Dangerous rip currents can pull even experienced swimmers away from shore. Entering the water is strongly discouraged. Gale Warning A Gale Warning is in effect until 2 a.m. Wednesday, October 28th, for nearshore waters from Sebastian Inlet to Jupiter Inlet and nearby offshore waters. One is in effect until 8 a.m. Wednesday, October 28th, for nearshore and offshore waters from Jupiter Inlet to Deerfield Beach. Northeast winds of 25 to 30 knots, with gusts up to 35 knots, and hazardous seas are expected. Small vessels could capsize or be damaged. Mariners should avoid these conditions and remain in port or seek safe harbor. Small Craft Advisory A Small Craft Advisory is scheduled from 8 a.m. Wednesday, October 28th, for nearshore and offshore waters from Jupiter Inlet to Deerfield Beach. Another is in effect until 8 p.m. Wednesday, October 28th, for Lake Okeechobee. Hazardous boating conditions are expected. Small craft operators should avoid heading out in these conditions.

entry.title: Is it cheaper to fly or drive this Thanksgiving?
entry.summary: If you're traveling for Thanksgiving, one question could have a big impact on your holiday budget: Is it cheaper to fly or drive? The answer can depend on where you're going, how many people are traveling, and when you plan to leave and return. Travelers we spoke with were divided. WATCH: Is it cheaper to fly or drive this Thanksgiving? Is it cheaper to fly or drive this Thanksgiving? It depends where you're going, Leticia Rivera said. But I would say fly right now. Others would rather stay on the road. For the preference, regardless of pricing, drive, Erik Eliassen said. Oh, definitely drive, Calvin Landau added. Carol Baxter, meanwhile, has already made her decision: I'm flying. Airfare can add up quickly for families According to Hopper data provided for this story, the average domestic round-trip flight for Thanksgiving is currently about $402 per person, compared with $307 last year. For a family of four, four tickets at the $402 average would total about $1,608 in airfare alone, before adding other potential travel expenses. Driving can look much different because expenses such as fuel are shared by everyone in the vehicle. Using the example in our comparison, the driving cost is about $160. That means families should consider the total cost of the trip rather than simply comparing the price of one plane ticket with one tank of gas. Your return date could make a big difference For people planning to fly, choosing a different return date could also affect the cost. Hopper data provided for this story shows a round trip with a return on the Sunday after Thanksgiving averaging about $604. Returning on Monday or Tuesday, however, could bring that average down to around $350. That's a difference of roughly $254 per ticket. For a family of four, that difference could potentially add up to more than $1,000. The bottom line There isn't one answer that works for every Thanksgiving traveler. Flying may save time on a long-distance trip, while driving can make the cost easier to spread across several people traveling together. Before booking, compare the total cost for everyone traveling, including airfare or fuel and any additional expenses associated with the trip. Also consider whether changing your travel dates could bring down the price. For families in particular, doing the math on the entire trip could make a significant difference in the Thanksgiving travel budget.

entry.title: Appeals court appears skeptical of Trump administration's California ballot lawsuit
entry.summary: A panel of federal appellate judges on Sunday questioned the timing, constitutionality and authority of the Justice Department's demand that California election officials set aside thousands of mail ballots from people the federal government suspects may not be citizens. The lawsuit accuses California officials of failing to meet a 48-hour deadline to review 20,000 names the administration flagged as likely noncitizens on the state's voter rolls. The administration asked a federal judge to require the state to withhold counting those ballots until the voters immigration status could be verified. entry.article_text: A panel of federal appellate judges on Sunday questioned the timing, constitutionality and authority of the Justice Department's demand that California election officials set aside thousands of mail ballots from people the federal government suspects may not be citizens.During rare weekend arguments, two of the three judges on the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals appeared skeptical of a lawsuit brought by President Donald Trump's administration in mid-October. The lawsuit accuses California officials of failing to meet a 48-hour deadline to review 20,000 names the administration flagged as likely noncitizens on the state's voter rolls.The administration asked a federal judge to require the state to withhold counting those ballots until the voters’ immigration status could be verified. The district judge scheduled a hearing for Oct. 27, days after the case was assigned, but the federal government appealed to the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals, seeking an expedited decision.Justice Department attorney Matthew Donnelly told the panel that California is causing irreparable harm “by allowing noncitizens to vote in violation of their own state laws. The damage is irreversible and irrevocable.”RELATED STORY | DOJ threatens California with legal action over claim of noncitizens on voter rollsThe Trump administration has made efforts to identify noncitizen voters a priority this year, even though noncitizen voting is exceptionally rare.Circuit Judge Mark Bennett, a Trump appointee, questioned whether the appellate court even has jurisdiction to hear the case even before a ruling by the lower court.Donnelly argued that the schedule set by the lower court judge was too slow and effectively a denial of the government's request, as state elections officials process thousands of mail ballots every day.Judge Gabriel Sanchez, appointed by former President Joe Biden, questioned whether the federal government was violating the Tenth Amendment, essentially commandeering the state to enforce a federal law that makes it a misdemeanor for a noncitizen to vote.The federal government is simply asking California to enforce their own law, which also bans noncitizens from voting, Donnelly said. He argued the state's refusal to comply with the federal request to set aside the ballots for review was “frustrating the purpose” of the federal law against noncitizen voting.The Elections Clause of the U.S. Constitution gives state legislatures the power to set the time, place and manner of congressional elections, Bennett said. The executive branch may be “unhappy with what they’re doing, and doesn’t like the manner,” Bennett said, but under the Election Clause the state has the right to determine those issues — including how it sorts out any noncitizen voters.Attorney Seth Waxman, representing Los Angeles County Clerk Dean Logan, said the federal government's list was unreliable and that segregating the ballots for a review process would effectively disenfranchise thousands of eligible voters.Even if election staffers spent just three minutes checking each of the expected 2.75 million mail ballots against the government's list, the process would take 140,000 man-hours, Waxman said — or about 16 years of working time.Waxman cited a review of 200 records from the Trump administration's list conducted by Los Angeles County staffers. Assistant Registrar-Recorder Monica Flores said in a court filing that the sample included canceled or inactive registrations, individuals with no voting history and voters who appeared to have been born in the United States, which the filing notes “is strong evidence of citizenship.”If the administration disagrees with how California runs its elections, it can ask Congress to change that process, said attorney Sam Siegel, representing California Secretary of State Shirley Weber.The federal government has provided no credible evidence to support its suspicions, said Siegal.“It has no basis in law or in fact,” he told the panel. “We just dispute the premise that noncitizens are voting."But Judge Patrick Bumatay, who was appointed by Trump, said everyone has an interest in ensuring that only eligible citizens vote. He suggested that granting the administration's request for an emergency order could provide clarity.“Without an injunction, you will never know” if that is happening, Bumatay told Seigel.Bennett said the panel would try to issue a ruling as quickly as possible.

entry.title: 23-year-old man killed after car enters I-95 crash scene, hits FHP cruiser in Lantana
entry.summary: A 23-year-old West Palm Beach man was killed early Sunday after a driver entered a lane closure at an Interstate 95 crash investigation scene and struck him before hitting a Florida Highway Patrol cruiser, according to FHP. The crash happened around 2:07 a.m. on northbound I-95 near Lantana Road in Palm Beach County. According to FHP, a 2019 Mercedes sedan driven by an 18-year-old Lake Worth woman was traveling north in the inside center lane. At the time, a marked FHP Dodge Charger was stationary across the inside and inside center lanes with its emergency lights activated as part of a lane closure for an ongoing crash investigation. Investigators said the Mercedes entered the closed lane and struck the 23-year-old man. The car then rotated and collided with the FHP cruiser. The man was pronounced dead at the scene. His identity has not been released. The 18-year-old driver suffered non-incapacitating injuries and was taken to JFK South for treatment. The outside northbound lane of I-95 reopened at 8:34 a.m., according to FHP.

entry.title: LagoonFest brings free family fun to West Palm Beach waterfront
entry.summary: LagoonFest returns to the downtown West Palm Beach waterfront Saturday with free boat tours, wildlife encounters, children's activities and opportunities to learn about the Lake Worth Lagoon. The free festival runs from 8:30 a.m. to 1:30 p.m. near the West Palm Beach GreenMarket. Benji Studt of Palm Beach County Environmental Resources Management said the event is designed to help residents and visitors connect with the lagoon. 'It's all about connecting people with the lagoon,' Studt said. Shell hunts, wildlife and more at LagoonFest Boat tours offer a closer look at the lagoon Visitors can explore the Lake Worth Lagoon aboard the Hakuna Matata or through Aqua Adventure tours, according to Studt. The boat tours provide a chance to experience the lagoon from the water while learning more about the natural area and the work being done around it. Wildlife encounters and hands-on activities Studt said participating organizations include the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, Busch Wildlife Sanctuary and Manatee Lagoon. The festival will feature touch tanks, wildlife experiences and a live python capture demonstration from FWC. Throughout the morning, families can also meet Laguna, the spotted eagle ray mascot representing Lake Worth Lagoon. Shell hunts and fishing lessons for children Studt said this year's children's zone includes a shell hunt, giveaways and calendars featuring work from local artists. Volunteers from the West Palm Beach Fishing Foundation will teach children how to cast and fish. Participating children will also get to take home a rod and reel, according to Studt. 'The kids can come, and they can do a little shell hunt, look for their shell treasures,' Studt said. Why LagoonFest matters now LagoonFest gives South Florida families a free way to spend time together while learning about a waterway that is part of Palm Beach County's environmental identity. Its location also allows visitors to pair the festival with a stop at the nearby West Palm Beach GreenMarket. Studt said the variety of activities makes the event accessible to visitors with different interests. 'There's something for everybody at LagoonFest,' Studt said. 'It's going to be an awesome time.' LagoonFest takes place Saturday from 8:30 a.m. to 1:30 p.m. along the downtown West Palm Beach waterfront. entry.title: Trump heads to Mississippi as more red states enter the midterm conversation with 8 days to go
entry.summary: The final full week of campaigning has begun after a weekend of bitter attacks on all sides. This week, more red states are entering the conversation for being potentially competitive and so are legal challenges from the Trump administration. President Donald Trump is heading to Mississippi Monday, another traditionally conservative state that few talked about as being competitive earlier this year. But after a number of high-profile visits by Democrats to campaign for Democrat Scott Colom, including former Vice President Kamala Harris, it has entered the conversation. RELATED STORY | Democrats tout momentum as early voting rises ahead of midterms While current Mississippi Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith is still favored, she has faced criticism for months after being asked about beef prices and suggesting there are other proteins to eat. Trump told reporters he thinks his frequent rallies are helping. 'I have heard we have turned the whole thing around and for whatever reason presidents don't win the midterms and I think we really turned it around and I think the rallies have turned it,' Trump said. Trump and Obama duel on the campaign trail Trump is also dueling with former President Barack Obama on the campaign trail this week, with Obama campaigning in Ohio and Michigan and mocking the former president in the process. 'Guy's building a ballroom bigger than White House, paved over the Rose Garden, put a helipad on the south lawn,' Obama said at one rally. 'And there is gold everywhere. What's up with the gold? He has got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.' MORE ELECTION NEWS | Young voter turnout could be pivotal in this year's midterms Polls show Democrats maintaining an edge in both House races and many Senate races with 8 days to go. But Republicans remain very skeptical of polling. A closely watched race in Alaska One of the biggest races is in Alaska, where Democratic nominee Mary Peltola was involved in a car accident over the weekend, sustaining minor injuries. This comes after the Department of Justice has sued to block Alaska certification, citing concerns that incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan is facing another Dan Sullivan on the ballot. 'That is very unfair, that's just outright cheating,' Trump said.

entry.title: Is it cheaper to fly or drive this Thanksgiving?
entry.summary: If you're traveling for Thanksgiving, one question could significantly affect your holiday budget: Is it cheaper to fly or drive? The answer can depend on where you're going, how many people are traveling, and when you plan to leave and return. Travelers we spoke with were divided. WATCH: Is it cheaper to fly or drive this Thanksgiving? Is it cheaper to fly or drive this Thanksgiving? 'It depends where you're going,' Leticia Rivera said. 'But I would say fly right now.' Others would rather stay on the road. 'For the preference, regardless of pricing, drive,' Erik Eliassen said. 'Oh, definitely drive,' Calvin Landau added. Carol Baxter, meanwhile, has already made her decision: 'I'm flying.' Airfare can add up quickly for families According to Hopper data provided for this story, the average domestic round-trip flight for Thanksgiving is currently about $402 per person, compared with $307 last year. For a family of four, four tickets at the $402 average would total about $1,608 in airfare alone, before adding other potential travel expenses. Driving can look very different because everyone in the vehicle shares expenses such as fuel. Using the example in our comparison, the driving cost is about $160. That means families should consider the total cost of the trip rather than simply comparing the price of one plane ticket with one tank of gas. Your return date could make a big difference For people planning to fly, choosing a different return date could also affect the cost. Hopper data provided for this story shows a round trip with a return on the Sunday after Thanksgiving averaging about $604. Returning on Monday or Tuesday, however, could bring that average down to around $350. That's a difference of roughly $254 per ticket. For a family of four, that difference could potentially add up to more than $1,000. The bottom line There isn't one answer that works for every Thanksgiving traveler. Flying may save time on a long-distance trip, while driving can make the cost easier to spread across several people traveling together. Before booking, compare the total cost for everyone traveling, including airfare or fuel and any additional expenses associated with the trip. Also consider whether changing your travel dates could bring down the price. For families in particular, doing the math on the entire trip could make a significant difference in the Thanksgiving travel budget.

entry.summary: Watches, warnings, and advisories in place across the Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches    WPEC
entry.article_text: A long list of watches, warnings and advisories is in place across the Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches, with coastal flooding, strong winds and dangerous beach and boating conditions among the main concerns. Note: Alert expiration times may differ across the region because Palm Beach County is covered by the Miami forecast office, while Indian River, St. Lucie, Martin and Okeechobee counties are covered by the Melbourne office. Coastal Flood Warning A Coastal Flood Warning is in effect until 8 p.m. Wednesday, October 28th for coastal Palm Beach County. One is in effect until 2 a.m. Thursday, October 29th for coastal Indian River, St. Lucie, and Martin counties. Coastal roads may be closed. Low lying property including homes, businesses and some critical infrastructure will be inundated. Significant shoreline erosion will occur. Wind Advisory A Wind Advisory is in effect from 11 a.m. Monday, October 26th, until 8 p.m. Tuesday, October 27th, for metro and coastal Palm Beach County. One is in effect until 8 p.m. Monday, October 26th, for coastal Indian River, St. Lucie and Martin counties. Northeast winds of 20 to 25 mph are expected, with gusts up to 40 mph in Palm Beach County and up to 35 mph along the Treasure Coast. Gusts could blow around unsecured objects, break tree limbs and cause isolated power outages. High Surf Advisory A High Surf Advisory is in effect until 8 p.m. Wednesday, October 28th, for coastal Palm Beach County. One is in effect until 2 a.m. Thursday, October 29th, for coastal Indian River, St. Lucie and Martin counties. Breaking waves of 8 to 13 feet are possible along the Palm Beaches, with 7 to 11 feet forecast for the Treasure Coast. Dangerous swimming and surfing conditions are expected, along with localized beach erosion. High Rip Current Risk A High Rip Current Risk is in effect through Wednesday evening, October 28th, for coastal Palm Beach County. One is in effect through late Wednesday night for coastal Indian River, St. Lucie and Martin counties. Dangerous rip currents can pull even experienced swimmers away from shore. Entering the water is strongly discouraged. Gale Warning A Gale Warning is in effect until 2 a.m. Wednesday, October 28th, for nearshore waters from Sebastian Inlet to Jupiter Inlet and nearby offshore waters. One is in effect until 8 a.m. Wednesday, October 28th, for nearshore and offshore waters from Jupiter Inlet to Deerfield Beach. Northeast winds of 25 to 30 knots, with gusts up to 35 knots, and hazardous seas are expected. Small vessels could capsize or be damaged. Mariners should avoid these conditions and remain in port or seek safe harbor. Small Craft Advisory A Small Craft Advisory is scheduled from 8 a.m. Wednesday, October 28th, for nearshore and offshore waters from Jupiter Inlet to Deerfield Beach. Another is in effect until 8 p.m. Wednesday, October 28th, for Lake Okeechobee. Hazardous boating conditions are expected. Small craft operators should avoid heading out in these conditions.

The investigation suggests a physical altercation took place among individuals known to one another before shots were fired near the Florida AM football stadium, Revell said. At this stage of the investigation, none of the victims appear to have been the intended targets, the police chief said. The investigation remains active and additional arrests are possible, Revell said. Six juveniles, including an 11-year-old, are among the injured, Revell said late Saturday. entry.title: From Jensen Beach to Louisiana Tech: Andrew Burnette gets one more shot at college football - WFLX
entry.summary: From Jensen Beach to Louisiana Tech: Andrew Burnette gets one more shot at college football    WFLX
entry.article_text: A young man from the Midwest with South Florida roots describes how Andrew Burnette moved from Michigan around the age of 12 and found home on the football field in Martin County. "I played football my whole life, and I can say football is a little harder in Florida than it is in Michigan," said Burnette. WATCH BELOW: Local football standout gets one more shot at college football While football was his first sport, during his high school days at Jensen Beach High School, he fell in love with takedowns and pins. "I wasn't zoned for that school, but I went there for wrestling originally; that was my first passion," said Burnette. While he was doing well in wrestling, football kept calling to him. "Moving through high school, I knew football was what I wanted to do," said Burnette. He established himself as a force at Jensen Beach High School, but he didn't receive much interest from college football programs, similar to many Treasure Coast football recruits. "One of my main struggles was recruitment out of high school, because I felt like our area was a little under-recruited," said Burnette. Betting on himself, he decided to play at Highland Community College in Kansas. Burnette played in nine games and rushed for 340 yards and two touchdowns, but he still wasn't on any other college football program's radar. "I transferred to Independence Junior College, and I was cut from the team," said Burnette. Independence was featured on the hit Netflix show Last Chance U, but once his chance there was short-lived, he reached out to Keiser University in West Palm Beach. "I spoke with the coach there and told him, 'You guys offered me in high school,' and he said, 'I don't really remember. Send me your film.' He saw my film and said, 'Hey, bring it,'" said Burnette. And he did "bring it." In the two years he played at Keiser, he rushed for over 2,300 yards and 30 touchdowns. With stats like that, Division I programs finally came calling, starting with Louisiana Tech. "Last year I played there; it was my first year at the Division I level, and then my eligibility ran out," said Burnette. At the time, the NCAA granted student-athletes only four years of eligibility unless they were injured, so Burnette rolled up his sleeves and got to work. "I called my dad and told him, 'Hey, I need to do something. I can't just sit here,' so I went and worked with my dad in Michigan," said Burnette. He worked with his dad at a steel mill in Detroit for a few months, but this summer the NCAA announced the 5-in-5 rule, meaning student-athletes can compete for up to five seasons across a continuous five-year period. So he hired a lawyer and went to court with the NCAA to get his final year of eligibility, and they granted him one last year, and now he's making the most of it. "It was amazing; I would rather play football than do anything, and for me to have this opportunity again, it's a blessing," said Burnette.

entry.title: USAA auto insurance rates dropping for nearly 500,000 Florida policies
entry.summary: Nearly half a million USAA auto insurance policies in Florida are set to see lower rates after state regulators approved a series of reductions, according to the Florida Office of Insurance Regulation. Florida Insurance Commissioner Mike Yaworsky approved several auto insurance program rate decreases for USAA Group that average 7%. The changes affect more than 498,000 policies across the state. Individual policyholders could see different savings depending on their program. According to the state, average rate changes range from a decrease of 0.4% to as much as 11.2%. USAA has its highest concentration of Florida business in Brevard, Escambia and Okaloosa counties. Average decreases in those counties are 5.8% in Brevard, 8% in Escambia and 8.4% in Okaloosa. 'The Office of Insurance Regulation is constantly reaching out to insurers to inquire about rate relief, and USAA is always stepping up to the plate and looking out for their consumers,' Yaworsky said in the release. He encouraged other insurers to consider additional rate reductions. Florida Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia pointed to the reductions as another sign of improvement in the state's insurance market and credited Florida's tort reforms. 'These auto insurance rate decreases will help Florida families keep more of their hard-earned money in their pockets, especially our military families,' Ingoglia said. The latest reductions follow other savings announced by USAA over the past year. According to the release, the company provided nearly $1 billion in rate reductions and direct member returns to Florida members between December 2025 and July 2026. That included a $500 million dividend distributed to approximately 830,000 members. State regulators also said Florida's five largest auto insurance groups are showing a combined indicated rate change of negative 12.6% for 2026. Those companies represent 81% of Florida's auto insurance market, according to the release. The state also reported that Florida had the nation's lowest personal auto liability loss ratio in 2025 at 52.5%, its lowest level in 15 years.

entry.article_text: Lucie County firefighter-paramedic died while on duty Saturday, more than a year after his younger brother, who also served as a firefighter-paramedic, died at age 26. Lucie County Fire District announced the line-of-duty death of Austin Hodge on Saturday, Oct. 24, calling his death a profound loss to the department and the fire service community. Hodge joined the district on July 17, 2017, and served the community for more than nine years. He was assigned to Station 9. Neighboring Indian River County Fire Rescue also shared condolences following the firefighter’s unexpected death Saturday morning. Lucie County Fire District asked the public to respect Hodge’s family as they grieve. Information about memorial arrangements will be shared as details are finalized. Read more: Missing 5-year-old girl found dead in Fort Pierce body of water Brothers shared a career in firefighting Austin Hodge’s death comes more than a year after his younger brother, Jarius Hodge, also a St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic, died on July 22, 2025. The brothers shared a close bond and a passion for serving their community. This was my best friend, my twin, Austin Hodge previously told CBS12 News. We had the same hairstyle. He described Jarius as someone who loved his family and his work as a first responder. He loved going to work, loved working beside me. I loved working beside him, Austin said. He always pushed me to keep going. He was someone who loved his family, his community and his country. Family sought accountability after Jarius’ death In an interview with CBS12 News , Austin said Jarius became ill after catching the flu from a patient at work in July 2025. Austin said his younger brother went to Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital in Port St. Lucie on July 22, struggling to breathe, but died hours later. He alleged that medical staff made critical errors in treating his brother, including taking three attempts to intubate him. He said Jarius had been healthy before becoming ill. Austin also spoke publicly about Florida’s medical malpractice laws, arguing that restrictions on who can pursue certain wrongful-death claims prevented his family from seeking legal accountability for Jarius’ death. This is unjust, and it's been going on for too long, Austin said in the earlier interview. He emphasized that his family was seeking accountability rather than financial compensation. For me personally, for my family, this has nothing to do with any type of dollar, he said. We just want those physicians to be held accountable. The circumstances surrounding Austin Hodge’s death have not been released. Lucie County Fire District said additional information about ways to honor his service will be shared in coordination with his family. entry.article_text: The race to be Florida's next governor is a competitive one — a statistical tie, according to a poll released last week by the University of North Florida.I caught up with Republican Byron Donalds and Democrat David Jolly as they each campaigned across the state, pitching different visions of Florida's future to voters.Donalds, a Republican congressman, told me in a video call from his campaign bus on the road that he wants to build on the policies he likes from Gov. Ron DeSantis' outgoing administration."We live in a great state, and what has separated us from the other states is we continue to choose common sense conservative policy," Donalds said.That includes immigration enforcement."We're going to continue that mission here in the great state of Florida because we are going to continue to follow the law. I think that's the appropriate use of state authority and state powers," Donalds said.It also includes Florida's Department of Government Efficiency, which DeSantis formed through an executive order in 2025 and has since conducted audits of multiple counties across Florida."We are going to DOGE all governments, both local and state agencies in the state of Florida, because it's not our tax money. It belongs to the people of Florida. We need to make sure that government lives within its means, the way families have to live within their means," Donalds said.Donalds told me that effort will be important if Amendment 3 passes, raising homestead tax exemptions and reducing local revenue. I asked him whether, as governor, he would be prepared if some of the municipalities that need help come to Tallahassee asking for it."Yes, we will, and we've already made a public commitment to the fiscally constrained counties in the state of Florida," Donalds said. "Those that we know that their budgets are going to change in a major way, that we're prepared to provide a funding formula for those fiscally constrained counties so that they can be able to make ends meet."Jolly, a Democrat who served as a Republican in Congress during the 2010s, visited WPTV as his campaign traveled through Palm Beach County. He has said he personally opposes Amendment 3, but will support the will of the voters if it passes."I think we all want the math behind Amendment 3 to work, but it just doesn't," Jolly said.Florida hasn't elected a Democrat as governor since the 1990s. I asked Jolly why he thinks that is and why he believes his campaign could overcome that."Look, we're a state that trended Republican, particularly in the last eight years, and we know by voter registration it's still a predominantly Republican state," Jolly said. "I think we're in a moment most akin to a 1974 post-Watergate moment, where voters are saying, 'Burn the ships. Let's go in a new direction.'"Jolly said that direction should be simple."Housing, healthcare, education, and no data centers. "The answers are not in ideology. The answers are in solutions."He also said he wants to reach across the aisle to achieve those goals."If we expand health care access, we reduce costs. So you can be a conservative that wants to save money or a progressive that wants more health care. When we invest in public education, we create a resilient economy that should be attractive to Republicans. The economic argument behind that, I think, on housing, when more people have stable housing, the economy is better. I think we can work with Republicans," Jolly said.One issue where the two candidates agree is on school choice. Both told me they support keeping universal vouchers in place.Jolly also emphasized his desire to increase transparency requirements in Florida's charter schools and increase teacher pay in public schools."Let's engage in a little bit of consumer protection here on behalf of kids and families, and say that if you're going to take a voucher as a school, you should have to provide the same services, standards and offerings and be measured by the same measuring stick that our public schools are," Jolly said.Asked whether financial records of charter schools should be public records, as they are for public schools, Donalds replied, "I think if you're talking about what parents are looking for, what they want to basically see, are the children being educated? What are the mathematical attainment scores of that school? What are the reading attainment scores of that school? And if you're talking about high school, what's the ACT scores and what's the SAT scores? I think that's the accountability and the transparency that parents are looking for in the state of Florida, because at the end of the day, they're looking to make sure that the output is where it needs to be."Donalds' wife, Erika Donalds, founded a charter school company and currently runs a nonprofit promoting school choice. "My wife is actually not in the charter school business anymore. She's actually been out of that business for a couple of years," Donalds told me. "But I just want to be clear: she will not be contracting with the state of Florida in any way, shape, or form."On data center policy, the candidates differ. Jolly said he supports a moratorium on data center construction, while Donalds believes those decisions should be left up to local governments."If a local government says no data centers, then no data centers. If they do, then where the state steps in is we make sure that utility bills, utility costs are not passed on to consumers, and we also make sure that we are going to protect water resources in our state," Donalds said.For the first time in decades, Florida voters did not get to see a gubernatorial debate for this election.Asked what he would say to Jolly had the two candidates faced one another on the debate stage, Donalds said, "I would like him to explain why and how the people of Florida are going to be able to pay for his insurance plan, because by independent analysis, his insurance plan will drive up premiums on the people of our state, and everybody will be hit with a $1,000 hurricane tax when the next time the big storm comes through," referring to the funding the sovereign wealth fund Jolly says he would like to create to cover windstorm damage for Florida homeowners. (Jolly has denied that the fund would impose a new tax.)"I'm not sure debates improve our politics at this point. I think they just platform the division and the vitriol and the ugliness," Jolly told me. "My wife says in a world of Donald Trump, I'm trying to be Ted Lasso. We have two young kids, and I want them to look back and know that Dad acted in a way that he spoke of, which was not to further devolve our politics into vitriol and ugliness and division. Debates are about who can score the greatest insult, and I just I don't think that helps."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

entry.title: 23-year-old Road Ranger hit, killed after car enters I-95 crash scene, hits FHP cruiser in Lantana
entry.summary: A 23-year-old Road Ranger from West Palm Beach was killed early Sunday after a driver entered a lane closure at an Interstate 95 crash investigation scene and struck him before hitting a Florida Highway Patrol cruiser, according to FHP. The crash happened around 2:07 a.m. on northbound I-95 near Lantana Road in Palm Beach County. According to FHP, a 2019 Mercedes sedan driven by an 18-year-old Lake Worth woman was traveling north in the inside center lane. At the time, a marked FHP Dodge Charger was stationary across the inside and inside center lanes with its emergency lights activated as part of a lane closure for an ongoing crash investigation. Investigators said the Mercedes entered the closed lane and struck the 23-year-old Road Ranger. The car then rotated and collided with the FHP cruiser. The man was pronounced dead at the scene. His identity has not been released. The 18-year-old driver suffered non-incapacitating injuries and was taken to JFK South for treatment. The outside northbound lane of I-95 reopened at 8:34 a.m., according to FHP. The name of the Road Ranger who was killed has not been released.

entry.title: Indiantown council sets November 5 meeting to consider data center moratorium - cw34.com
entry.summary: Indiantown council sets November 5 meeting to consider data center moratorium    cw34.com
entry.article_text: The Village of Indiantown is moving forward with plans to consider a temporary moratorium on large-scale data center development, but three sites already in the works would be excluded from the proposed restrictions. During Thursday night's Village Council meeting, members voted to schedule a special meeting for November 5, when they will take up the first reading of an ordinance that would temporarily halt new data center development applications, reviews, approvals and the start of construction on projects subject to the restrictions. The council also identified three sites that would be excluded from the proposed moratorium: Project Silver Fox Associated with Silver Fox 606 LLC. Project Growler Associated with Warfield 18 LLC. Tesoro Groves A large, planned development associated with Florida Power & Light property. The exemptions would allow those sites to remain outside the proposed restrictions while the village considers how to regulate future large-scale data center development. Council seeks negotiations and an end to litigation Council members also called for lawsuits surrounding the developments to be dropped as the village seeks to negotiate with developers. The request comes amid ongoing legal disputes involving data center development in Indiantown. Silver Fox 606 LLC filed a lawsuit against the village challenging its handling of an appeal involving the project's development approvals. A Martin County circuit judge issued an injunction earlier this month blocking a planned zoning appeals hearing while the legal dispute proceeds. It remains unclear whether the developers will agree to dismiss pending litigation or what conditions could be attached to any negotiations. Councilwoman pushes for community benefits See also: Palm Beach County district says 12 K-8 schools made Florida’s top 100 in new rankings During Thursday's meeting, Councilwoman Vernestine Williams-Palmer expressed frustration over the lengthy discussions surrounding data centers and emphasized the need to secure financial benefits for Indiantown residents. Palmer said the village needs additional tax revenue and investments in community infrastructure, particularly improvements to its water system. We need all the things, all the things that's been promised. We need the community impacts. We need all of that," Palmer said, according to a transcript of the meeting. She also encouraged residents to identify improvements they would like developers to help fund, mentioning a proposed $3 million gymnasium as one example discussed. Palmer said she has visited a data center in Texas and spoken with facility managers as part of her efforts to better understand the industry. While acknowledging that residents remain divided over data center development, Palmer said council members are working to protect the community's interests. The November 5 special meeting will focus on the first reading of the proposed moratorium ordinance. If ultimately adopted, the measure would temporarily restrict new large-scale data center applications and development activity covered by the ordinance while excluding the three identified sites. The length of the proposed moratorium and the precise conditions governing the exemptions still need to be established. The council's October 22 vote scheduled the special meeting and addressed the proposed exclusions. It did not enact the moratorium. Village leaders are expected to continue discussions over development restrictions, infrastructure needs and potential community benefits as the ordinance moves forward. entry.title: King tides cause coastal flooding, beach closures in Palm Beach County and Treasure Coast - WPEC
entry.summary: King tides cause coastal flooding, beach closures in Palm Beach County and Treasure Coast    WPEC
entry.article_text: Turn around, don’t drown is the message for drivers as king tides are expected to bring the highest tides of the season to Florida’s Atlantic coast. A coastal flood warning covers low-lying areas near the water in Palm Beach, Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties. Flooding is more likely in places with poor drainage, especially around high tide. The National Weather Service says the warning runs through 8 p.m. Wednesday in coastal Palm Beach County and 2 a.m. Thursday in coastal Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties. The highest tides are expected at these times: Monday: 9:06 p.m. In Palm City, the Martin County Sheriff’s Office reported significant flooding along SW Dyer Point Road, making it impassable. Additional flooding was reported on SW 34th Street and Cornell Avenue. The Sheriff’s Office is deploying high-water rescue vehicles to help anyone stranded in a vehicle or home. Residents should avoid the area, never drive through floodwater and call 911 for emergency assistance. See also: Florida Amendment 3 debate centers on property taxes, police protection and spending Photos shared by the Sheriff’s Office show extensive street flooding and people wading through ankle-deep water. Another video that was shared by a CBS12 viewer shows flooded streets on Indian River Drive as a car drives through it. In Boynton Beach, the intersection of Ocean Avenue and Federal Highway is closed because of heavy flooding. Drivers should avoid the area and use alternate routes. Officials will provide an update once the water recedes and the intersection reopens. The Ocean Inlet Marina is also closed because of high tides. Midtown Beach is temporarily closed because of large surf and exceptionally high tides. Officials say conditions are unsafe for beach access. The northbound lane of South Ocean Boulevard between Chilean Avenue and Australian Avenue will be closed from 10 a.m. to noon while crews relocate the lifeguard tower. The City of Delray Beach says red flags are flying at its beach because of high surf and flooding. The Juno Beach Pier is closed until further notice because of damage from a recent offshore surge and high surf.

entry.title: St. Lucie County firefighter paramedic Austin Hodge dies after being found unresponsive on duty
entry.summary: A St. Lucie County Fire District firefighter who died unexpectedly Saturday morning has been identified as Austin Hodge, a firefighter paramedic and nine-year veteran of the department. The fire district announced Hodge was found unresponsive in his bunk during a shift change. He was taken to the hospital and passed away. WATCH REPORT BELOW: St. Lucie County firefighter dies on duty St. Lucie County community mourns firefighter who died on duty 'Today, our St. Lucie County Fire District family mourns the loss of one of our own,' the district said in a statement. In the hours following his death, firefighters, the department's Honor Guard and fellow first responders gathered to honor Hodge and support one another. The district said the response reflected the strong bond shared throughout the fire service. The district thanked the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Fort Pierce Police Department, Port St. Lucie Police Department and peer support teams from Martin and Indian River counties for providing assistance and standing alongside firefighters during the difficult day. 'Together, they offered strength, compassion, and support while ensuring Austin was honored with the dignity and respect he deserves,' the district said. The district said its thoughts are with Hodge's family, loved ones and everyone who served alongside him. They respectfully ask that Hodge's family be given privacy during this time. 'We are deeply grateful to our fellow first responders and community for the outpouring of support during this tremendous loss,' the district said. 'Today and always, we stand together.' The tragedy comes more than a year after the community mourned the sudden loss of his brother, Jarius Hodge , 26, who was also a St. Lucie County firefighter and died from septic shock in July 2025. The district said it will share information on funeral and memorial services in coordination with the family when it becomes available.

entry.title: St. Lucie County Fire District confirms firefighter’s death - WPBF
entry.summary: St. Lucie County Fire District confirms firefighter’s death    WPBF
entry.article_text: A firefighter/paramedic died Saturday morning while on duty, one year after his brother, also with the St. Lucie County Fire District, passed away, the agency said. Austin Hodge, 34, joined the St. Lucie County Fire District on July 17, 2017. He was assigned to Station 9 in Fort Pierce. A procession of firefighters and personnel from other agencies went from HCA Lawnwood Hospital to the morgue in Fort Pierce on Saturday morning. His brother, Jarius Hodge, died on July 22, 2025, after falling ill at work at Station 3. His family said he had the flu, felt weak and was later rushed to the hospital, where he died hours later. People gathered on May 30 to celebrate what would have been his 27th birthday with a cookout and balloon release. Austin Hodge told WPBF at the time: "He was a quiet leader, and we take a lot from him. He was my younger brother, but I looked up to him in many ways to keep me poised, keep me patient. And I think that's what he's teaching everybody today." In June, another firefighter, Connor Whitehead, 21, died on May 31 but the cause of death wasn't released. Stay up to date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 There are 20 fire stations and 523 firefighters in the county, according to the agency's website. Information regarding memorial arrangements and opportunities to honor Hodge's service iwll be shared in coordination with his family as details are finalized. "His death is a profound loss to the St. Lucie County Fire District and the fire service community," the agency said. "The District extends its heartfelt condolences to Hodge’s family, friends, and fellow firefighters during this difficult time." Several agencies offered their condolences, including Port St. Lucie Fire Rescue, Fort Pierce Police Officers Association, Port St. Lucie Police Department, Indian River County Sheriff's Office, Indian River County Emergency Services Department, Indian River County Fire Rescue, Palm Beach County Fire Rescue, Riviera Beach Fire Rescue. https://www.facebook.com/stluciesheriff/posts/pfbid0cPopWYk7mLx2z6QfJqkd99ZUoP9dWGSRx3Y7yjuN21oLAqBUmr6n8RYoUYP9RGaZl The St. Lucie agency thanked other agencieson Facebook. https://www.facebook.com/slcfd/posts/pfbid02FGoAgmLryFmnkCkLqRQfwhzpBpGAX3Bh285A6jFqKysGajonPUPDHeKjxdFm2KQvl "In the hours following this heartbreaking loss, our firefighters, Honor Guard, and public safety partners came together to honor our fallen brother and stand alongside one another during an incredibly difficult time. The brotherhood of the fire service extends far beyond the walls of a fire station. It is a bond built on trust, shared experiences, and an unwavering commitment to one another. "Today, that bond was especially evident through the incredible support of the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Fort Pierce Police Department, Port St. Lucie Police Department, and peer support teams from Martin and Indian River counties. "Together, they offered strength, compassion, and support while ensuring Austin was honored with the dignity and respect he deserves. Our hearts are with Austin’s family, loved ones, and everyone who had the privilege of serving alongside him. We are deeply grateful to our fellow first responders and community for the outpouring of support during this tremendous loss." Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

entry.title: Buc-ee's plan for St. Lucie County moves forward, with opening still listed for 2027
entry.summary: Plans to bring a Buc-ee's travel center to the Treasure Coast are continuing to move forward. During questioning from a St. Lucie County commissioner last week, county Planning Director Ben Balser said Buc-ee's has received site plan approval and its building permits are currently under review. Balser said the county is ready to move forward once Buc-ee's addresses the remaining comments from county staff. Plans for the travel center were first announced in 2023. The project calls for a 120-pump location off Indrio Road off Interstate 95 in St. Lucie County. Buc-ee's website continues to list the location as opening in 2027. The Texas-based travel center chain is known for its large stores and expansive fueling areas. The St. Lucie County location would bring the popular chain to the Treasure Coast.

entry.title: Air defense systems spotted on barge outside Mar-a-Lago as security measures expand
entry.summary: More defense capabilities are being added outside Mar-a-Lago to protect President Donald Trump when he visits his private club. On Monday, WPTV spotted two ground-based air defense assets aboard a barge that was floating in the Intracoastal Waterway outside Mar-a-Lago. WATCH BELOW: Barge with air defense assets spotted outside Mar-a-Lago Air defense systems spotted on barge outside Mar-a-Lago These new details come after WPTV reported Friday that NORAD and USNORTHCOM confirmed they deployed assets in and around Mar-a-Lago at the Secret Service's request. It's unclear if a specific threat prompted the deployment of these defense systems. 'Due to security considerations, we cannot provide tactics, techniques and procedural specifics,' NORAD said in a statement. Also, NORAD said one of its F-16s intercepted a plane that flew into restricted airspace Saturday near Mar-a-Lago. 'After the fighter jet executed a standard headbutt maneuver to gain the pilots attention, the civilian aircraft established communication and safely exited the restricted airspace in full compliance with flight instructions,' NORAD said in a statement. According to the military, pilots who violate restricted airspace may also be met by federal authorities upon landing and subject to enforcement action. WPTV reporter Joel Lopez reported this month that fighter pilots have intercepted more than 60 aircraft violating temporary flight restrictions around Palm Beach since January 2025.

entry.title: Trump heads to Mississippi as more red states enter the midterm conversation with 8 days to go
entry.summary: The final full week of campaigning has begun after a weekend of bitter attacks on all sides. This week, more red states are entering the conversation for being potentially competitive and so are legal challenges from the Trump administration. President Donald Trump is heading to Mississippi Monday, another traditionally conservative state that few talked about as being competitive earlier this year. But after a number of high-profile visits by Democrats to campaign for Democrat Scott Colom, including former Vice President Kamala Harris, it has entered the conversation. RELATED STORY | Democrats tout momentum as early voting rises ahead of midterms While current Mississippi Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith is still favored, she has faced criticism for months after being asked about beef prices and suggesting there are other proteins to eat. Trump told reporters he thinks his frequent rallies are helping. 'I have heard we have turned the whole thing around and for whatever reason presidents don't win the midterms and I think we really turned it around and I think the rallies have turned it,' Trump said. Trump and Obama duel on the campaign trail Trump is also dueling with former President Barack Obama on the campaign trail this week, with Obama campaigning in Ohio and Michigan and mocking the former president in the process. 'Guy's building a ballroom bigger than White House, paved over the Rose Garden, put a helipad on the south lawn,' Obama said at one rally. 'And there is gold everywhere. What's up with the gold? He has got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.' MORE ELECTION NEWS | Young voter turnout could be pivotal in this year's midterms Polls show Democrats maintaining an edge with 8 days to go before the midterms. But Republicans remain very skeptical of polling. A closely watched race in Alaska One of the biggest races is in Alaska, where Democratic nominee Mary Peltola was involved in a car accident over the weekend, sustaining minor injuries. This comes after the Department of Justice has sued to block Alaska certification, citing concerns that incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan is facing another Dan Sullivan on the ballot. 'That is very unfair, that's just outright cheating,' Trump said.

entry.title: St. Lucie County firefighter paramedic Austin Hodge dies after being found unresponsive on duty - WFLX
entry.summary: St. Lucie County firefighter paramedic Austin Hodge dies after being found unresponsive on duty    WFLX
entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire District firefighter who died unexpectedly Saturday morning has been identified as Austin Hodge, a firefighter paramedic and nine-year veteran of the department. The fire district announced Hodge was found unresponsive in his bunk during a shift change. He was taken to the hospital and passed away. Lucie County firefighter dies on duty "Today, our St. Lucie County Fire District family mourns the loss of one of our own," the district said in a statement. In the hours following his death, firefighters, the department's Honor Guard and fellow first responders gathered to honor Hodge and support one another. The district said the response reflected the strong bond shared throughout the fire service. The district thanked the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Fort Pierce Police Department, Port St. Lucie Police Department and peer support teams from Martin and Indian River counties for providing assistance and standing alongside firefighters during the difficult day. "Together, they offered strength, compassion, and support while ensuring Austin was honored with the dignity and respect he deserves," the district said. The district said its thoughts are with Hodge's family, loved ones and everyone who served alongside him. They respectfully ask that Hodge's family be given privacy during this time. "We are deeply grateful to our fellow first responders and community for the outpouring of support during this tremendous loss," the district said. "Today and always, we stand together." The tragedy comes more than a year after the community mourned the sudden loss of his brother, Jarius Hodge , 26, who was also a St. Lucie County firefighter and died from septic shock in July 2025. The district said it will share information on funeral and memorial services in coordination with the family when it becomes available.

entry.title: Watches, warnings, and advisories in place across the Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches - WPEC
entry.summary: Watches, warnings, and advisories in place across the Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches    WPEC
entry.article_text: A long list of watches, warnings and advisories is in place across the Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches, with coastal flooding, strong winds and dangerous beach and boating conditions among the main concerns. Note: Alert expiration times may differ across the region because Palm Beach County is covered by the Miami forecast office, while Indian River, St. Lucie, Martin and Okeechobee counties are covered by the Melbourne office. Coastal Flood Warning A Coastal Flood Warning is in effect until 8 p.m. Wednesday, October 28th for coastal Palm Beach County. One is in effect until 2 a.m. Thursday, October 29th for coastal Indian River, St. Lucie, and Martin counties. Coastal roads may be closed. Low lying property including homes, businesses and some critical infrastructure will be inundated. Significant shoreline erosion will occur. Wind Advisory A Wind Advisory is in effect from 11 a.m. Monday, October 26th, until 8 p.m. Tuesday, October 27th, for metro and coastal Palm Beach County. One is in effect until 8 p.m. Monday, October 26th, for coastal Indian River, St. Lucie and Martin counties. Northeast winds of 20 to 25 mph are expected, with gusts up to 40 mph in Palm Beach County and up to 35 mph along the Treasure Coast. Gusts could blow around unsecured objects, break tree limbs and cause isolated power outages. High Surf Advisory A High Surf Advisory is in effect until 8 p.m. Wednesday, October 28th, for coastal Palm Beach County. One is in effect until 2 a.m. Thursday, October 29th, for coastal Indian River, St. Lucie and Martin counties. Breaking waves of 8 to 13 feet are possible along the Palm Beaches, with 7 to 11 feet forecast for the Treasure Coast. Dangerous swimming and surfing conditions are expected, along with localized beach erosion. High Rip Current Risk A High Rip Current Risk is in effect through Wednesday evening, October 28th, for coastal Palm Beach County. One is in effect through late Wednesday night for coastal Indian River, St. Lucie and Martin counties. Dangerous rip currents can pull even experienced swimmers away from shore. Entering the water is strongly discouraged. Gale Warning A Gale Warning is in effect until 2 a.m. Wednesday, October 28th, for nearshore waters from Sebastian Inlet to Jupiter Inlet and nearby offshore waters. entry.title: Seminole Ridge flag football eyes third straight state title
entry.summary: Greatness doesn't happen overnight; it takes countless hours and endless repetition. Over the past two years, the girls' flag football team at Seminole Ridge High School has won 37 games and lost only four, while winning two straight championships. WATCH BELOW: Seminole Ridge flag football eyes 3rd straight state title Seminole Ridge flag football eyes 3rd straight state title 'It's an amazing feeling that the girls are so hungry and into flag football. They love what they do and work so hard. It's really a joy to be the coach,' head coach Scott O'Hara said. His joy as a coach comes from having the best team in Florida. The girls are sure-handed, disciplined, and have fun while doing it. 'If we're too serious with the team, then it's going to be a lot of tension with the team, but adding the jokes and the calmness helps keep the balance between everything,' said Samantha Musgrave, the team captain. She knows the girls have a chance to win three straight titles, but takes it day by day. 'This upcoming season I expect for us to win some games. It's all about who puts in the most work, and I think our team puts in even more work than we need to, for sure,' said Musgrave. One reason the girls can let their hair down and be free is thanks to Chachi Saunders, but on the field she's a playmaker. From game-winning catches in the championship to leading the team in almost every statistical category, 17 interceptions last season, and even earning First Team All-Defensive honors. To cap it all off, she's the first flag footballer in Palm Beach County to commit to a Division I school for flag football. 'I didn't know this would ever happen, but I'm so proud and so happy to have all of my coaches to help me and my team being on my back,' said Saunders.

entry.article_text: A proposal that could provide property-tax relief to Florida homeowners is raising concerns among Palm Beach County nonprofit leaders who worry the savings could come with consequences for organizations serving families already struggling to make ends meet.Nearly 100 people gathered in Wellington Monday for a presentation hosted by the Nonprofit Chamber of Palm Beach County focused on the potential community impact of Amendment 3, including what organizers say it could mean for nonprofit funding and local services.WATCH BELOW: Nonprofits raise concerns over Amendment 3A statewide survey by the Florida Nonprofit Alliance found that 92% of nonprofits surveyed said they would face an impact if Amendment 3 passes. Of those surveyed, 65% reported they may have to cut programs or services or turn clients away.Monday's panel featured the following speakers:Leah McDermott, vice president of Policy & Programs at the Florida Nonprofit AllianceFormer Palm Beach County Deputy Administrator Tammy Fields Jennifer Sullivan, senior vice president of the Cultural Council for Palm Beach CountyPastor Rae Whitely of Faith in Florida"The nonprofit chamber is really trying to educate the community about Amendment 3 and its impact specifically on the nonprofit community as it relates to programming that is funded through the county and special taxing districts like Children's Services Council and the Healthcare District," said Michelle Gonzalez, president of the Nonprofit Chamber.Gonzalez said nonprofits across Palm Beach County provide a wide range of services."They're serving pregnant women, children, families, education, childcare, health, you name it. The nonprofit community is doing it, and I don't think people realize the impact on the hundreds of thousands of residents throughout Palm Beach County that are utilizing these services," Gonzalez said.She said the discussion surrounding Amendment 3 is complicated by the potential savings for homeowners."When you look at the property tax valuations, you're talking about $166 on an average home that's about $350,000. So that's how much they would invest in a year in that property tax," Gonzalez said.But Gonzalez said nonprofit organizations rely on funding from several sources, including special taxing districts."It's absolutely crucial. The nonprofit community is working with private funders and individual donors, but we also do rely on special taxing districts like Children's Services Council, like the Healthcare District, to provide services that those entities can't, that the county government cannot," Gonzalez said.She said Children's Services Council could face a significant reduction."When you talk about special taxing districts like Children's Services Council, they're looking at a $25 million reduction in their budget by 2028. And so that's a huge hit to the more than 700 nonprofits that are being funded through them," Gonzalez said.That potential ripple effect was one of the biggest concerns raised during the event.Ruth, who said she is with CROS Ministries, an organization that helps provide people with access to healthy food, said she came to learn how Amendment 3 could affect both nonprofit organizations and the residents walking through their doors."What brought me out here is to hear what the impact of Amendment 3 is on our community and also on the people that we serve, because it's going to affect the funding that's coming to nonprofits, but also, at the end of the day, affect the people that are coming in through our doors," she said.She said one of her biggest takeaways was that the impact could reach beyond homeowners."So one of the things that I learned is the fact that renters are going to be affected, that there's a trickle down, and although some funds, although some agencies may not be getting funding directly from property taxes, it's going to increase the number of people who are coming into our agencies," Ruth said.She described the potential impact as a "circle domino effect.""Yes, it's a circle domino effect that will affect everybody, and I think if we really look at it, even for those of us who may not be affected financially, at the end of the day, our community, we have our brothers, we have our sisters, we have our neighbors. So at the end of the day, what affects one affects all of us," Ruth said.Whiteley, an organizer with Faith in Florida and CEO of Trinity Counseling Center, was one of the panel speakers."Saving money shouldn't come at the cost of somebody else's expense," Whiteley said.He acknowledged that property taxes are a concern but said he does not believe Amendment 3 is the answer."Absolutely. I think that property taxes are definitely a problem and we have to address it. This is just not the way," Whiteley said."We really have to study impact or consequences before we make decisions, and I don't think that we've had a, we haven't had an opportunity to study the consequences or the long-term impact on the state of Florida. This was rushed, so we have to do something. I just don't believe that Amendment 3 is that option because we haven't studied the consequences," he added.Then came a question Whiteley said churches may eventually have to confront."If they can't meet that need, you have people who are already struggling, struggle more, and they always come back to the church. And with the church itself struggling, we, we will have our doors open," he said. "But how long can we sustain it? The collection plate should not be a substitute for a county budget," Whiteley said.Whiteley said some nonprofits are already dealing with financial challenges even before any potential effects from Amendment 3."Yeah, there are nonprofit organizations that we're speaking with that are saying that their budget has already been cut 20 to 30% and they had to make layoffs, right? And that's not post Amendment 3," Whiteley said."When they lose more funding, they will have to decide whether they're gonna keep those doors open, or they're gonna try to find funding in other areas," he added.Trudy Crowetz with Nonprofits First said the gathering brought together organizations working in different areas of the community."So I'm out here to help the nonprofit sector understand the implications of Amendment 3, the property tax amendment, so we are involved with all of our different types of nonprofits, health and human services, arts and culture, family services, education, so we serve every cause, so we want to make sure that our constituents are well informed about the implications of property tax amendment number 3," Crowetz said.She said Palm Beach County's economic diversity is an important part of the conversation."Because I know that Palm Beach County is a very diverse county and so there are, like I mentioned, areas of wealth and pockets of poverty as well so, keeping that in mind we talk about that as a statewide perspective but we also, we need to figure that out as a county how that's going to affect the different areas within our county," Crowetz said.Gonzalez said those economic differences are also why nonprofits are focused on residents who may have jobs but continue to struggle with basic expenses."There's this population called the ALICE population that United Way of Palm Beach County is really pushing forward. It's asset-limited, income-constrained, but employed, and it's this pocket of individuals and families across the community that are working sometimes two and three jobs, but they're still struggling to make ends meet. That's the area, that's the population that we're trying to serve," Gonzalez said.With Election Day approaching, Gonzalez said the chamber's goal is to get information in front of voters who are still making their decision."Very much so. We are trying to do our part in advocating through the nonprofit chamber so that we can really educate the community, those who really haven't made their decision yet on which way they want to vote. That's what today is all about," Gonzalez said.Whiteley said the gathering now needs to translate into greater community involvement."I think today went really well. I think that whenever you have over 100 people in a room sharing a message, that's important, right? Now, how do we move from being attendees to being organizers?" Whiteley said.His final message focused less on organizations and more on the people who make up the community."Stay involved. Think about the impact that it will have on your neighbor, and let's start thinking more as a collective and not individually," Whiteley said.In Florida, all constitutional amendments require a 60% vote to be approved.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: 85-year-old West Palm Beach woman says hospital stay cost her $10K My Safe Florida Home grant
entry.summary: A West Palm Beach homeowner says she was locked out of the My Safe Florida Home program while she was in the hospital with a broken hip. 'I applied for it, and they told me you're doing fine, and then when I got out of the hospital and got here, I called them up, or I texted them, and they said, 'You haven't responded to our emails, so it's over,'' Barbara Madewell said. WATCH BELOW: Woman, 85, says hospital stay cost her $10K home grant Woman, 85, says hospital stay cost her $10K home grant She tells me she had recently completed her second home inspection with the program after replacing windows and a roof before she broke her hip during a fall in early September. The 85-year-old said she spent more than weeks in two hospitals for surgery and then had physical therapy. She was hoping to resume the process with the program to get a $10,000 grant to offset her costs of over $60,000. 'It's very frustrating to me, very frustrating,' she said. 'I'm all by myself. I have no income other than my husband's pension and Social Security.' The My Safe Florida Home program has helped thousands of homeowners with storm-strengthening repairs to lower insurance costs. In the last two years, the program was changed by lawmakers to prioritize low-income and senior homeowners. The program can take months to complete, and it is also known for strict deadlines, forcing many homeowners to keep close watch on emails and texts. I have reached out to the state Department of Financial Services with information about Madewell's situation.
