entry.article_text: The race to be Florida's next governor is a competitive one — a statistical tie, according to a poll released last week by the University of North Florida.I caught up with Republican Byron Donalds and Democrat David Jolly as they each campaigned across the state, pitching different visions of Florida's future to voters.WATCH BELOW: Donalds, Jolly pitch competing visions in tight governor's raceDonalds, a Republican congressman, told me in a video call from his campaign bus on the road that he wants to build on the policies he likes from Gov. Ron DeSantis' outgoing administration."We live in a great state, and what has separated us from the other states is we continue to choose common sense conservative policy," Donalds said.That includes immigration enforcement."We're going to continue that mission here in the great state of Florida because we are going to continue to follow the law. I think that's the appropriate use of state authority and state powers," Donalds said.It also includes Florida's Department of Government Efficiency, which DeSantis formed through an executive order in 2025 and has since conducted audits of multiple counties across Florida."We are going to DOGE all governments, both local and state agencies in the state of Florida, because it's not our tax money. It belongs to the people of Florida. We need to make sure that government lives within its means, the way families have to live within their means," Donalds said.Donalds told me that effort will be important if Amendment 3 passes, raising homestead tax exemptions and reducing local revenue. I asked him whether, as governor, he would be prepared if some of the municipalities that need help come to Tallahassee asking for it."Yes, we will, and we've already made a public commitment to the fiscally constrained counties in the state of Florida," Donalds said. "Those that we know that their budgets are going to change in a major way, that we're prepared to provide a funding formula for those fiscally constrained counties so that they can be able to make ends meet."Jolly, a Democrat who served as a Republican in Congress during the 2010s, visited WPTV as his campaign traveled through Palm Beach County. He has said he personally opposes Amendment 3, but will support the will of the voters if it passes."I think we all want the math behind Amendment 3 to work, but it just doesn't," Jolly said.Florida hasn't elected a Democrat as governor since the 1990s. I asked Jolly why he thinks that is and why he believes his campaign could overcome that."Look, we're a state that trended Republican, particularly in the last eight years, and we know by voter registration it's still a predominantly Republican state," Jolly said. "I think we're in a moment most akin to a 1974 post-Watergate moment, where voters are saying, 'Burn the ships. Let's go in a new direction.'"Jolly said that direction should be simple."Housing, healthcare, education, and no data centers. "The answers are not in ideology. The answers are in solutions."He also said he wants to reach across the aisle to achieve those goals."If we expand health care access, we reduce costs. So you can be a conservative that wants to save money or a progressive that wants more health care. When we invest in public education, we create a resilient economy that should be attractive to Republicans. The economic argument behind that, I think, on housing, when more people have stable housing, the economy is better. I think we can work with Republicans," Jolly said.One issue where the two candidates agree is on school choice. Both told me they support keeping universal vouchers in place.Jolly also emphasized his desire to increase transparency requirements in Florida's charter schools and increase teacher pay in public schools."Let's engage in a little bit of consumer protection here on behalf of kids and families, and say that if you're going to take a voucher as a school, you should have to provide the same services, standards and offerings and be measured by the same measuring stick that our public schools are," Jolly said.Asked whether financial records of charter schools should be public records, as they are for public schools, Donalds replied, "I think if you're talking about what parents are looking for, what they want to basically see, are the children being educated? What are the mathematical attainment scores of that school? What are the reading attainment scores of that school? And if you're talking about high school, what's the ACT scores and what's the SAT scores? I think that's the accountability and the transparency that parents are looking for in the state of Florida, because at the end of the day, they're looking to make sure that the output is where it needs to be."Donalds' wife, Erika Donalds, founded a charter school company and currently runs a nonprofit promoting school choice. "My wife is actually not in the charter school business anymore. She's actually been out of that business for a couple of years," Donalds told me. "But I just want to be clear: she will not be contracting with the state of Florida in any way, shape, or form."On data center policy, the candidates differ. Jolly said he supports a moratorium on data center construction, while Donalds believes those decisions should be left up to local governments."If a local government says no data centers, then no data centers. If they do, then where the state steps in is we make sure that utility bills, utility costs are not passed on to consumers, and we also make sure that we are going to protect water resources in our state," Donalds said.For the first time in decades, Florida voters did not get to see a gubernatorial debate for this election.Asked what he would say to Jolly had the two candidates faced one another on the debate stage, Donalds said, "I would like him to explain why and how the people of Florida are going to be able to pay for his insurance plan, because by independent analysis, his insurance plan will drive up premiums on the people of our state, and everybody will be hit with a $1,000 hurricane tax when the next time the big storm comes through," referring to the funding the sovereign wealth fund Jolly says he would like to create to cover windstorm damage for Florida homeowners. (Jolly has denied that the fund would impose a new tax.)"I'm not sure debates improve our politics at this point. I think they just platform the division and the vitriol and the ugliness," Jolly told me. "My wife says in a world of Donald Trump, I'm trying to be Ted Lasso. We have two young kids, and I want them to look back and know that Dad acted in a way that he spoke of, which was not to further devolve our politics into vitriol and ugliness and division. Debates are about who can score the greatest insult, and I just I don't think that helps."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Trump heads to Mississippi as more red states enter the midterm conversation with 8 days to go
entry.summary: The final full week of campaigning has begun after a weekend of bitter attacks on all sides. This week, more red states are entering the conversation for being potentially competitive and so are legal challenges from the Trump administration. President Donald Trump is heading to Mississippi Monday, another traditionally conservative state that few talked about as being competitive earlier this year. But after a number of high-profile visits by Democrats to campaign for Democrat Scott Colom, including former Vice President Kamala Harris, it has entered the conversation. WATCH: Latino voters in Texas are a critical constituency as the race gets close Texas candidates reach out to Latino voters as midterm deadline looms RELATED STORY | Democrats tout momentum as early voting rises ahead of midterms While current Mississippi Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith is still favored, she has faced criticism for months after being asked about beef prices and suggesting there are other proteins to eat. Trump told reporters he thinks his frequent rallies are helping. 'I have heard we have turned the whole thing around and for whatever reason presidents don't win the midterms and I think we really turned it around and I think the rallies have turned it,' Trump said. Trump and Obama duel on the campaign trail Trump is also dueling with former President Barack Obama on the campaign trail this week, with Obama campaigning in Ohio and Michigan and mocking the former president in the process. 'Guy's building a ballroom bigger than White House, paved over the Rose Garden, put a helipad on the south lawn,' Obama said at one rally. 'And there is gold everywhere. What's up with the gold? He has got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.' MORE ELECTION NEWS | Young voter turnout could be pivotal in this year's midterms Polls show Democrats maintaining an edge with 8 days to go before the midterms. But Republicans remain very skeptical of polling. A closely watched race in Alaska One of the biggest races is in Alaska, where Democratic nominee Mary Peltola was involved in a car accident over the weekend, sustaining minor injuries. This comes after the Department of Justice has sued to block Alaska certification, citing concerns that incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan is facing another Dan Sullivan on the ballot. 'That is very unfair, that's just outright cheating,' Trump said.

entry.title: St. Lucie County firefighter paramedic Austin Hodge dies after being found unresponsive on duty
entry.summary: A St. Lucie County Fire District firefighter who died unexpectedly Saturday morning has been identified as Austin Hodge, a firefighter paramedic and nine-year veteran of the department. The fire district announced Hodge was found unresponsive in his bunk during a shift change. He was taken to the hospital and passed away. WATCH REPORT BELOW: St. Lucie County firefighter dies on duty St. Lucie County community mourns firefighter who died on duty 'Today, our St. Lucie County Fire District family mourns the loss of one of our own,' the district said in a statement. In the hours following his death, firefighters, the department's Honor Guard and fellow first responders gathered to honor Hodge and support one another. The district said the response reflected the strong bond shared throughout the fire service. The district thanked the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Fort Pierce Police Department, Port St. Lucie Police Department and peer support teams from Martin and Indian River counties for providing assistance and standing alongside firefighters during the difficult day. 'Together, they offered strength, compassion, and support while ensuring Austin was honored with the dignity and respect he deserves,' the district said. The district said its thoughts are with Hodge's family, loved ones and everyone who served alongside him. They respectfully ask that Hodge's family be given privacy during this time. 'We are deeply grateful to our fellow first responders and community for the outpouring of support during this tremendous loss,' the district said. 'Today and always, we stand together.' The tragedy comes more than a year after the community mourned the sudden loss of his brother, Jarius Hodge , 26, who was also a St. Lucie County firefighter and died from septic shock in July 2025. The district said it will share information on funeral and memorial services in coordination with the family when it becomes available.

entry.title: 'A smile that lights up the room': Loved ones remember St. Lucie County firefighter - WPEC
entry.summary: 'A smile that lights up the room': Loved ones remember St. Lucie County firefighter    WPEC
entry.article_text: Family and friends are mourning St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge, a man those closest to him describe as endlessly positive and devoted to serving his community. A funeral procession for Hodge left the Medical Examiner’s Office in Fort Pierce at 2 p.m. Monday and traveled to Stone Brothers Funeral Home. Lucie County Sheriff's Office went to the station at 7:25 a.m. 24, regarding a "full cardiac arrest," and Hoge was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. His death comes about 15 months after his younger brother, Jarius Hodge, also a St. Lucie County Fire District firefighter and paramedic, died in July 2025 after falling ill during a shift. The district honored Jarius with line-of-duty honors. After his brother’s death, Austin spent months searching for answers. He told CBS12 News in January that Jarius caught the flu from a patient and died hours after arriving at Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital in Port St. Lucie, struggling to breathe. Austin said medical records showed doctors made critical mistakes, including needing three attempts to intubate his brother. CBS12 reached out to the hospital at the time and did not receive a response before that story was published. Because Jarius was over 25 and had no spouse or children, Florida’s so-called free kill law barred his family from suing for medical malpractice. Austin pushed state lawmakers to repeal it and started a petition in his brother’s honor. He said the fight was about accountability, not money. Bernard Taylor has known Austin since their school days in Sebastian. Taylor was a senior and Austin a freshman when they met at the Boys and Girls Club, where Taylor worked as a counselor and Austin was one of the kids he mentored. Taylor said Austin always wanted to keep up with the older kids, and the two formed a bond that lasted for years. Later, when Taylor decided to change careers, Austin was one of the first people he called. Taylor said Austin supported him through becoming a firefighter, from answering questions to helping him with his conditioning. Just a ball of positive energy. A smile that lights up the room. No matter what you’re going through, he had the right words to kind of get you through it, Taylor said. Taylor said he spoke with Austin about a week before his death to make sure he was doing well. He said he is most heartbroken for Austin’s mother, who has now lost both of her sons. That’s one of the strongest people I’ve ever met in my life. I don’t know if I can hold it together if I was her, Taylor said. Bonnie Hill, a family friend who helped raise Austin’s mother, said she has been by her side and that the family is leaning on its faith and a strong circle of support. I say on my watch, I’m not going to let you die. You’re going to live, and we’re going to get through this, Hill said of what she has told Austin’s mother. Hill said that faith is what is carrying the family now. See also: King tides cause coastal flooding, beach closures in Palm Beach County and Treasure Coast We believe God even in this. We believe God, and we stand on the promises because they won’t fail, Hill said. Taylor said he hopes people remember Austin for his love of serving others. He was a person who loved what he did. He was a person who loved serving his community, Taylor said. Lucie County Fire District has not released details about Austin Hodge’s death.

entry.title: Strong winds, king tides flood parts of Martin County as officials warn of more high water
entry.summary: WPTV has been following flooding on the Treasure Coast caused by strong winds and king tides on Monday. In Martin County, off Dyer Point Road in Palm City, parts of the area were completely underwater. WATCH BELOW: Flooding swamps parts of Palm City amid king tides, strong winds King tides, strong winds flood areas of Martin County Terresa Baldwin, who lives off the roadway, said it was flooded for a few hours, but water has since retreated. 'You could smell the sewage; it was really stinky, it was bad,' Baldwin said. 'There were dead copperheads, so the snakes are coming out. They're getting flushed out with the water.' Baldwin said she was also dealing with flooding in her backyard along one of the finger canals. She showed WPTV the water over her dock and in her new patio. 'The wind was blowing so hard, so it was like waves crashing in your backyard, and you're like, no, nobody wants to see that,' Baldwin said. Despite the water going down, she is still worried about what could happen in the next few days. 'The biggest concern for us is getting water from both sides. What do you do, especially when you're trying to sleep, and you don't know if the water's going to come up more or what's going to get damaged at night when you really can't see,' Baldwin said.  With high tide later Monday night, the sheriffs office told WPTV the situation could get worse. Lt. Dave Rosko said they have three high-water vehicles ready for rescue efforts and urged neighbors to think twice before driving through the water. 'Understand the limitations of your vehicle and do not drive through the high waters,' Rosko said. 'If your vehicle gets disabled there, it may turn into a rescue event where we need to come out and ensure your safety.' Rosko said neighbors living in coastal communities should be aware of future tides before traveling.

entry.title: 23-year-old Road Ranger hit, killed after car enters I-95 crash scene, hits FHP cruiser in Lantana
entry.summary: A 23-year-old Road Ranger from West Palm Beach was killed early Sunday after a driver entered a lane closure at an Interstate 95 crash investigation scene and struck him before hitting a Florida Highway Patrol cruiser, according to FHP. The crash happened around 2:07 a.m. on northbound I-95 near Lantana Road in Palm Beach County. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Road Ranger hit, killed on I-95 in Lantana According to FHP, a 2019 Mercedes sedan driven by an 18-year-old Lake Worth woman was traveling north in the inside center lane. At the time, a marked FHP Dodge Charger was stationary across the inside and inside center lanes with its emergency lights activated as part of a lane closure for an ongoing crash investigation. Investigators said the Mercedes entered the closed lane and struck the 23-year-old Road Ranger. The car then rotated and collided with the FHP cruiser. The man was pronounced dead at the scene. His identity has not been released. The 18-year-old driver suffered non-incapacitating injuries and was taken to JFK South for treatment. The outside northbound lane of I-95 reopened at 8:34 a.m., according to FHP. The name of the Road Ranger who was killed has not been released.

entry.title: Palm Beach Co. voters to decide whether to renew school tax funding teacher pay, safety and student programs
entry.summary: Palm Beach County voters will decide Nov. 3 whether to renew an existing 1-mill property tax for public schools for four more years, continuing funding for teacher pay, school safety, mental health services and student programs through June 30, 2031. The referendum is a renewal, not a new tax. According to the School District of Palm Beach County, the 1-mill levy has supported local schools since 2019. Voters approved the levy in 2018 and renewed it in 2022. If approved again, the measure would take effect July 1, 2027, after the current authorization expires, and automatically end June 30, 2031. What would the Palm Beach County school referendum fund? The ballot language says money from the tax would be dedicated to school safety, school police, mental health services, arts, music, physical education, career and choice program teachers, and improved teacher pay. An independent committee of citizens and experts would oversee the funds. According to the district, half of the funding currently supports teacher salary supplements, while 25% supports more than 900 career and choice, arts, music and other specialized teaching positions. The remaining 25% supports mental health services, school police and security staff. Students speak out in support Some students who are too young to cast ballots are speaking in support of the referendum and highlighting the impact they believe the measure has on their schools. 'Teacher issues are everybody's issues,' referendum supporter Sawyer Tinsley told WPTV. Tinsley said the issue extends beyond what students experience inside the classroom. 'It goes much further than just high school and high school education. It really impacts our future and the future of our country,' Tinsley said. What happens if the referendum fails? The School District of Palm Beach County says the local funding currently provides teachers salary supplements averaging about $8,000 annually. The money also funds more than 900 teaching positions in areas including art, music and physical education. According to the district, those teaching positions and programs would face cuts without the funding. entry.article_text: Palm Beach County voters will decide Nov. 3 whether to renew an existing 1-mill property tax for public schools for four more years, continuing funding for teacher pay, school safety, mental health services and student programs through June 30, 2031.The referendum is a renewal, not a new tax. According to the School District of Palm Beach County, the 1-mill levy has supported local schools since 2019. Voters approved the levy in 2018 and renewed it in 2022. If approved again, the measure would take effect July 1, 2027, after the current authorization expires, and automatically end June 30, 2031.The ballot language says money from the tax would be dedicated to school safety, school police, mental health services, arts, music, physical education, career and choice program teachers, and improved teacher pay. An independent committee of citizens and experts would oversee the funds. According to the district, half of the funding currently supports teacher salary supplements, while 25% supports more than 900 career and choice, arts, music and other specialized teaching positions. The remaining 25% supports mental health services, school police and security staff. Some students who are too young to cast ballots are speaking in support of the referendum and highlighting the impact they believe the measure has on their schools."Teacher issues are everybody's issues," referendum supporter Sawyer Tinsley told WPTV.Tinsley said the issue extends beyond what students experience inside the classroom."It goes much further than just high school and high school education. It really impacts our future and the future of our country," Tinsley said.The School District of Palm Beach County says the local funding currently provides teachers salary supplements averaging about $8,000 annually. The money also funds more than 900 teaching positions in areas including art, music and physical education. According to the district, those teaching positions and programs would face cuts without the funding. The League of Women Voters of Palm Beach County's referendum synopsis also states that if voters reject the measure, teachers would face an average $8,000 annual reduction in pay and more than 900 teaching positions in the arts, physical education and choice programs would be eliminated.Ultimately, Palm Beach County voters will determine whether the existing levy continues for another four years when they cast their ballots Nov. 3.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Dangerous surf, king tides bring coastal flooding and beach erosion concerns to Juno Beach
entry.summary: Strong winds, rough surf and king tides are creating dangerous beach conditions and raising concerns about coastal flooding along Juno Beach, while nearby Jupiter has temporarily closed four dune crossovers because of beach erosion. WATCH: Powerful waves hit the Palm Beach County coast Powerful Waves, King Tides Impact Juno Beach Coast | WPTV Despite the hazardous conditions, the powerful waves are drawing people to the Palm Beach County coastline to see the surf firsthand. Residents who spoke with WPTV said they kept their distance as waves crashed along the shore. Dangerous conditions are expected to continue through midweek, making the combination of breaking waves, erosion and possible flooding in low-lying areas an ongoing concern for beachgoers. Powerful waves draw spectators to Juno Beach Jupiter resident Rachel Hooker brought visiting family members to the coast specifically to see the waves. 'My aunt's 86. My uncle's 91. We traveled all the way here just to see the waves actually,' Hooker said. 'They heard that it was going to be powerful and beautiful, and that's why we're here.' Hooker told WPTV she saw people venturing into the water but was more comfortable watching the conditions from shore. 'Terrifying. How crazy is it to be out here?' Hooker said. 'You know, they're really brave, honestly, but yeah, I'm not sure I'm that brave, but it's really cool to see.' For her family, the attraction was the ocean's power, viewed from a safer distance. 'Powerful and beautiful,' Hooker said. 'Yeah, we wouldn't miss it.' Jupiter closes four dune crossovers The rough conditions are also affecting beaches in nearby Jupiter. The Town of Jupiter has temporarily closed dune crossovers 48, 49 and 50, along with the Civic Center crossover, because of beach erosion. The town asks beachgoers to use other access points and avoid walking on the dunes, which officials say can contribute to further erosion. Coastal flooding remains a concern Along with dangerous surf, coastal flooding is a concern around high tide as king tides and strong winds affect the coastline. Beachgoers should stay clear of breaking waves and watch for flooding in low-lying coastal areas as rough conditions continue. For people like Hooker and her family, the ocean may offer a dramatic sight, but their approach is simple: admire it from a distance. entry.title: St. Lucie County honors firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge after line-of-duty death
entry.summary: St. Lucie County firefighters and community members gathered to honor firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge, escorting him through the community he served after the fire district said he died Saturday and is being honored with a line-of-duty death designation. WATCH: St. Lucie County Honors Firefighter-Paramedic Austin Hodge St. Lucie County Honors Firefighter-Paramedic Austin Hodge | WPTV Hodge served the St. Lucie County Fire District for more than nine years. According to the district, he was found unresponsive in his bunk at the firehouse during shift change. Firefighters escorted Hodge from the medical examiner's office to the funeral home as colleagues and community members paid their respects along his final journey through Fort Pierce. 'A bright light' Dr. Aleta Paschal, who worked alongside Hodge outside the fire district, described him as someone whose personality made an impression on those around him. 'Austin is just a bright light,' Paschal said. 'He always made me smile. He had the biggest bear hugs. Everybody loved him.' Paschal said Hodge had a way of making the people around him feel welcomed. 'Anybody he interacted with, he made you feel like family for sure,' she said. His service extended beyond the firehouse Hodge's work caring for people extended beyond his role as a firefighter-paramedic. Paschal said Hodge also worked as a respiratory therapist, where the two cared for critically ill patients together. 'Everybody loved him,' Paschal said. 'He was a critical part of our team. He's going to be very missed at the hospital.' Within the St. Lucie County Fire District, Hodge also served on the Honor Guard and the district's Firefighter Challenge Team. Those roles added to a legacy of service that spanned more than nine years with the district. Community says goodbye As Hodge's colleagues escorted him through Fort Pierce, Paschal said she hopes people remember the qualities that made him special to those who knew him. 'Remember his smile. Remember his presence,' Paschal said. 'Just remember his strength and who he was.' The procession offered firefighters, colleagues and members of the community a chance to pay tribute to someone who spent years helping others, both at the fire district and in health care. entry.article_text: The race to be Florida's next governor is a competitive one — a statistical tie, according to a poll released last week by the University of North Florida.I caught up with Republican Byron Donalds and Democrat David Jolly as they each campaigned across the state, pitching different visions of Florida's future to voters.WATCH BELOW: Donalds, Jolly pitch competing visions in tight governor's raceDonalds, a Republican congressman, told me in a video call from his campaign bus on the road that he wants to build on the policies he likes from Gov. Ron DeSantis' outgoing administration."We live in a great state, and what has separated us from the other states is we continue to choose common sense conservative policy," Donalds said.That includes immigration enforcement."We're going to continue that mission here in the great state of Florida because we are going to continue to follow the law. I think that's the appropriate use of state authority and state powers," Donalds said.It also includes Florida's Department of Government Efficiency, which DeSantis formed through an executive order in 2025 and has since conducted audits of multiple counties across Florida."We are going to DOGE all governments, both local and state agencies in the state of Florida, because it's not our tax money. It belongs to the people of Florida. We need to make sure that government lives within its means, the way families have to live within their means," Donalds said.Donalds told me that effort will be important if Amendment 3 passes, raising homestead tax exemptions and reducing local revenue. I asked him whether, as governor, he would be prepared if some of the municipalities that need help come to Tallahassee asking for it."Yes, we will, and we've already made a public commitment to the fiscally constrained counties in the state of Florida," Donalds said. "Those that we know that their budgets are going to change in a major way, that we're prepared to provide a funding formula for those fiscally constrained counties so that they can be able to make ends meet."Jolly, a Democrat who served as a Republican in Congress during the 2010s, visited WPTV as his campaign traveled through Palm Beach County. He has said he personally opposes Amendment 3, but will support the will of the voters if it passes."I think we all want the math behind Amendment 3 to work, but it just doesn't," Jolly said.Florida hasn't elected a Democrat as governor since the 1990s. I asked Jolly why he thinks that is and why he believes his campaign could overcome that."Look, we're a state that trended Republican, particularly in the last eight years, and we know by voter registration it's still a predominantly Republican state," Jolly said. "I think we're in a moment most akin to a 1974 post-Watergate moment, where voters are saying, 'Burn the ships. Let's go in a new direction.'"Jolly said that direction should be simple."Housing, healthcare, education, and no data centers. "The answers are not in ideology. The answers are in solutions."He also said he wants to reach across the aisle to achieve those goals."If we expand health care access, we reduce costs. So you can be a conservative that wants to save money or a progressive that wants more health care. When we invest in public education, we create a resilient economy that should be attractive to Republicans. The economic argument behind that, I think, on housing, when more people have stable housing, the economy is better. I think we can work with Republicans," Jolly said.One issue where the two candidates agree is on school choice. Both told me they support keeping universal vouchers in place.Jolly also emphasized his desire to increase transparency requirements in Florida's charter schools and increase teacher pay in public schools."Let's engage in a little bit of consumer protection here on behalf of kids and families, and say that if you're going to take a voucher as a school, you should have to provide the same services, standards and offerings and be measured by the same measuring stick that our public schools are," Jolly said.Asked whether financial records of charter schools should be public records, as they are for public schools, Donalds replied, "I think if you're talking about what parents are looking for, what they want to basically see, are the children being educated? What are the mathematical attainment scores of that school? What are the reading attainment scores of that school? And if you're talking about high school, what's the ACT scores and what's the SAT scores? I think that's the accountability and the transparency that parents are looking for in the state of Florida, because at the end of the day, they're looking to make sure that the output is where it needs to be."Donalds' wife, Erika Donalds, founded a charter school company and currently runs a nonprofit promoting school choice. "My wife is actually not in the charter school business anymore. She's actually been out of that business for a couple of years," Donalds told me. "But I just want to be clear: she will not be contracting with the state of Florida in any way, shape, or form."On data center policy, the candidates differ. Jolly said he supports a moratorium on data center construction, while Donalds believes those decisions should be left up to local governments."If a local government says no data centers, then no data centers. If they do, then where the state steps in is we make sure that utility bills, utility costs are not passed on to consumers, and we also make sure that we are going to protect water resources in our state," Donalds said.For the first time in decades, Florida voters did not get to see a gubernatorial debate for this election.Asked what he would say to Jolly had the two candidates faced one another on the debate stage, Donalds said, "I would like him to explain why and how the people of Florida are going to be able to pay for his insurance plan, because by independent analysis, his insurance plan will drive up premiums on the people of our state, and everybody will be hit with a $1,000 hurricane tax when the next time the big storm comes through," referring to the funding the sovereign wealth fund Jolly says he would like to create to cover windstorm damage for Florida homeowners. (Jolly has denied that the fund would impose a new tax.)"I'm not sure debates improve our politics at this point. I think they just platform the division and the vitriol and the ugliness," Jolly told me. "My wife says in a world of Donald Trump, I'm trying to be Ted Lasso. We have two young kids, and I want them to look back and know that Dad acted in a way that he spoke of, which was not to further devolve our politics into vitriol and ugliness and division. Debates are about who can score the greatest insult, and I just I don't think that helps."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.article_text: Lucie County firefighter-paramedic died while on duty Saturday, more than a year after his younger brother, who also served as a firefighter-paramedic, died at age 26. Lucie County Fire District announced the line-of-duty death of Austin Hodge on Saturday, Oct. 24, calling his death a profound loss to the department and the fire service community. Hodge joined the district on July 17, 2017, and served the community for more than nine years. He was assigned to Station 9. Neighboring Indian River County Fire Rescue also shared condolences following the firefighter’s unexpected death Saturday morning. Lucie County Fire District asked the public to respect Hodge’s family as they grieve. Information about memorial arrangements will be shared as details are finalized. Read more: Missing 5-year-old girl found dead in Fort Pierce body of water Brothers shared a career in firefighting Austin Hodge’s death comes more than a year after his younger brother, Jarius Hodge, also a St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic, died on July 22, 2025. The brothers shared a close bond and a passion for serving their community. This was my best friend, my twin, Austin Hodge previously told CBS12 News. We had the same hairstyle. He described Jarius as someone who loved his family and his work as a first responder. He loved going to work, loved working beside me. I loved working beside him, Austin said. He always pushed me to keep going. He was someone who loved his family, his community and his country. Family sought accountability after Jarius’ death In an interview with CBS12 News , Austin said Jarius became ill after catching the flu from a patient at work in July 2025. Austin said his younger brother went to Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital in Port St. Lucie on July 22, struggling to breathe, but died hours later. He alleged that medical staff made critical errors in treating his brother, including taking three attempts to intubate him. He said Jarius had been healthy before becoming ill. Austin also spoke publicly about Florida’s medical malpractice laws, arguing that restrictions on who can pursue certain wrongful-death claims prevented his family from seeking legal accountability for Jarius’ death. This is unjust, and it's been going on for too long, Austin said in the earlier interview. He emphasized that his family was seeking accountability rather than financial compensation. For me personally, for my family, this has nothing to do with any type of dollar, he said. We just want those physicians to be held accountable. The circumstances surrounding Austin Hodge’s death have not been released. Lucie County Fire District said additional information about ways to honor his service will be shared in coordination with his family.

Lucie County firefighter dies on duty "Today, our St. Lucie County Fire District family mourns the loss of one of our own," the district said in a statement. In the hours following his death, firefighters, the department's Honor Guard and fellow first responders gathered to honor Hodge and support one another. The district said the response reflected the strong bond shared throughout the fire service. The district thanked the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Fort Pierce Police Department, Port St. Lucie Police Department and peer support teams from Martin and Indian River counties for providing assistance and standing alongside firefighters during the difficult day. "Together, they offered strength, compassion, and support while ensuring Austin was honored with the dignity and respect he deserves," the district said. The district said its thoughts are with Hodge's family, loved ones and everyone who served alongside him. They respectfully ask that Hodge's family be given privacy during this time. "We are deeply grateful to our fellow first responders and community for the outpouring of support during this tremendous loss," the district said. "Today and always, we stand together." The tragedy comes more than a year after the community mourned the sudden loss of his brother, Jarius Hodge , 26, who was also a St. Lucie County firefighter and died from septic shock in July 2025. The district said it will share information on funeral and memorial services in coordination with the family when it becomes available.

entry.title: St. Lucie County firefighter paramedic Austin Hodge dies after being found unresponsive on duty - WFLX
entry.summary: St. Lucie County firefighter paramedic Austin Hodge dies after being found unresponsive on duty    WFLX
entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire District firefighter who died unexpectedly Saturday morning has been identified as Austin Hodge, a firefighter paramedic and nine-year veteran of the department. The fire district announced Hodge was found unresponsive in his bunk during a shift change. He was taken to the hospital and passed away. Lucie County firefighter dies on duty "Today, our St. Lucie County Fire District family mourns the loss of one of our own," the district said in a statement. In the hours following his death, firefighters, the department's Honor Guard and fellow first responders gathered to honor Hodge and support one another. The district said the response reflected the strong bond shared throughout the fire service. The district thanked the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Fort Pierce Police Department, Port St. Lucie Police Department and peer support teams from Martin and Indian River counties for providing assistance and standing alongside firefighters during the difficult day. "Together, they offered strength, compassion, and support while ensuring Austin was honored with the dignity and respect he deserves," the district said. The district said its thoughts are with Hodge's family, loved ones and everyone who served alongside him. They respectfully ask that Hodge's family be given privacy during this time. "We are deeply grateful to our fellow first responders and community for the outpouring of support during this tremendous loss," the district said. "Today and always, we stand together." The tragedy comes more than a year after the community mourned the sudden loss of his brother, Jarius Hodge , 26, who was also a St. Lucie County firefighter and died from septic shock in July 2025. The district said it will share information on funeral and memorial services in coordination with the family when it becomes available.

entry.summary: King tides cause coastal flooding, beach closures in Palm Beach County and Treasure Coast    WPEC
entry.article_text: King tides flooded streets and reached homes across Palm Beach County on Monday, while beach and road closures were reported as more high tides were expected through Wednesday. In Palm City, flooding made SW Dyer Point Road impassable. Martin County Sheriff’s Office deputies brought in three high-water vehicles to help reach anyone stranded in a vehicle or home. Flooding also was reported on SW 34th Street and Cornell Avenue. One driver told CBS12 the water was about waist-deep in part of the area. Resident Terresa Baldwin said water came up around both the front and back of her home, and that Monday’s flooding was the worst she had seen in eight years. Baldwin also raised concerns about the water’s source and smell. This is not only runoff water, it’s sewage and it’s bad and you can smell it, she said. Deputies urged people to avoid flooded areas and not to drive through standing water. These vehicles can travel through several feet of water safely, Martin County Sheriff’s Office Lt. Flooding also reached Flagler Drive in downtown West Palm Beach and Sunset Avenue on Palm Beach Island, where water covered parts of the roadway and disrupted pedestrians and cyclists. In Boynton Beach, flooding led to road closures, including at Ocean Avenue and Federal Highway. The Ocean Inlet Marina also closed because of high tides. In Boca Raton, water reached a Cub Scout pack’s campsite at Spanish River Park, prompting campers to move supplies to higher ground. Elsewhere, Midtown Beach was temporarily closed because of large surf and high tides. The northbound lane of South Ocean Boulevard between Chilean and Australian avenues was scheduled to close from 10 a.m. to noon while crews moved a lifeguard tower. Delray Beach officials raised red flags because of high surf and flooding, and the Juno Beach Pier remained closed because of damage from a recent offshore surge and high surf. See also: 15-year-old FAMU shooting suspect ordered to be held as prosecutors seek adult charges A coastal flood warning covers low-lying areas near the water in Palm Beach, Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties. The National Weather Service said the warning runs through 8 p.m. Wednesday in coastal Palm Beach County and 2 a.m. Thursday in coastal Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties. The forecast high tides were: Monday: 9:06 p.m. The sheriff’s office advised residents not to drive through floodwater and to call 911 if they need emergency assistance.

entry.title: From Jensen Beach to Louisiana Tech: Andrew Burnette gets one more shot at college football - WFLX
entry.summary: From Jensen Beach to Louisiana Tech: Andrew Burnette gets one more shot at college football    WFLX
entry.article_text: A young man from the Midwest with South Florida roots describes how Andrew Burnette moved from Michigan around the age of 12 and found home on the football field in Martin County. "I played football my whole life, and I can say football is a little harder in Florida than it is in Michigan," said Burnette. WATCH BELOW: Local football standout gets one more shot at college football While football was his first sport, during his high school days at Jensen Beach High School, he fell in love with takedowns and pins. "I wasn't zoned for that school, but I went there for wrestling originally; that was my first passion," said Burnette. While he was doing well in wrestling, football kept calling to him. "Moving through high school, I knew football was what I wanted to do," said Burnette. He established himself as a force at Jensen Beach High School, but he didn't receive much interest from college football programs, similar to many Treasure Coast football recruits. "One of my main struggles was recruitment out of high school, because I felt like our area was a little under-recruited," said Burnette. Betting on himself, he decided to play at Highland Community College in Kansas. Burnette played in nine games and rushed for 340 yards and two touchdowns, but he still wasn't on any other college football program's radar. "I transferred to Independence Junior College, and I was cut from the team," said Burnette. Independence was featured on the hit Netflix show Last Chance U, but once his chance there was short-lived, he reached out to Keiser University in West Palm Beach. "I spoke with the coach there and told him, 'You guys offered me in high school,' and he said, 'I don't really remember. Send me your film.' He saw my film and said, 'Hey, bring it,'" said Burnette. And he did "bring it." In the two years he played at Keiser, he rushed for over 2,300 yards and 30 touchdowns. With stats like that, Division I programs finally came calling, starting with Louisiana Tech. "Last year I played there; it was my first year at the Division I level, and then my eligibility ran out," said Burnette. At the time, the NCAA granted student-athletes only four years of eligibility unless they were injured, so Burnette rolled up his sleeves and got to work. "I called my dad and told him, 'Hey, I need to do something. I can't just sit here,' so I went and worked with my dad in Michigan," said Burnette. He worked with his dad at a steel mill in Detroit for a few months, but this summer the NCAA announced the 5-in-5 rule, meaning student-athletes can compete for up to five seasons across a continuous five-year period. So he hired a lawyer and went to court with the NCAA to get his final year of eligibility, and they granted him one last year, and now he's making the most of it. "It was amazing; I would rather play football than do anything, and for me to have this opportunity again, it's a blessing," said Burnette.

entry.summary: Watches, warnings, and advisories in place across the Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches    WPEC
entry.article_text: A long list of watches, warnings and advisories is in place across the Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches, with coastal flooding, strong winds and dangerous beach and boating conditions among the main concerns. Note: Alert expiration times may differ across the region because Palm Beach County is covered by the Miami forecast office, while Indian River, St. Lucie, Martin and Okeechobee counties are covered by the Melbourne office. Coastal Flood Warning A Coastal Flood Warning is in effect until 8 p.m. Wednesday, October 28th for coastal Palm Beach County. One is in effect until 2 a.m. Thursday, October 29th for coastal Indian River, St. Lucie, and Martin counties. Coastal roads may be closed. Low lying property including homes, businesses and some critical infrastructure will be inundated. Significant shoreline erosion will occur. Wind Advisory A Wind Advisory is in effect from 11 a.m. Monday, October 26th, until 8 p.m. Tuesday, October 27th, for metro and coastal Palm Beach County. One is in effect until 8 p.m. Monday, October 26th, for coastal Indian River, St. Lucie and Martin counties. Northeast winds of 20 to 25 mph are expected, with gusts up to 40 mph in Palm Beach County and up to 35 mph along the Treasure Coast. Gusts could blow around unsecured objects, break tree limbs and cause isolated power outages. High Surf Advisory A High Surf Advisory is in effect until 8 p.m. Wednesday, October 28th, for coastal Palm Beach County. One is in effect until 2 a.m. Thursday, October 29th, for coastal Indian River, St. Lucie and Martin counties. Breaking waves of 8 to 13 feet are possible along the Palm Beaches, with 7 to 11 feet forecast for the Treasure Coast. Dangerous swimming and surfing conditions are expected, along with localized beach erosion. High Rip Current Risk A High Rip Current Risk is in effect through Wednesday evening, October 28th, for coastal Palm Beach County. One is in effect through late Wednesday night for coastal Indian River, St. Lucie and Martin counties. Dangerous rip currents can pull even experienced swimmers away from shore. Entering the water is strongly discouraged. Gale Warning A Gale Warning is in effect until 2 a.m. Wednesday, October 28th, for nearshore waters from Sebastian Inlet to Jupiter Inlet and nearby offshore waters. One is in effect until 8 a.m. Wednesday, October 28th, for nearshore and offshore waters from Jupiter Inlet to Deerfield Beach. Northeast winds of 25 to 30 knots, with gusts up to 35 knots, and hazardous seas are expected. Small vessels could capsize or be damaged. Mariners should avoid these conditions and remain in port or seek safe harbor. Small Craft Advisory A Small Craft Advisory is scheduled from 8 a.m. Wednesday, October 28th, for nearshore and offshore waters from Jupiter Inlet to Deerfield Beach. Another is in effect until 8 p.m. Wednesday, October 28th, for Lake Okeechobee. Hazardous boating conditions are expected. Small craft operators should avoid heading out in these conditions.

entry.summary: Strong winds, king tides flood parts of Martin County as officials warn of more high water    WFLX
entry.article_text: WPTV has been following flooding on the Treasure Coast caused by strong winds and king tides on Monday. In Martin County, off Dyer Point Road in Palm City, parts of the area were completely underwater. WATCH BELOW: Flooding swamps parts of Palm City amid king tides, strong winds Terresa Baldwin, who lives off the roadway, said it was flooded for a few hours, but water has since retreated. "You could smell the sewage; it was really stinky, it was bad," Baldwin said. "There were dead copperheads, so the snakes are coming out. They're getting flushed out with the water." Baldwin said she was also dealing with flooding in her backyard along one of the finger canals. She showed WPTV the water over her dock and in her new patio. "The wind was blowing so hard, so it was like waves crashing in your backyard, and you're like, no, nobody wants to see that," Baldwin said. Despite the water going down, she is still worried about what could happen in the next few days. "The biggest concern for us is getting water from both sides. What do you do, especially when you're trying to sleep, and you don't know if the water's going to come up more or what's going to get damaged at night when you really can't see," Baldwin said. With high tide later Monday night, the sheriff’s office told WPTV the situation could get worse. Dave Rosko said they have three high-water vehicles ready for rescue efforts and urged neighbors to think twice before driving through the water. "Understand the limitations of your vehicle and do not drive through the high waters," Rosko said. "If your vehicle gets disabled there, it may turn into a rescue event where we need to come out and ensure your safety." Rosko said neighbors living in coastal communities should be aware of future tides before traveling.

entry.title: Martin County approves 1-year pause on new data center development
entry.summary: By a 4-0 vote, commissioners in Martin County on Tuesday unanimously passed a one-year moratorium on data centers as county leaders consider how to handle future development of the facilities. This was the second reading after commissioners moved forward with the moratorium during a meeting held Oct. 13. PREVIOUS COVERAGE BELOW: Martin County eyes pause on data center development Tuesday's vote comes after Martin County recently received an application to build its first data center proposed in unincorporated Martin County. That application is for the construction of a hyperscale data center off Kanner Highway west of Interstate 95. However, because the application was submitted before the moratorium, it will not be affected by Tuesday's vote. The proposal comes amid residents' concerns about the future of data center development.

entry.title: Frankel, Adeimy outline affordability priorities in race for Florida's redrawn 23rd congressional district
entry.summary: With just a week left until the General Election, the candidates vying for the newly redrawn 23rd congressional district in Florida sat down with WPTV morning anchor Hollani Davis to talk about their priorities for voters here at home if they're elected. U.S. Rep. Louis Frankel, D-Fla., is fighting to continue representing South Florida. She says affordability is at the top of her list to tackle. WATCH REPORT BELOW: District 23 candidates focus on affordability Candidates vying to represent Florida's 23rd District lay out priorities to tackle affordability 'When I'm at the supermarket, and people can't afford their food, that's a pretty big message,' says Frankel. Frankel, who is seeking an eighth term in Congress, says Democrats must seek to end the war with Iran and rein in the Trump administration's tariffs to help bring costs under control. She also says there is another glaring issue that can't be ignored. '(There's) probably nothing more important for the people of Palm Beach County, where we have a big senior population, is (the need) to protect Social Security and Medicare,' Frankel said. Challenging Frankel in the race is Deborah Adeimy. The Republican, is a native of Palm Beach County who's worked as a financial adviser to companies like Morgan Stanley, JP Morgan Chase. She says she'd use her financial acumen to help solve South Florida's affordable housing problem by rewriting the playbook. 'Currently in Palm Beach County, there are real estate developers who are taking advantage of antiquated tax incentives, tax breaks that are driving up costs here in Palm Beach County (including) rent,' says Adeimy. Florida's 23rd congressional district previously straddled the Palm Beach-Broward County line with a heavy focus on Broward County. After the districts were redrawn this year, it now covers a portion of West Palm Beach and extends south to include Boynton Beach.

entry.title: Boca Raton Fire Rescue expands lifesaving whole blood program through new health network partnership
entry.summary: A new partnership between Boca Raton Fire Rescue and Palm Beach Health Network is strengthening a whole blood program that has already saved lives in the field this summer. Boca Raton's fire rescue crews have had access to whole blood since a new program kicked off this summer; paramedics say the capability is transforming how they treat patients before they reach the hospital. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Boca Raton expands whole blood program According to Red Cross Blood Services, whole blood is blood as it flows in our bodies, with none of its components separated or removed. 'Whole blood has been shown to save lives, and now that we have the capability in our arsenal, it's a world of difference in treating patients and getting the right care,' Kacper Palej, Boca Raton firefighter paramedic, said. Jo Thomas was critically injured in a motorcycle crash this summer. Crews administered whole blood for the first time under the new program. 'I've been told I got flown from the bike into a crosswalk pole about 20 to 30 feet and then hit a crosswalk pole with my body,' Thomas said. 'When somebody's bleeding out on the street, the one thing that will really help out is being able to feed blood back into them to keep them alive, just until they can make it to the hospital to be fully treated.' Months later, Thomas is surrounded by fire rescue again, but for a different reason. Crew members who responded to his crash call received a firefighter challenge coin as a token of appreciation. 'Seeing him walking into the station today and we're gonna go and have something to eat, break bread with him... It's a great day,' Steven Wright, driver engineer, said. A recent partnership with Palm Beach Health Network now means that when blood in fire rescue units is close to expiring, crews return it to Palm Beach Health Network for patient care. In exchange, crews receive fresh blood for future emergency calls.

entry.title: 'A smile that lights up the room': Loved ones remember St. Lucie County firefighter - WPEC
entry.summary: 'A smile that lights up the room': Loved ones remember St. Lucie County firefighter    WPEC
entry.article_text: Family and friends are mourning St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge, a man those closest to him describe as endlessly positive and devoted to serving his community. A funeral procession for Hodge left the Medical Examiner’s Office in Fort Pierce at 2 p.m. Monday and traveled to Stone Brothers Funeral Home. Lucie County Sheriff's Office went to the station at 7:25 a.m. 24, regarding a "full cardiac arrest," and Hoge was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. His death comes about 15 months after his younger brother, Jarius Hodge, also a St. Lucie County Fire District firefighter and paramedic, died in July 2025 after falling ill during a shift. The district honored Jarius with line-of-duty honors. After his brother’s death, Austin spent months searching for answers. He told CBS12 News in January that Jarius caught the flu from a patient and died hours after arriving at Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital in Port St. Lucie, struggling to breathe. Austin said medical records showed doctors made critical mistakes, including needing three attempts to intubate his brother. CBS12 reached out to the hospital at the time and did not receive a response before that story was published. Because Jarius was over 25 and had no spouse or children, Florida’s so-called free kill law barred his family from suing for medical malpractice. Austin pushed state lawmakers to repeal it and started a petition in his brother’s honor. He said the fight was about accountability, not money. Bernard Taylor has known Austin since their school days in Sebastian. Taylor was a senior and Austin a freshman when they met at the Boys and Girls Club, where Taylor worked as a counselor and Austin was one of the kids he mentored. Taylor said Austin always wanted to keep up with the older kids, and the two formed a bond that lasted for years. Later, when Taylor decided to change careers, Austin was one of the first people he called. Taylor said Austin supported him through becoming a firefighter, from answering questions to helping him with his conditioning. Just a ball of positive energy. A smile that lights up the room. No matter what you’re going through, he had the right words to kind of get you through it, Taylor said. Taylor said he spoke with Austin about a week before his death to make sure he was doing well. He said he is most heartbroken for Austin’s mother, who has now lost both of her sons. That’s one of the strongest people I’ve ever met in my life. I don’t know if I can hold it together if I was her, Taylor said. Bonnie Hill, a family friend who helped raise Austin’s mother, said she has been by her side and that the family is leaning on its faith and a strong circle of support. I say on my watch, I’m not going to let you die. You’re going to live, and we’re going to get through this, Hill said of what she has told Austin’s mother. Hill said that faith is what is carrying the family now. See also: King tides cause coastal flooding, beach closures in Palm Beach County and Treasure Coast We believe God even in this. We believe God, and we stand on the promises because they won’t fail, Hill said. Taylor said he hopes people remember Austin for his love of serving others. He was a person who loved what he did. He was a person who loved serving his community, Taylor said. Lucie County Fire District has not released details about Austin Hodge’s death.

entry.article_text: Lucie County Sheriff’s Office deputy was arrested on allegations of driving while impaired. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office announced on Monday, Oct. 26, that Detective Tyler A. Horstman turned himself in to the Indian River County jail on Monday afternoon. Jail records indicate Horstman is facing a charge of DUI causing serious bodily injury to another. "Our responsibility to uphold the law comes with an expectation that we follow it ourselves. When an employee is accused of violating that responsibility, we must address it fairly and hold them accountable through the appropriate process," St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard R. said in a statement on Monday. entry.title: King tides cause coastal flooding, beach closures in Palm Beach County and Treasure Coast - WPEC
entry.summary: King tides cause coastal flooding, beach closures in Palm Beach County and Treasure Coast    WPEC
entry.article_text: King tides flooded streets and reached homes across Palm Beach County on Monday, while beach and road closures were reported as more high tides were expected through Wednesday. In Palm City, flooding made SW Dyer Point Road impassable. Martin County Sheriff’s Office deputies brought in three high-water vehicles to help reach anyone stranded in a vehicle or home. Flooding also was reported on SW 34th Street and Cornell Avenue. One driver told CBS12 the water was about waist-deep in part of the area. Resident Terresa Baldwin said water came up around both the front and back of her home, and that Monday’s flooding was the worst she had seen in eight years. Baldwin also raised concerns about the water’s source and smell. This is not only runoff water, it’s sewage and it’s bad and you can smell it, she said. Deputies urged people to avoid flooded areas and not to drive through standing water. These vehicles can travel through several feet of water safely, Martin County Sheriff’s Office Lt. Flooding also reached Flagler Drive in downtown West Palm Beach and Sunset Avenue on Palm Beach Island, where water covered parts of the roadway and disrupted pedestrians and cyclists. In Boynton Beach, flooding led to road closures, including at Ocean Avenue and Federal Highway. The Ocean Inlet Marina also closed because of high tides. In Boca Raton, water reached a Cub Scout pack’s campsite at Spanish River Park, prompting campers to move supplies to higher ground. Elsewhere, Midtown Beach was temporarily closed because of large surf and high tides. The northbound lane of South Ocean Boulevard between Chilean and Australian avenues was scheduled to close from 10 a.m. to noon while crews moved a lifeguard tower. Delray Beach officials raised red flags because of high surf and flooding, and the Juno Beach Pier remained closed because of damage from a recent offshore surge and high surf. See also: 15-year-old FAMU shooting suspect ordered to be held as prosecutors seek adult charges A coastal flood warning covers low-lying areas near the water in Palm Beach, Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties. The National Weather Service said the warning runs through 8 p.m. Wednesday in coastal Palm Beach County and 2 a.m. Thursday in coastal Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties. The forecast high tides were: Monday: 9:06 p.m. The sheriff’s office advised residents not to drive through floodwater and to call 911 if they need emergency assistance.

entry.title: Strong winds, king tides flood parts of Martin County as officials warn of more high water
entry.summary: WPTV has been following flooding on the Treasure Coast caused by strong winds and king tides on Monday. In Martin County, off Dyer Point Road in Palm City, parts of the area were completely underwater. WATCH BELOW: Flooding swamps parts of Palm City amid king tides, strong winds King tides, strong winds flood areas of Martin County Terresa Baldwin, who lives off the roadway, said it was flooded for a few hours, but water has since retreated. 'You could smell the sewage; it was really stinky, it was bad,' Baldwin said. 'There were dead copperheads, so the snakes are coming out. They're getting flushed out with the water.' Baldwin said she was also dealing with flooding in her backyard along one of the finger canals. She showed WPTV the water over her dock and in her new patio. 'The wind was blowing so hard, so it was like waves crashing in your backyard, and you're like, no, nobody wants to see that,' Baldwin said. Despite the water going down, she is still worried about what could happen in the next few days. 'The biggest concern for us is getting water from both sides. What do you do, especially when you're trying to sleep, and you don't know if the water's going to come up more or what's going to get damaged at night when you really can't see,' Baldwin said.  With high tide later Monday night, the sheriffs office told WPTV the situation could get worse. Lt. Dave Rosko said they have three high-water vehicles ready for rescue efforts and urged neighbors to think twice before driving through the water. 'Understand the limitations of your vehicle and do not drive through the high waters,' Rosko said. 'If your vehicle gets disabled there, it may turn into a rescue event where we need to come out and ensure your safety.' Rosko said neighbors living in coastal communities should be aware of future tides before traveling.

entry.title: Buc-ee's plan for St. Lucie County moves forward, with opening still listed for 2027
entry.summary: Plans to bring a Buc-ee's travel center to the Treasure Coast are continuing to move forward. During questioning from a St. Lucie County commissioner last week, county Planning Director Ben Balser said Buc-ee's has received site plan approval and its building permits are currently under review. Balser said the county is ready to move forward once Buc-ee's addresses the remaining comments from county staff. Plans for the travel center were first announced in 2023. The project calls for a 120-pump location off Indrio Road off Interstate 95 in St. Lucie County. Buc-ee's website continues to list the location as opening in 2027. The Texas-based travel center chain is known for its large stores and expansive fueling areas. The St. Lucie County location would bring the popular chain to the Treasure Coast.

entry.title: From Jensen Beach to Louisiana Tech: Andrew Burnette gets one more shot at college football - WFLX
entry.summary: From Jensen Beach to Louisiana Tech: Andrew Burnette gets one more shot at college football    WFLX
entry.article_text: A young man from the Midwest with South Florida roots describes how Andrew Burnette moved from Michigan around the age of 12 and found home on the football field in Martin County. "I played football my whole life, and I can say football is a little harder in Florida than it is in Michigan," said Burnette. WATCH BELOW: Local football standout gets one more shot at college football While football was his first sport, during his high school days at Jensen Beach High School, he fell in love with takedowns and pins. "I wasn't zoned for that school, but I went there for wrestling originally; that was my first passion," said Burnette. While he was doing well in wrestling, football kept calling to him. "Moving through high school, I knew football was what I wanted to do," said Burnette. He established himself as a force at Jensen Beach High School, but he didn't receive much interest from college football programs, similar to many Treasure Coast football recruits. "One of my main struggles was recruitment out of high school, because I felt like our area was a little under-recruited," said Burnette. Betting on himself, he decided to play at Highland Community College in Kansas. Burnette played in nine games and rushed for 340 yards and two touchdowns, but he still wasn't on any other college football program's radar. "I transferred to Independence Junior College, and I was cut from the team," said Burnette. Independence was featured on the hit Netflix show Last Chance U, but once his chance there was short-lived, he reached out to Keiser University in West Palm Beach. "I spoke with the coach there and told him, 'You guys offered me in high school,' and he said, 'I don't really remember. Send me your film.' He saw my film and said, 'Hey, bring it,'" said Burnette. And he did "bring it." In the two years he played at Keiser, he rushed for over 2,300 yards and 30 touchdowns. With stats like that, Division I programs finally came calling, starting with Louisiana Tech. "Last year I played there; it was my first year at the Division I level, and then my eligibility ran out," said Burnette. At the time, the NCAA granted student-athletes only four years of eligibility unless they were injured, so Burnette rolled up his sleeves and got to work. "I called my dad and told him, 'Hey, I need to do something. I can't just sit here,' so I went and worked with my dad in Michigan," said Burnette. He worked with his dad at a steel mill in Detroit for a few months, but this summer the NCAA announced the 5-in-5 rule, meaning student-athletes can compete for up to five seasons across a continuous five-year period. So he hired a lawyer and went to court with the NCAA to get his final year of eligibility, and they granted him one last year, and now he's making the most of it. "It was amazing; I would rather play football than do anything, and for me to have this opportunity again, it's a blessing," said Burnette.

entry.title: LagoonFest brings free family fun to West Palm Beach waterfront
entry.summary: LagoonFest returns to the downtown West Palm Beach waterfront Saturday with free boat tours, wildlife encounters, children's activities and opportunities to learn about the Lake Worth Lagoon. The free festival runs from 8:30 a.m. to 1:30 p.m. near the West Palm Beach GreenMarket. Benji Studt of Palm Beach County Environmental Resources Management said the event is designed to help residents and visitors connect with the lagoon. 'It's all about connecting people with the lagoon,' Studt said. Shell hunts, wildlife and more at LagoonFest Boat tours offer a closer look at the lagoon Visitors can explore the Lake Worth Lagoon aboard the Hakuna Matata or through Aqua Adventure tours, according to Studt. The boat tours provide a chance to experience the lagoon from the water while learning more about the natural area and the work being done around it. Wildlife encounters and hands-on activities Studt said participating organizations include the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, Busch Wildlife Sanctuary and Manatee Lagoon. The festival will feature touch tanks, wildlife experiences and a live python capture demonstration from FWC. Throughout the morning, families can also meet Laguna, the spotted eagle ray mascot representing Lake Worth Lagoon. Shell hunts and fishing lessons for children Studt said this year's children's zone includes a shell hunt, giveaways and calendars featuring work from local artists. Volunteers from the West Palm Beach Fishing Foundation will teach children how to cast and fish. Participating children will also get to take home a rod and reel, according to Studt. 'The kids can come, and they can do a little shell hunt, look for their shell treasures,' Studt said. Why LagoonFest matters now LagoonFest gives South Florida families a free way to spend time together while learning about a waterway that is part of Palm Beach County's environmental identity. Its location also allows visitors to pair the festival with a stop at the nearby West Palm Beach GreenMarket. Studt said the variety of activities makes the event accessible to visitors with different interests. 'There's something for everybody at LagoonFest,' Studt said. 'It's going to be an awesome time.' LagoonFest takes place Saturday from 8:30 a.m. to 1:30 p.m. along the downtown West Palm Beach waterfront. entry.title: St. Lucie County firefighter paramedic Austin Hodge dies after being found unresponsive on duty - WPTV
entry.summary: St. Lucie County firefighter paramedic Austin Hodge dies after being found unresponsive on duty    WPTV
entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire District firefighter who died unexpectedly Saturday morning has been identified as Austin Hodge, a firefighter paramedic and nine-year veteran of the department.The fire district announced Hodge was found unresponsive in his bunk during a shift change. He was taken to the hospital and passed away.WATCH REPORT BELOW: St. Lucie County firefighter dies on duty"Today, our St. Lucie County Fire District family mourns the loss of one of our own," the district said in a statement. In the hours following his death, firefighters, the department's Honor Guard and fellow first responders gathered to honor Hodge and support one another. The district said the response reflected the strong bond shared throughout the fire service. The district thanked the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Fort Pierce Police Department, Port St. Lucie Police Department and peer support teams from Martin and Indian River counties for providing assistance and standing alongside firefighters during the difficult day."Together, they offered strength, compassion, and support while ensuring Austin was honored with the dignity and respect he deserves," the district said. The district said its thoughts are with Hodge's family, loved ones and everyone who served alongside him. They respectfully ask that Hodge's family be given privacy during this time."We are deeply grateful to our fellow first responders and community for the outpouring of support during this tremendous loss," the district said. "Today and always, we stand together." The tragedy comes more than a year after the community mourned the sudden loss of his brother, Jarius Hodge, 26, who was also a St. Lucie County firefighter and died from septic shock in July 2025.The district said it will share information on funeral and memorial services in coordination with the family when it becomes available.

entry.summary: A group of faith leaders and immigration advocates gathered near U.S. Sen. Ashley Moody's Palm Beach Gardens office to deliver a message, urging her to support Senate Bill 4814, which would extend Temporary Protected Status for Haitians living in the U.S. for three years. Since 2010, that status has allowed Haitian immigrants to legally live and work in the U.S. because of dangerous conditions in their country. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Advocates urge Sen. Moody to back Haitian TPS extension Homeland Security revoked Haitian TPS in July following a Supreme Court decision allowing it to do so. Advocates say more than 150,000 Haitian TPS beneficiaries live in Florida, contributing $2.6 billion to the state's economy, and that they became unable to legally work when Homeland Security revoked their status. Among those affected is Farah Larrieux, who ran her own marketing company and is now unable to work. I introduced you to Larrieux earlier this year , before TPS was revoked. 'Because of TPS, I'm able to rebuild my life,' Larrieux said in February. entry.title: New $17 million Boys & Girls Club opens in West Palm Beach, offering opportunities for hundreds of kids
entry.summary: A new Boys Girls Club officially opened its doors Tuesday in West Palm Beach, bringing a new place for hundreds of children and teens to learn, explore their interests and prepare for their futures. The Julie Mike Connors Boys Girls Club, located at 1150 Southern Blvd., celebrated its grand opening after years of planning. WATCH REPORT BELOW: New Boys Girls Club opens in West Palm Beach 'To have this come to fruition is more beautiful than I ever thought it could be,' Julie Connors said during the celebration. The $17 million, 31,000-square-foot facility is the 21st location for the Boys Girls Clubs of Palm Beach County and is expected to serve approximately 800 children and teens each year, with about 220 attending daily. The club will serve kids ages 6 to 18. For the Connors, however, the bigger story is the need they say exists in the surrounding community. 'People don't realize how big a need there is in West Palm Beach,' Mike Connors said. 'There are a lot of single families that need a lot of help, especially to get kids off the streets.' Inside the new facility are spaces designed for academics, recreation, the arts and career exploration. The club includes a gym and stage, academic center, cultural arts center, computer labs, dance studio, cafeteria, commercial kitchen, sound and recording studio, maker space and outdoor playground. Students will also have access to daily homework help and tutoring programs with certified teachers, along with STEM education, sports, health and fitness programs, cultural arts and leadership programs. For teens, the opportunities extend into career exploration and workforce readiness. They can get hands-on experience in areas such as robotics, health care, content creation, design and culinary arts while being introduced to potential college and career pathways. 'I can be a journalist, a content creator; I can do anything that's possible because we provide essential tools, systems and environment to help them grow,' said Pablo Tejada, Chief Impact Officer for the Boys Girls Club. WPTV reporter Christy Waite spoke with one family who came to the grand opening to tour the new facility. College student Christian Smith said he believes the opportunities being offered could help break cycles of poverty and create new opportunities for young people in the community.
